D1 reports agriculture-sector GVA growth of 4.6 per cent for full-year 2024-25; D2 reports aggregate real GVA growth of 6.2 per cent for H1 FY25. The two differ in both scope (one sector vs all sectors) and coverage (full year vs half year), so they are not competing measurements.

D1's 11.0 per cent industrial GVA growth is explicitly for the preceding year 2023-24, from which growth 'eased' in 2024-25; D2's 6.2 per cent is the FY25 first-advance estimate. Different fiscal years for the same sector, so the gap is the slowdown D1 describes.
D1 gives 11.0 per cent industrial GVA growth for 2023-24; D2 gives 6 per cent for H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024). Same sector, different periods a year apart, so the values are not in conflict.
D1's 11.0 per cent is full-year 2023-24 industrial GVA growth; D2's 8.3 per cent is the single quarter Q1 FY25 (Apr-Jun 2024). Different, non-overlapping periods for the same sector.

D1's 11.0 per cent refers to the industrial sector in 2023-24; D2's 3.8 per cent refers to the agriculture sector in FY25. Different sectors and different years — the pair is a false match on the shared 'GVA growth' label.
D1 measures industrial-sector GVA growth for 2023-24 (11.0 per cent); D2 measures agriculture-sector GVA growth for Q2 FY25 (3.5 per cent). Different sectors entirely, so no comparison holds.

D1's 80 per cent is manufacturing's share of industrial-sector GVA (a composition weight), while D2's 6.2 per cent is the industrial sector's growth rate in FY25. Different attributes — a share versus a growth rate — that only share the word 'industrial'.

D1 reports manufacturing GVA growth of 4.3 per cent in 2024-25, while D2 reports 6.2 per cent for the whole industrial sector in FY25. Manufacturing is a component of industry (about 80 per cent of it per D1), and the two documents also use different national-accounts vintages (D2's Jan-2025 first advance estimates vs D1's post-year-end figures), so scope plus vintage explain the gap.

D1's 4.3 per cent is manufacturing-only GVA growth for 2024-25; D2's 6.4 per cent is total real GVA growth for the same FY25. A sub-sector growing below the aggregate is not a disagreement — the measures differ in scope.

D1 gives manufacturing GVA growth of 4.3 per cent for full-year 2024-25; D2 gives economy-wide real GVA growth of 6.2 per cent for H1 FY25. The figures differ in scope (one sub-sector vs all sectors) and in coverage (full year vs half year).
D1's 4.3 per cent is manufacturing GVA growth; D2's 3.8 per cent is agriculture GVA growth. Same year but different sectors, so the near-similar numbers are coincidental rather than competing.
Manufacturing GVA growth for 2024-25 (D1, 4.3 per cent) and agriculture GVA growth for Q2 FY25 (D2, 3.5 per cent) measure different sectors over different windows; they are not the same quantity.

D1's 12.3 per cent is the manufacturing 'high base' for 2023-24; D2's 6.2 per cent is industrial-sector growth for FY25. The periods differ by a year (and the scope by manufacturing vs all industry), so the drop is the base effect D1 explicitly cites.

D1 reports 12.3 per cent manufacturing GVA growth in 2023-24 as a prior-year base; D2 reports 6.4 per cent total real GVA growth for FY25. Different years and different scope (one sub-sector vs the aggregate), so no conflict arises.
D1's 12.3 per cent covers manufacturing in 2023-24; D2's 6.2 per cent covers aggregate real GVA in H1 FY25. Non-overlapping periods and differing scope explain the gap entirely.

D1's 12.3 per cent is manufacturing GVA growth for 2023-24; D2's 3.8 per cent is agriculture GVA growth for FY25. Different sector and different year — a false match on the generic 'GVA growth' attribute.
Manufacturing GVA growth in 2023-24 (12.3 per cent) and agriculture GVA growth in Q2 FY25 (3.5 per cent) refer to different sectors in different periods, so they make no comparable claim.

D1's 3.6 per cent is Index of Industrial Production growth for Q4 2024-25 (Jan-Mar 2025), a volume index; D2's 6 per cent is industrial-sector real GVA growth for H1 FY25. Different statistical measures (IIP vs national-accounts GVA) over different periods.

IIP growth of 3.6 per cent in Q4 2024-25 (D1) and industrial GVA growth of 8.3 per cent in Q1 FY25 (D2) are distinct indicators covering distinct quarters, so they are not two readings of the same quantity.

D1's 4.4 per cent is Eight Core Industries output growth for Q4 2024-25, a narrow eight-commodity infrastructure index; D2's 6 per cent is industrial-sector GVA growth for H1 FY25. Different indicator and different period.
Eight Core Industries growth of 4.4 per cent in Q4 2024-25 (D1) is not the same attribute as industrial-sector GVA growth of 8.3 per cent in Q1 FY25 (D2); the indicators and the quarters both differ.

D1 reports headline food inflation averaging 6.7 per cent over the full fiscal year 2024-25 (Apr 2024-Mar 2025). D2's 4.3 per cent is an explicitly narrower basket — food inflation excluding vegetables and pulses — over the shorter Apr-Dec FY25 window, and D2 itself says this is 4.1 pp below overall food inflation (implying ~8.4 per cent headline food inflation over Apr-Dec). Both the excluded items and the shorter, higher-inflation nine-month window explain the gap.

D1's 6.7 per cent is full-year 2024-25 headline food inflation; D2's 6.5 per cent excludes tomato, onion and potato and covers only Apr-Dec 2024. D2 states this is 1.9 pp lower than current food inflation, implying ~8.4 per cent headline food inflation over Apr-Dec — so the near-identical 6.7 vs 6.5 figures are not the same measure despite looking alike. Different basket definition plus different window.

D1 gives a food inflation rate (6.7 per cent); D2's 32.3 per cent is a contribution share of vegetables and pulses to headline inflation, not an inflation rate. Different attribute and different unit of meaning.

D1's 2.9 per cent is a single-month reading (March 2025) for headline food inflation, cited as the end-point of a sharp decline; D2's 4.3 per cent is a nine-month average (Apr-Dec 2024) for food inflation excluding vegetables and pulses. A point-in-time March 2025 value legitimately sits below an Apr-Dec average, and the baskets also differ.

D1's 2.9 per cent is March 2025 alone, after what it calls a dramatic decline; D2's 6.5 per cent is the Apr-Dec 2024 average excluding tomato, onion and potato. D2 (published 31 Jan 2025) predates the March 2025 disinflation, and a monthly print versus a nine-month average of a different basket are not the same measure.
D1's 2.9 per cent is food inflation in March 2025; D2's 5.4 per cent is headline CPI retail inflation for FY24. Different index and different period entirely.
D1 reports food inflation of 2.9 per cent for March 2025; D2 reports headline CPI retail inflation of 4.9 per cent for Apr-Dec FY25. Different attribute (food sub-index vs headline CPI).

D1's figure is an inflation rate (2.9 per cent, March 2025); D2's 32.3 per cent is the share of headline inflation contributed by vegetables and pulses. Different attribute type, not comparable values.

D1's 3.2 per cent of GDP is the consolidated states' gross fiscal deficit (budget estimate, 2024-25); D2's 1.3 per cent of GDP is the external current account deficit in Q2 FY24. Both are 'deficit as % of GDP' but of entirely different accounts (fiscal vs balance of payments).

D1 states a fiscal deficit for state governments (3.2 per cent of GDP, 2024-25 BE); D2 states India's current account deficit (1.2 per cent of GDP, Q2 FY25). Different attribute and different entity/account — a false match on the '% of GDP deficit' phrasing.

D1's 4.7 per cent of GDP is the central government's gross fiscal deficit for 2024-25 (RE); D2's 1.2 per cent of GDP is the external current account deficit for Q2 FY25. Fiscal account versus balance-of-payments account — different attributes.

D1 reports the Centre's gross fiscal deficit (4.7 per cent of GDP, 2024-25 RE); D2 reports the current account deficit (1.3 per cent of GDP, Q2 FY24). Different measures and different periods; the similarity is only the '% of GDP' denominator.

D1's 5.5 per cent of GDP is the central government gross fiscal deficit in 2023-24; D2's 1.2 per cent of GDP is the current account deficit in Q2 FY25. Different attribute (fiscal vs external) and different period.
D1's 5.5 per cent of GDP is a fiscal deficit for FY2023-24; D2's 1.3 per cent of GDP is the balance-of-payments current account deficit for Q2 FY24. Same denominator, unrelated numerators.

D1 reports 5.2 per cent growth in the Centre's effective capital expenditure for the whole of 2024-25 (RE), while D2 reports 8.2 per cent growth in Union capex over just July-November 2024 with the expectation it would 'pick up further pace'. A five-month within-year run-rate need not equal the full-year RE growth, and 'effective capex' (capex plus grants-in-aid for capital asset creation) is a broader definition than plain capex.

D1's 19.8 per cent is effective capital expenditure growth in 2023-24; D2's 8.2 per cent is Union capex growth over July-November 2024 (FY25). These are different fiscal years — and different definitions (effective capex vs capex) — so the divergence is expected rather than conflicting.

D1's 5.8 per cent is revenue expenditure growth of the central government in 2024-25 (RE); D2's 12 per cent is the aggregate states' revenue expenditure growth over Apr-Nov 2024. Different tiers of government (Centre vs states), so the figures describe different entities, not a disagreement.
D1 reports revenue expenditure growth (5.8 per cent, 2024-25 RE); D2 reports capital expenditure growth (8.2 per cent, July-November 2024). Revenue and capital expenditure are distinct budget heads.

D1's 0.1 per cent is merchandise exports alone for FY2024-25; D2's 6 per cent (USD 602.6 billion) is total exports including services for Apr-Dec 2024. Services exports grew far faster than goods, so a combined aggregate legitimately grows much faster; the periods also differ (full year vs nine months).
D1's 0.1 per cent is export growth; D2's 5.2 per cent is import growth. Opposite sides of the trade account — different attributes.
D1 reports merchandise exports growing 0.1 per cent; D2 reports merchandise imports rising 5.2 per cent. Different flow direction, so not comparable figures.

D1's 6.2 per cent is merchandise (goods) import growth in value terms for FY2024-25; D2's 0.7 per cent is national-accounts imports of goods and non-factor services at constant prices for H1 FY25. Different basket (goods vs goods plus services), different valuation (nominal customs data vs constant-price national accounts) and a shorter half-year window all separate the two.
D1's 6.2 per cent is merchandise import growth; D2's 1.6 per cent is merchandise export growth. Opposite trade flows, so the pair is a false match on 'merchandise trade growth'.
D1 states imports grew 6.2 per cent in 2024-25; D2 states exports grew 1.6 per cent in Apr-Dec 2024. Different attribute (imports vs exports).

D1's -4.4% is merchandise EXPORTS growth in Q4 2024-25; D2's 5.2% is merchandise IMPORTS growth in April-December 2024. Different attribute and different period — the pair is a false match on the shared 'merchandise trade' scope label.
Exports versus imports: D1 states merchandise exports fell 4.4% in Q4 2024-25, D2 states merchandise imports rose 5.2% in April-December FY25. Neither the measured flow nor the period matches.

D2's 6% growth is TOTAL exports including services (USD 602.6 billion, merchandise plus services) over April-December FY25; D1's -4.4% is merchandise exports alone for Q4 2024-25. Different aggregate and different window, so the figures are not measuring the same quantity.
D1's 1.2% is merchandise imports (Q4 2024-25); D2's 1.6% is merchandise exports (April-December 2024). The near-identical numbers are coincidental — different trade flow and different period.
Imports versus exports: D1 reports merchandise imports growing 1.2% in Q4 2024-25, D2 reports merchandise exports growing 1.6% YoY in April-December 2024. Different attribute and different period.

D1's 1.2% is nominal merchandise import value growth for Q4 2024-25; D2's 0.7% is growth of imports of goods and non-factor services at constant prices (national-accounts basis) in H1 FY25. Different coverage (goods only vs goods plus services), different basis (nominal customs data vs real national accounts) and different period, so the two numbers are not measuring the same series.

D1's 3.3% is a single month (March 2025) headline CPI print; D2's 4.9% is the average over April-December 2024. A single terminal-month reading below the earlier nine-month average is exactly the 'sharp moderation in food inflation' D1 describes, and March 2025 lies outside D2's window entirely.

D1 reports 3.3% CPI for March 2025; D2 reports 5.4% as the FY24 (April 2023-March 2024) full-year average. Different periods a year apart, and both documents describe the same downward path (D2: softening from 5.4% in FY24; D1: easing to 3.3% by March 2025).

D1 gives a full-year 2024-25 average of 4.6%; D2 gives 4.9% for April-December 2024, the first nine months of that same year. The full-year figure is lower because Q4 prints were soft (D1 puts March 2025 at 3.3%): roughly (0.75 x 4.9) + (0.25 x ~3.7) ≈ 4.6, so the two are consistent rather than conflicting.
D1's 4.6% is the average for 2024-25; D2's 5.4% is the average for FY24 (2023-24). Consecutive but distinct fiscal years — both documents record moderation from the 5.4% base.

Both report headline CPI-Combined inflation of 5.4% for the same period: D1 'from 5.4 per cent during 2023-24' and D2 '5.4 per cent in FY24', where FY24 = 1 Apr 2023-31 Mar 2024. Identical value, period and scope from two independent official sources.

D1's 5.4% is the 2023-24 average; D2's 4.9% is April-December 2024 (within FY25). Different years — indeed D2's own sentence pairs exactly these two numbers as a decline from FY24 to April-December 2024, so the gap is the intended year-on-year moderation.

D1 cites the CPI-Combined weight of the 'Food and Beverages' group at 45.9%, which includes non-alcoholic beverages and prepared meals/snacks; D2's 'about two-fifths' (~40%) matches the narrower 'Food' sub-basket (roughly 39%) once those items are excluded. The gap is a group-definition difference in the same 2012-base CPI basket, not a disagreement about weights. To confirm, one would check the official CPI weighting diagram for the Food versus Food-and-Beverages split.

D1's 0.9 is a standard deviation (dispersion of monthly headline inflation across 2024-25, in percentage points); D2's 4.9% is the level of average inflation over April-December 2024. Different statistics measured on the same series — a dispersion figure cannot corroborate or contradict a mean.

A standard deviation of 0.9 pp for 2024-25 monthly inflation (D1) and an FY24 average inflation level of 5.4% (D2) are different attributes over different periods; the pair is a false match on the shared CPI subject.

D1's 4.8 is the MEDIAN of monthly headline inflation over the full year 2024-25; D2's 4.9% is the MEAN over April-December 2024. Different central-tendency statistics over different windows, yet mutually consistent (4.8 vs 4.9), so the small gap reflects median-vs-average and the inclusion of the softer Q4 rather than a conflict.

D1's median monthly inflation of 4.8 is for 2024-25; D2's 5.4% average is for FY24. Both the year and the statistic differ (median vs mean), and the lower 2024-25 median is consistent with the moderation D2 itself describes from the FY24 base.

D1's 6.2 is the maximum single-month headline inflation print during 2024-25 (the October 2024 peak); D2's 4.9% is the average over April-December 2024. A period maximum and a period mean are different attributes, so no corroboration or contradiction is implied — a maximum above the mean is expected.
D1 reports the highest monthly reading of 2024-25 (6.2%); D2 reports the FY24 full-year average (5.4%). Different statistic and different year — the numbers are not comparable measures.

D1's 3.3 is the minimum monthly headline print in 2024-25 (equal to its March 2025 reading); D2's 5.4% is the FY24 average. An extremum of one year against the mean of another is a different attribute over a different period.

D1's 3.3 is the lowest monthly CPI inflation of 2024-25 — a figure that occurs in March 2025, outside D2's April-December 2024 window — whereas D2's 4.9% is the mean over that window. Minimum versus average are different statistics, so the pair is a false match.

D1's 4.8% covers just April-May 2024, a two-month sub-window inside D2's April-December 2024 average of 4.9%. A sub-period value close to but not identical with the nine-month mean is expected, particularly given D1's note that inflation dipped to 3.6% in July 2024 before rising later.

D1's 4.8% is for April-May 2024 (start of FY25); D2's 5.4% is the FY24 (2023-24) full-year average. Different, non-overlapping periods — the lower early-FY25 reading is part of the same moderation from the FY24 base that D2 documents.

Both give industrial-sector growth for the full FY2024-25: D2 says 6.2% on first advance estimates (Jan 2025), D1 says growth 'moderated to 4.3 per cent in 2024-25' citing deceleration in manufacturing GVA. The RBI report post-dates the Survey and uses later NSO estimates, so the 1.9pp gap is a downward revision of the same series. To confirm, one would check the NSO Provisional Estimates (May 2025) industrial GVA figure against both.

D2's 6% is explicitly 'in H1 FY25' (Apr-Sep 2024); D1's 4.3% is the full 2024-25 year. D2 itself notes growth 'moderated in Q2', so a full-year figure below the H1 figure is coherent; the periods differ.

D2's 8.3% is a single quarter (Q1 FY25, Apr-Jun 2024) described as 'strong growth' that then 'moderated in Q2'; D1's 4.3% averages the whole of 2024-25. A quarter cannot be compared directly with the annual average.
D1's 4.3% is industrial-sector GVA growth; D2's 6.4% is economy-wide real GDP growth. Same period but different aggregates — one is a sector component, the other the headline total.

D1's 64.1% is the services sector's share of GVA (a composition ratio); D2's 7.2% is the services sector's GVA growth rate. Same sector and period, but different attributes, so the values are not comparable.

Both state services-sector growth for FY2024-25: D2 expects 7.2% on first advance estimates (Jan 2025), D1 reports 7.5% for 2024-25 using later estimates. The 0.3pp difference is within a normal FAE-to-SAE/PE revision, and D2's wording ('expected to remain robust') marks it as a forecast rather than an outturn.

D2's 7.1% is explicitly H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024) growth resulting from Q1 and Q2; D1's 7.5% covers the full year 2024-25. The higher annual number implies stronger H2 services activity, so the windows, not the data, differ.

D1's 7.5% is domestic services-sector GVA growth for 2024-25; D2's 11.6% is growth in services exports over the first nine months of FY25. Different attribute (output versus exports) and different window.

D1's 7.5% measures services-sector GVA growth; D2's 0.7% measures growth in imports of goods and services at constant prices in H1 FY25. Different attributes entirely — a supply-side sector aggregate versus an expenditure-side import flow.
D1's 7.5% is services GVA growth for 2024-25; D2's -2.9% is the Q2 FY25 contraction in imports of goods and services attributed to falling commodity prices. Different attribute and different period.

D2's 4.9% covers April-December 2024 only (nine months of FY25, provisional); D1's 4.6% is the average across the full 2024-25 year. Adding the Jan-Mar 2025 quarter, when CPI inflation fell sharply, pulls the twelve-month average below the nine-month figure, so the two are consistent.

Same reconciliation as D2 page 28: D2's 4.9% is labelled 'FY25 (April-December)', a nine-month average, whereas D1's 4.6% is the full 2024-25 average. The gap is the excluded Q4 FY25 months, not a disagreement over the same window.

D2's 5.4% is FY24 (Apr 2023-Mar 2024); D1's 4.6% is 2024-25. D1 explicitly frames its figure as moderating 'from 5.4 per cent in the previous year', so the two documents agree on the trajectory and simply report different years.
D2 page 76 gives 5.4% for FY24; D1 gives 4.6% for 2024-25. Different fiscal years, and D1's own prior-year reference of 5.4% matches D2's FY24 value exactly.

D1 states headline CPI averaged 5.4 per cent in 2023-24 (the previous year); D2 states retail headline CPI inflation was 5.4 per cent in FY24 (1 Apr 2023-31 Mar 2024). Identical measure, identical period, identical value.
D2 page 76 repeats that 'retail inflation moderated from 5.4 per cent in FY24', matching D1's 5.4 per cent average for 2023-24. Same CPI headline series, same fiscal year, same figure.

D1's 5.4% is the 2023-24 average; D2's 4.9% is the April-December 2024 (FY25) average. These are consecutive but different periods — D2's own sentence contrasts the two ('softened from 5.4 per cent in FY24 to 4.9 per cent').

D1's 5.4% covers 2023-24; D2's 4.9% is labelled 'FY25 (April-December)'. Different years and a partial-year window for the latter, so the decline is a genuine time trend rather than conflicting measurements.

D1 gives a level — core CPI (ex food and fuel) averaging 3.5 per cent in 2024-25 — while D2 gives a change, a 0.9pp reduction in core inflation between FY24 and April-December 2024. They are arithmetically compatible: FY24 core of roughly 4.3-4.4 per cent less 0.9pp lands near 3.4-3.5 per cent, matching D1's level. Different attribute (level versus delta) and different end-window.

D1's 3.5% is core CPI, defined as headline excluding food and fuel, for 2024-25. D2's 3.2% is headline CPI excluding only vegetables and pulses for April-December 2024 — a different exclusion basket (it retains fuel and most food) and a different window. The near-identical magnitudes are coincidental.

D1's 3.5% is core CPI excluding food and fuel; D2's 4.3% is food inflation (CFPI) excluding vegetables and pulses. Core inflation excludes food by construction, so the two measure disjoint parts of the index.

D1's 3.5% is core CPI excluding food and fuel for 2024-25; D2's 6.5% is food inflation excluding tomato, onion and potato for April-December 2024. Different index components (core excludes food entirely) and different windows.

Both quote 3.3 per cent global growth, but for different years: D1 says "the growth of 3.3 per cent in 2024" while D2 says "The global economy grew by 3.3 per cent in 2023." Identical values for different reference years, so this is not the same measurement being confirmed. Note D1 elsewhere puts 2023 at 3.5 per cent (IMF WEO April 2025), so the 2023 figure itself differs by vintage.
D1: "Global inflation eased to 5.7 per cent in 2024"; D2: "to 5.7 per cent in 2024" for global headline inflation. Same subject, same attribute, same calendar year 2024, identical value.

D1's 5.7 per cent is global inflation in 2024; D2's 3.3 per cent is global GDP growth in 2023. Different attributes (price inflation vs output growth) and different years — a false match on the shared 'World' subject.

Same measure (global headline inflation) at different points of the disinflation path: D2 records the peak of "8.7 per cent in 2022" while D1 records the easing "to 5.7 per cent in 2024". The gap is entirely the two-year interval, and both documents describe inflation as falling.

D1's 6.6 per cent is global inflation in 2023; D2's 5.7 per cent is global headline inflation in 2024. D1's own sentence ("eased to 5.7 per cent in 2024 from 6.6 per cent in 2023") shows the two values are consecutive years of the same series, consistent with D2.
D1's 6.6 per cent for 2023 is inflation; D2's 3.3 per cent for 2023 is GDP growth. Same year and same subject (World) but different attributes, so the apparent pairing is spurious.

Both are global headline inflation, one year apart: D2 gives the 2022 peak of 8.7 per cent, D1 gives 6.6 per cent for 2023. The decline from 8.7 to 6.6 is the same disinflation narrative, not a disagreement about one period.

Both refer to 2024 global goods/merchandise trade growth. D2 (published 31 Jan 2025) states it "is projected to grow by about 2 per cent in 2024", an ex-ante nowcast; D1 cites the WTO Global Trade Outlook of April 2025 reporting the outturn, "expanded by 2.9 per cent in 2024". The 2.9 vs ~2 gap is a projection later superseded by the realised WTO figure.

D1's -1.0 per cent is merchandise trade volume in 2023 ("after contracting by 1.0 per cent in 2023"); D2's ~2 per cent is the projection for 2024. Different reference years of the same series — D1 explicitly frames 2024 as a rebound from the 2023 contraction.

D1's 3.7 per cent is a twenty-year average ("the historical average (2000-19)"), whereas D2's 3.3 per cent is the single year 2023. A benchmark average and one year's outturn are not competing values; D1 itself uses the 3.7 per cent average to say recent growth is below trend.

D1 reports "global growth at 3.3 per cent in 2024" (IMF WEO April 2025); D2 reports "3.3 per cent in 2023". Same value but different calendar years, so they are not measuring the same period — D1 puts 2023 at 3.5 per cent in the same sentence.

Both give IMF global growth for 2024: D2 (Jan 2025) cites the IMF's projection of 3.2 per cent, while D1 cites IMF WEO April 2025 with the outturn at 3.3 per cent. The 0.1 pp gap is an ex-ante projection later replaced by the estimated actual.

D1's 3.3 per cent is the 2024 outturn; D2's 3.3 per cent is the IMF projection for 2025. Identical numbers but different reference years, so this is coincidence of value rather than confirmation of the same measurement.

D1 states 3.3 per cent for 2024 (IMF WEO April 2025); D3 quotes the IMF July 2024 WEO update that "global economic growth for 2025 will likely hold steady at 3.3%". Different reference years (2024 actual vs 2025 projection), so no conflict.

Both state global growth for calendar 2023: D2 (Jan 2025) says 3.3 per cent, D1 says 3.5 per cent citing IMF WEO April 2025 ("3.5 per cent a year ago"). Same period and scope with a 0.2 pp gap explained by successive IMF WEO revisions of 2023 world growth; to confirm one would check the 2023 figure printed in the Oct 2024 vs April 2025 WEO.
D1's 3.5 per cent refers to 2023 ("a year ago" relative to 2024); D2's 3.2 per cent is the IMF projection for 2024. Different reference years of the same global growth series.
D1's 3.5 per cent is the 2023 outturn; D2's 3.3 per cent is the IMF's projection for 2025. Two years apart, one historical and one forecast, so the difference is not a disagreement.
D1 gives 3.5 per cent for 2023; D3 quotes the IMF's July 2024 projection of 3.3 per cent for 2025. Different periods (realised 2023 vs projected 2025) and different vintages of IMF data.

Both cover agriculture GVA growth in FY2024-25: D2 (tabled 31 Jan 2025) uses the First Advance Estimates, "expected to rebound to a growth of 3.8 per cent in FY25"; D1, reporting after year-end, states "4.6 per cent" for 2024-25. The 3.8 vs 4.6 gap reflects the advance estimate being revised up in the later provisional estimates, not a dispute over the same vintage.

D1's 4.6 per cent is full-year 2024-25 agriculture and allied GVA growth; D2's 3.5 per cent is Q2 FY25 (Jul-Sep 2024) only. A single quarter within the year can differ from the annual average, and D2 notes Q2 was itself "an improvement over the previous four quarters".

D1's 4.6 per cent is the agriculture and allied sector alone for full-year 2024-25; D2's 6.2 per cent is economy-wide real GVA for H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024). Sector versus total, and half-year versus full year — different measures, not conflicting ones.

Same period (FY2024-25) but different aggregates: D1 reports agriculture and allied GVA growth of 4.6 per cent, D2 reports total economy real GVA growth of 6.4 per cent. A sectoral component naturally differs from the all-sector total.

D1's 4.6 per cent is agriculture and allied GVA for FY25; D2's 6.2 per cent is the industrial sector for FY25. Different sectors of the economy, so the two numbers describe different entities and are not comparable.

D1's 2.7 per cent is agriculture GVA growth in 2023-24 ("a year ago" relative to 2024-25); D2's 3.8 per cent is the FY25 first advance estimate. Consecutive fiscal years, and D2's word "rebound" is consistent with the weaker prior-year base.
D1's 2.7 per cent covers full-year FY2023-24 agriculture GVA; D2's 3.5 per cent is Q2 of FY25 (Jul-Sep 2024). Different fiscal years and different frequency (annual vs quarterly).

D1's 2.7 per cent is the agriculture and allied sector in FY2023-24; D2's 6.2 per cent is total real GVA in H1 FY25. Both scope (one sector vs whole economy) and period (FY24 vs first half of FY25) differ.

D1 gives agriculture-and-allied GVA growth of 2.7 per cent for FY2023-24; D2 gives all-economy real GVA growth of 6.4 per cent estimated for FY25. Different aggregate (segment vs total) and different fiscal year.
D1's 2.7 per cent refers to the agriculture and allied sector in FY24; D2's 6.2 per cent refers to the industrial sector in FY25. Different sectors and different years — no shared measurement.

Both measure real (constant-price) exports of goods and services for India in FY25 on the national-accounts basis, but over different windows: D1's 7.1% is the full year 2024-25 (Apr 2024-Mar 2025), while D2's 5.6% covers only H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024). A stronger second half lifting the annual figure above the half-year rate is arithmetically consistent, so the gap is a period difference, not a disagreement.

D1 reports 7.1% real constant-price export growth for the full year 2024-25; D2 reports 6% growth in the nominal US$ value of combined merchandise and services exports (USD 602.6 billion) over the first nine months of FY25 only. The two differ in both window (9 months vs 12) and measurement (nominal dollar value vs constant-price volume), so the values are not expected to match.

D1's 7.1% is real growth of total exports (goods plus services) for the full year 2024-25; D2's 1.6% is nominal merchandise-only export growth for April-December 2024. Services exports, which grew much faster than goods in FY25, are excluded from D2's figure, and the window is nine months, so the narrower scope explains the lower number.

Same scope difference as the other merchandise series: D2 states merchandise exports grew 1.6% YoY in April-December 2024, excluding services, while D1's 7.1% is constant-price growth of total exports for the whole of 2024-25. Excluding fast-growing services exports and truncating to nine months accounts for the gap.

D1's 7.1% is aggregate real export growth for the economy in 2024-25; D2's 9.9% refers specifically to engineering goods exports in April-December 2024. Different attribute (one sub-sector vs all exports), so the two numbers are not comparable claims.

Both are constant-price import growth on the national-accounts basis. D2's +0.7% covers H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024); D1's -1.1% is the full year 2024-25. A flat first half followed by contraction in the second half yields a mildly negative annual figure, so the difference is one of window, not of fact.

D2's -2.9% is a single quarter (Q2 FY25, Jul-Sep 2024) of constant-price imports, attributed to falling commodity prices; D1's -1.1% is the full year 2024-25 on the same real basis. A quarterly contraction being deeper than the annual average is consistent; the periods simply differ.

D1's -1.1% is real (constant-price) import growth for full-year 2024-25; D2's +6.9% is growth in the nominal US$ value of total imports (USD 682.2 billion) over the first nine months of FY25. Nominal dollar value growth and constant-price volume growth are different measures over different windows, so the opposite signs do not conflict.

D2's 5.2% is nominal merchandise-only import growth for April-December 2024; D1's -1.1% is real growth of total imports (goods and services) for the full year 2024-25. Different scope (goods only vs goods and services), different valuation (nominal vs constant prices) and a nine-month window explain the divergence.

The same merchandise series as stated elsewhere in D2: imports grew 5.2% during April-December 2024 in nominal merchandise trade terms, whereas D1's -1.1% is constant-price total imports for the whole of 2024-25. Narrower scope and nominal valuation account for the sign difference.

D1 reports Q1:2024-25 real GDP growth of 6.5% y-o-y; D2 reports 6.0% for H1 FY25, i.e. Q1 and Q2 combined. Averaging D1's own Q1 (6.5%) and Q2 (5.6%) figures gives roughly 6.0%, so D2's half-year number is the aggregate of the quarters rather than a competing estimate.

D1's 6.5% is a single quarter (Q1:2024-25, Apr-Jun 2024) actual; D2's 6.4% is the First Advance Estimate for the entire FY25 (Apr 2024-Mar 2025) published 31 Jan 2025. A quarterly outturn and a full-year estimate are different quantities, and the two are in any case close.

Same relationship as the other FY25 estimate in D2: 6.4% is the constant-price First Advance Estimate for the full year FY25, while D1's 6.5% is the Q1:2024-25 y-o-y outturn. Quarter versus full year, so no conflict.

D1's 6.2% refers to Q3:2024-25 (Oct-Dec 2024); D2's 6.0% is H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024). The windows do not overlap at all, so the higher third-quarter figure simply reflects the recovery after the softer first half.

D2's 6.4% is the FY25 First Advance Estimate covering Apr 2024-Mar 2025; D1's 6.2% is the Q3 (Oct-Dec 2024) y-o-y outturn reported later in the RBI's annual report. A quarter within the year need not equal the annual estimate, and the values are within 0.2 pp.

Same as the other FY25 advance-estimate statement: 6.4% is a full-year constant-price estimate, 6.2% is D1's Q3:2024-25 quarterly growth. Different periods, so the two are complementary rather than conflicting.

D1 reports Q2:2024-25 growth softening to 5.6% on excess rainfall; D2's 6.0% covers H1 FY25, which includes both the stronger Q1 (6.5% per D1) and this weaker Q2. The half-year average lying between the two quarters is exactly what one expects.

D2's 6.4% is a full-year FY25 First Advance Estimate; D1's 5.6% is the Q2:2024-25 quarterly outturn, explicitly described as a softening driven by excess rainfall. Quarter versus full year, so the gap is a period difference.

5.6% is one quarter (Jul-Sep 2024) of D1's quarterly series; 6.4% is D2's constant-price advance estimate for the whole of FY25. Different periods, and D1's own quarters (6.5, 5.6, 6.2) bracket the annual figure.

Both state constant-price PFCE growth for the same year (FY25 / 2024-25) with the same rural-demand explanation, but D2's 7.3% is the First Advance Estimate published 31 Jan 2025, while D1's 7.6% comes from the RBI's annual report using later provisional estimates for the completed year. A 0.3 pp upward revision between advance and later estimates is a data-vintage difference, not a disagreement.

D2's 6.7% YoY PFCE growth covers H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024); D1's 7.6% is the full year 2024-25. Consumption strengthening in the second half lifts the annual rate above the first-half rate, so the two are consistent readings of different windows.

D3 reports PFCE growth of 4.0% in FY24 (Apr 2023-Mar 2024), citing RBI data; D1 reports 7.6% for 2024-25. These are consecutive, non-overlapping fiscal years, and D1 describes 2024-25 as an improvement, which matches a rise from the weak FY24 base.
D3's 6.8% is PFCE growth in FY23 (Apr 2022-Mar 2023); D1's 7.6% is for 2024-25. Two years apart, so the difference is purely one of period.

D3's 6.8% is FY23 PFCE growth; D2's 6.7% is H1 FY25 YoY growth. The near-identical values cover completely different periods two years apart, so they are not the same measurement despite the coincidence.

Both give the PFCE share of GDP for the same year (2024-25 / FY25), but on different valuation bases: D1's 56.7% is the share of real (constant-price) GDP, while D2's 61.8% is explicitly 'at current prices'. Current- and constant-price shares routinely differ by several percentage points, so the gap is definitional.

D2's 60.3% is the current-price PFCE share of GDP in FY24, whereas D1's 56.7% is the constant-price share in 2024-25. Both the valuation basis (current vs real) and the year differ, either of which alone would prevent a direct comparison.

D1's 3.8% is government final consumption expenditure (GFCE) growth in 2024-25; D2's 7.3% is private final consumption expenditure (PFCE). These are separate components of aggregate demand, so the figures measure different attributes.

D1 reports GFCE (government consumption) growing 3.8% in 2024-25; D2 reports PFCE (private consumption) growing 6.7% in H1 FY25. Different expenditure aggregates, so they are not competing values for the same quantity.

D1's 8.1% is government final consumption expenditure growth in 2023-24, quoted as the prior-year comparator; D2's 7.3% is private final consumption expenditure for FY25. Both the component (government vs private) and the year differ, so the pair is a false match.
D1's 8.1% refers to GFCE in 2023-24; D2's 6.7% refers to PFCE in H1 FY25. Different demand component and different period — not the same measurement.

Both describe the same series (all-India CPI-Combined headline inflation) but over different windows: D1 gives a single month, 3.6% in July 2024, while D2 gives the 4.9% average over April–December 2024. A single trough month sitting below a nine-month average is arithmetically consistent, and D1's own sentence shows the path (4.8% in April-May, 3.6% in July, 6.2% in October) that averages out near 4.9%. No disagreement once the period difference is applied.

Same CPI headline series, different periods: D1's 3.6% is a July 2024 monthly print, D2's 5.4% is the full FY24 (April 2023–March 2024) average. A month inside FY25 and an annual average for the preceding fiscal year cannot be compared directly, and D2 itself frames 5.4% as the FY24 base from which inflation 'softened'.

D1's 6.2% is a single month (October 2024), the peak of the FY25 food-driven spike; D2's 4.9% is the April–December 2024 average of the same CPI headline series. A peak month above the period mean is consistent, not contradictory — D1's quote explicitly frames 6.2% as a rise from the 3.6% July low within the same window D2 averages.

D1's 6.2% covers October 2024 (inside FY25) whereas D2's 5.4% is the FY24 (April 2023–March 2024) annual average of the same CPI headline measure. The values differ because one is a monthly observation in the following fiscal year and the other a prior-year annual average; there is no same-period disagreement.

D1's 68% is the contribution of the entire food and beverages group to headline inflation in 2024-25; D2's 32.3% is the contribution of just two sub-items, vegetables and pulses, in April–December FY25. The narrower basket necessarily contributes less than the full food group (32.3% is roughly half of 68%), and the windows also differ (full fiscal year vs April–December), so the two figures are compatible rather than conflicting.

D1's 61% is the whole food and beverages group's contribution to headline inflation in 2023-24; D2's 32.3% is vegetables and pulses alone in April–December FY25. Both scope (full food group vs two sub-items) and period (2023-24 vs FY25 April–December) differ, so the numbers measure different quantities and do not conflict.

D1's 9.7 is the CPI weight of one food sub-group (cereals); D2's 'about two-fifths' is the share of all food items in the CPI basket. A single item weighing 9.7% inside a food block of roughly 40-46% is consistent — cereals is the largest food component but far from the whole. The figures describe a part and its container, not the same quantity.

D1 lists pulses at 2.4 and vegetables at 6.0; D2 states vegetables and pulses together hold 8.42% of the CPI basket. 2.4 + 6.0 = 8.4, which matches 8.42 to D1's one-decimal rounding, so D1's component weight is a subset of D2's combined weight and the two are arithmetically consistent.

D1's 2.4 is the CPI weight of pulses alone; D2's 'about two-fifths' is the weight of all food items. A 2.4% sub-item inside a ~40% food block is consistent; the two facts describe a component and the aggregate that contains it.

D1's 6.0 is the CPI weight of vegetables only; D2's 'about two-fifths' is the share of the entire food group in the CPI. A 6% sub-item within a ~40% food block is compatible — part versus whole, not competing estimates of one number.

D1 reports vegetables at 6.0 and pulses at 2.4; D2 reports the pair jointly at 8.42% of the CPI basket. 6.0 + 2.4 = 8.4 ≈ 8.42 within D1's one-decimal rounding, so D1's vegetables weight is the larger half of D2's combined figure and the two agree.

D1's 2.9 is the CPI weight of fruits alone, a single food sub-group; D2's 'about two-fifths' covers all food items in the CPI basket. A 2.9% component sitting inside a ~40% aggregate is consistent, so the difference is purely one of scope.

D1's 6.6 is the milk sub-group's CPI weight; D2's 'about two-fifths' is the whole food block's share of the CPI. Milk at 6.6% is one of the larger food components but well within a ~40% food aggregate, so the two figures are compatible part-and-whole measures.

D1's 2.5 is the CPI weight of spices only; D2's 'about two-fifths' is the aggregate food share of the CPI. A 2.5% sub-item inside a ~40% food group is consistent; the numbers are not rival estimates of the same weight.

D1's 1.4 is the sugar sub-group's CPI weight; D2's 'about two-fifths' is the total food share of the CPI basket. Sugar at 1.4% is one of the smallest food components and fits comfortably inside a ~40% food block, so the two are consistent at different levels of aggregation.

D1's 5.6 is the CPI weight of processed food and beverages; D2's 'about two-fifths' is the share of all food items. A 5.6% sub-group within a ~40% food aggregate is arithmetically compatible — the facts differ only in the level of the basket they describe.

D1's (-)2.5% is the fuel and light group of the CPI averaged over 2024-25; D2's 5.4% is overall retail (headline) CPI inflation for FY24. These are a component and the aggregate, and the periods also differ (2024-25 vs FY24). A deflating fuel component alongside positive headline inflation is exactly what D1 describes ('significantly lower than 1.2 per cent a year ago'), so there is no conflict.

D1's (-)2.5% covers only the fuel and light group for 2024-25, while D2's 4.9% is headline retail inflation for April–December FY25. A negative component print and a positive headline average are consistent — falling LPG/kerosene prices pulled fuel and light negative while food kept headline near 5%. Scope differs (group vs headline), and the windows differ slightly (full year vs April–December).

Both address core (ex food and fuel) CPI inflation. D1 reports 3.5% in 2024-25 against 4.3% a year earlier, a fall of 0.8 pp over the full fiscal year; D2 reports a 0.9 pp reduction measured between FY24 and April–December 2024. The 0.8 vs 0.9 pp gap is explained by D1 including the January–March 2025 quarter, when core edged up, whereas D2's window stops in December; D2 is also the earlier (31 Jan 2025) pre-Budget vintage using partial-year data.

D1's 3.5% is core CPI, defined as headline excluding food and fuel, for 2024-25. D2's 4.3% is food inflation (CFPI) excluding vegetables and pulses for April–December FY25 — a food-basket measure that core explicitly excludes. The apparent link is only that 4.3 also happens to be D1's prior-year core figure; the two facts measure different baskets.

D1's 3.5% is core inflation, i.e. CPI stripped of the entire food and fuel groups, for 2024-25. D2's 3.2% strips only vegetables and pulses from headline, retaining all other food items and all fuel. Despite similar magnitudes these are different exclusion definitions over different windows (full FY25 vs April–December), so they are not two readings of one quantity.

D1's 3.5% is core CPI inflation, which excludes food entirely; D2's 6.5% is food inflation excluding tomato, onion and potato. One measure deliberately removes food, the other is a food index — different attributes over different windows, so no comparison is available.

D1's 3.5% is core inflation (headline less food and fuel) for 2024-25, whereas D2's 4.2% is headline inflation with only tomato, onion and potato removed for April–December FY25. The baskets and the exclusion rules are different constructs; the pair matched only on both being 'ex-something' inflation rates.

D1 gives the full-year merchandise trade deficit for FY2024-25 (Apr 2024-Mar 2025) at US$282.8 bn; D2 gives a single quarter, Q2 FY25 (Jul-Sep 2024), at USD 75.3 bn. A quarter of roughly 75 bn is entirely consistent with an annual 282.8 bn (about 70.7 bn per quarter on average). Different aggregation period, not a disagreement.

D1's US$282.8 bn covers the full fiscal year 2024-25 (Apr 2024-Mar 2025); D2's USD 210.8 bn covers only April-December 2024, the first nine months of that same year. The implied Q4 (Jan-Mar 2025) deficit of about 72 bn is plausible and in line with D2's Q2 FY25 figure of 75.3 bn, so the two are consistent partial/full-year cuts.

D1's US$282.8 bn is the annual FY2024-25 merchandise trade deficit, while D2's USD 64.5 bn is Q2 of FY24 (Jul-Sep 2023) — a single quarter of the prior fiscal year. Same attribute and scope, but neither the length nor the year of the period matches, so the values are not comparable as stated.

D1 reports US$282.8 bn for the whole of FY2024-25; D2's USD 189.7 bn is April-December 2023, i.e. nine months of the preceding fiscal year. The gap reflects both a shorter window and an earlier year — D1 itself puts full FY2023-24 at 241.1 bn, which sits consistently above the 189.7 bn nine-month figure.

D1's US$282.8 bn is a merchandise-only deficit for FY2024-25, whereas D2's USD 69.7 bn is the overall trade deficit for April-December 2023, explicitly 'merchandise and services combined' — India's large services surplus nets most of the goods deficit away. Scope (goods only vs goods plus services) plus a different, shorter period fully explains the gap.

D1 states the FY2023-24 merchandise trade deficit was US$241.1 bn for the full year; D2 reports USD 189.7 bn for April-December 2023, the first nine months of that same year. The residual Q4 (Jan-Mar 2024) deficit of about 51.4 bn is plausible, so the figures are consistent nine-month vs twelve-month cuts of the same series.

D1's US$241.1 bn is the full FY2023-24 merchandise trade deficit; D2's USD 64.5 bn is Q2 FY24 (Jul-Sep 2023) alone. One quarter at 64.5 bn against an annual 241.1 bn (about 60.3 bn average per quarter) is coherent — a quarter-vs-year period difference, not a conflict.

D1's US$241.1 bn covers all of FY2023-24, while D2's USD 75.3 bn is Q2 of FY25 (Jul-Sep 2024) — a single quarter in the following fiscal year. Both the length and the year of the period differ, so no comparison of levels is implied.

D1 reports US$241.1 bn for full-year FY2023-24; D2's USD 210.8 bn is April-December 2024, nine months of the next fiscal year. D2 itself notes the comparable April-December 2023 figure was 189.7 bn, so the two documents describe adjacent periods of a widening series rather than disagreeing.

D1's US$241.1 bn is merchandise-only for the full FY2023-24; D2's USD 69.7 bn is the 'overall trade deficit' for April-December 2023, which combines merchandise and services and is therefore netted down by India's services surplus. Different measure and a shorter window explain the difference.

D1 puts the CAD at 1.3 per cent of GDP for April-December 2024 (nine months of FY25); D2 reports 1.2 per cent for Q2 FY25 (Jul-Sep 2024) alone. A single quarter at 1.2 per cent is compatible with a nine-month average of 1.3 per cent, so the difference is one of aggregation period.

Same attribute and scope, different windows: D1's 1.3 per cent covers April-December 2024, D2's 1.2 per cent is the Q2 FY25 quarter only. The quarterly reading is a component of the nine-month figure and the 0.1 pp gap is consistent with quarter-to-quarter variation.

D1's 1.1 per cent is the April-December 2023 (FY24) CAD; D2's 1.2 per cent is Q2 FY25 (Jul-Sep 2024). Different fiscal years and different window lengths — the figures describe separate periods rather than conflicting readings of one.

D1 reports 1.1 per cent of GDP for April-December 2023, while D2 reports 1.2 per cent for Q2 FY25 (Jul-Sep 2024). The year and the aggregation window both differ, so the 0.1 pp difference carries no contradiction.

D1's US$0.4 bn is net FDI on a BoP basis for full FY2024-25 (after repatriation/disinvestment and Indian outward FDI), whereas D2's USD 55.6 bn is explicitly 'gross FDI inflows' for the first eight months of FY25 (Apr-Nov 2024). Gross inflows of tens of billions netting down to under a billion is the well-known FY25 pattern; the periods also differ (8 months vs 12).

D1 reports net BoP-basis FDI of US$0.4 bn for FY2024-25; D2's USD 47.2 bn is gross FDI inflows for April-November of FY24. The measures differ (net of repatriation and outward FDI vs gross inflows) and so do the year and window, so the two cannot be read as competing values.

D1's US$0.4 bn is a single-year net BoP flow for FY2024-25; D2's USD 1,033.4 bn is a DPIIT cumulative stock of inflows from April 2000 to September 2024 including equity, reinvested earnings and other capital. Cumulative-since-2000 gross inflows versus one year's net flow are entirely different constructs.

D1's US$0.4 bn concerns foreign direct investment (BoP basis, FY2024-25); D2's USD 10.6 bn concerns net foreign portfolio investment for April-December 2024. Different investment categories in the financial account — the similarity is only that both are capital inflows.

D1 measures FDI (net, BoP, FY2024-25, US$0.4 bn); D2's USD 31.7 bn is net FPI for April-December 2023. Different attribute (direct vs portfolio investment) and different period, so the pair is a false match.

D1's US$1.7 bn net FPI is for FY2024-25; D2's USD 31.7 bn is April-December 2023, i.e. nine months of the previous fiscal year. D2 itself records the collapse to 10.6 bn in the comparable FY25 window, so the two figures track a sharp year-on-year decline across different periods.

D1's US$1.7 bn is total net FPI (equity plus debt) for the full FY2024-25; D2's USD 3.1 bn is one month (December 2024) of net inflow into Indian equities only. A single strong month can exceed the annual net when other months record outflows — scope (equity-only vs all FPI) and period both differ.

D2's USD 11.5 bn is a net equity outflow in the single month of October 2024, while D1's US$1.7 bn is the net inflow across all FPI for the entire FY2024-25. A large one-month equity outflow offset by inflows in other months and by debt flows is exactly how a small positive annual net arises.

D2's USD 2.5 bn is an equity-only net outflow over the first half of November 2024; D1's US$1.7 bn is the net FPI figure for all of FY2024-25 across instruments. Sub-monthly equity flows and a full-year all-instrument net are different slices, so the signs and magnitudes need not align.

D1's US$23.8 bn is a flow — accretion to reserves on a BoP basis over H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024) — while D2's USD 704.9 bn is the reserves stock level at September 2024. D2's own stock path (616.7 bn end-Jan 2024 rising to 704.9 bn in Sep 2024) exceeds 23.8 bn because stock changes also include valuation effects and a longer window; flow vs level, not conflicting values.

D1 states an H1 FY25 BoP accretion of US$23.8 bn; D2's USD 616.7 bn is the outstanding reserves stock at end-January 2024, before D1's window even begins. A flow over Apr-Sep 2024 and a stock level at 31 Jan 2024 measure different things over different dates.

D1 reports the BoP-basis accretion of US$23.8 bn during H1:2024-25, whereas D2 reports the reserves level of USD 640.3 bn as at end-December 2024. One is a half-year flow, the other an end-period stock at a later date, so no direct comparison of the numbers is implied.

D1's US$23.8 bn is reserve accretion (a BoP flow) over April-September 2024; D2's USD 640.3 bn is the stock of reserves at end-December 2024, described as having 'moderated' from its September peak. Flow versus level over non-identical periods explains the entire difference.

D1 gives an H1 FY25 accretion flow of US$23.8 bn; D2 gives the reserves stock of USD 634.6 bn as on 3 January 2025. The two are a flow and a level measured on different dates, and the post-September moderation D2 describes is separate from the April-September BoP accretion D1 reports.

D1's full sentence is "Global inflation eased to 5.7 per cent in 2024 from 6.6 per cent a year ago", so D1 puts 2024 global inflation at exactly 5.7 per cent — the same figure and same calendar year D2 reports ("to 5.7 per cent in 2024"). The extracted D1 value (6.6 per cent) is the 2023 comparator inside that same sentence, so the two documents describe one consistent disinflation path rather than conflicting values.

Both are the same series (global headline inflation) at different points in time: D2 gives the 2022 peak of 8.7 per cent, D1 gives 6.6 per cent for 2023. Read together with D1's 5.7 per cent for 2024, the sequence 8.7 (2022) → 6.6 (2023) → 5.7 (2024) is a single declining path, so the gap is purely the different reference year.

D1's 6.6 per cent is global consumer inflation in 2023; D2's 3.3 per cent is global real economic growth in 2023 ("The global economy grew by 3.3 per cent in 2023"). Same subject and year but different attributes — a price measure versus an output measure — so the numbers are not comparable.

D1 reports 3.8 per cent for 2024 on global goods AND services trade volume, an outturn stated in the RBI's FY2024-25 annual report; D2 (published 31 Jan 2025) projects "about 2 per cent in 2024" for goods trade only. Services trade grew far faster than goods in 2024, so a goods-only measure is expected to sit well below a goods-plus-services measure; the gap is also partly vintage, since D2's figure is a projection made before the year's data were complete.

D1's 1.0 per cent is goods-and-services trade volume growth in 2023, the base year from which it says growth "recovered to 3.8 per cent in 2024"; D2's ~2 per cent is a projection for 2024 and covers goods trade only. The values differ because they refer to different years (2023 vs 2024) and, secondarily, to different trade coverage.

D3 reports 8.2 per cent for FY24 (Apr 2023–Mar 2024), "the highest among the major economies"; D1 reports 6.5 per cent for 2024-25 and describes it as a moderation. The two refer to consecutive fiscal years, so the lower later figure is the documented slowdown, not a conflict.

D3's US$3.9 trillion is the level of India's GDP in calendar 2024 per the IMF; D1's 6.5 per cent is the real growth rate for fiscal 2024-25. A stock/level in US dollars and a growth rate in per cent are different attributes and cannot corroborate or contradict each other.

D2's 6.7 per cent is Q1 FY25 (Apr–Jun 2024) at constant 2011-12 prices; D1's 6.5 per cent is the full year 2024-25 on the same price basis. A single quarter sitting slightly above the annual average is a period difference, not a discrepancy.

D2's 5.4 per cent is the Q2 FY25 (Jul–Sep 2024) quarterly rate at constant 2011-12 prices, the weakest quarter of the year; D1's 6.5 per cent is the full-year 2024-25 figure. Averaging a soft Q2 with stronger later quarters yields the higher annual number.
D1's 9.2 per cent is annual FY2023-24 growth; D2's 6.7 per cent is the single quarter Q1 FY25 (Apr–Jun 2024) at constant 2011-12 prices. Different year and different periodicity.

D1's 9.2 per cent is the FY2023-24 annual rate used as a comparator; D2's 5.4 per cent is Q2 FY25 (Jul–Sep 2024). Non-overlapping periods of different length, so the decline is a time-series movement.

D1's 8.8 per cent GFCF growth is the "previous year" comparator, i.e. FY2023-24, in a sentence saying growth "moderated to 6.1 per cent in 2024-25 from 8.8 per cent"; D2's 6.4 per cent is the FY25 estimate at constant prices. Different fiscal years account for the difference.

Both refer to FY2023-24 GFCF growth, but D2's 10.1 per cent is H1 FY24 (Apr–Sep 2023) only, while D1's 8.8 per cent is the full year. A stronger first half than full year implies slower H2 FY24 investment growth, which is consistent rather than conflicting.

D1's 8.8 per cent is full-year FY24 GFCF growth; D2's 6.4 per cent is H1 FY25 (Apr–Sep 2024). Different fiscal year and half-year versus full-year coverage; D2 itself frames this as "a softening" from H1 FY24.

D1's 5.8 per cent for 2024-25 is Gross Capital Formation (the table row "II. Gross Capital Formation"), which includes change in stocks and valuables, whereas D2's 6.4 per cent is Gross FIXED Capital Formation only. Same period, different aggregate, so GCF growing more slowly than GFCF reflects weaker inventory/valuables accumulation, not a conflicting estimate.
