D1's 5.1 per cent is WPI inflation for primary articles (22.6 per cent weight in the WPI basket) in 2024-25; D2's 5.4 per cent is CPI headline retail inflation in FY24. Different price index, different sub-basket and different year — the closeness of 5.1 and 5.4 is coincidental.

WPI primary-articles inflation (5.1 per cent, 2024-25, D1) and CPI headline retail inflation (4.9 per cent, April-December FY25, D2) are distinct indices with different baskets and weights; they are not two readings of the same attribute.

D1 reports the GDP deflator inflation rate (3.0 per cent in April-December 2024, up from 2.3 per cent a year earlier); D2 reports a 0.9 percentage point fall in CPI core (non-food, non-fuel) inflation between FY24 and April-December 2024. One is a level of deflator inflation, the other a change in a CPI sub-aggregate — different attributes that neither confirm nor conflict.

D1's 13.4 per cent is y-o-y bank credit growth by scheduled commercial banks to the services sector as at end-March 2025; D2's 7.1 per cent is real growth of services sector output (GVA) in H1 FY25. Credit outstanding growth and value-added growth are different attributes.

D1's 20.8 per cent is y-o-y growth in bank credit to services as at end-March 2024; D2's 7.1 per cent is services sector output growth in H1 FY25. Different attribute (lending versus value added) and different period, so no comparison is implied.

D1 states headline CPI inflation fell below 4.0 per cent in July and August 2024 for the first time since September 2019; D2 states core inflation reached a decade low in FY25. Headline CPI and core (non-food, non-fuel) inflation are different aggregates over different windows, so the two milestone claims are complementary rather than the same fact.

D1's ₹1.5 lakh crore is total FPI investment in debt across the General route, VRR and FAR for the whole of 2024-25; D2's ₹62,431 crore covers only July-November 2024, the five months after JP Morgan index inclusion took effect. The smaller figure is a sub-period of the larger one (≈0.62 lakh crore of ≈1.5 lakh crore), so the two are consistent.

D1 reports ₹1.5 lakh crore (≈US$ 17-18 billion) of FPI investment in debt instruments over full-year 2024-25; D2 reports net FPI inflows of USD 10.6 billion in April-December 2024 across all segments, a figure depressed by the equity outflows D2 itself documents for October-November. Debt-only versus all-segment net flows, over a nine-month versus a twelve-month window, explains the gap; a currency conversion would be needed to test them precisely.

D1's ₹1.5 lakh crore is debt-segment FPI investment in 2024-25; D2's USD 31.7 billion is total net FPI inflows in April-December 2023, quoted only as a prior-year comparator. Different segment coverage and non-overlapping periods make this a false match rather than a disagreement.

D1 reports the rupee closing 2024-25 (to 31 Mar 2025) 2.4 per cent weaker against the dollar; D2, published 31 Jan 2025, measures 2.9 per cent depreciation over the first nine months of FY25 up to 6 January 2025. The full-year figure is smaller because the rupee recovered part of its loss in the closing months, so a partial-year and a full-year window explain the difference.

Both describe net FPI outflows from Indian equities in October 2024: D1 says 'more than US$ 11 billion' and D2 gives USD 11.5 billion. Same segment, same month, and 11.5 satisfies D1's 'more than 11' statement.

D1's outflow of more than US$ 11 billion is for October 2024; D2's USD 2.5 billion is for the first half of November 2024. D2 presents them as the two legs of the same reversal ('October and the first half of November 2024, resulting in a net outflow of USD 11.5 billion and 2.5 billion, respectively'), so the different magnitudes are purely a matter of different windows.

D1 records an equity FPI outflow of more than US$ 11 billion in October 2024; D2 records a net inflow of USD 3.1 billion in December 2024. Opposite signs, but they are different months of the same year and D2 describes December as a reversal of the October-November selling, so this is a time path rather than a conflict.

D1's figure is a single-month equity-segment outflow (>US$ 11 billion, October 2024); D2's USD 10.6 billion is net FPI inflow across all segments over April-December 2024. The one-month equity outflow sits inside the nine-month all-segment net figure — indeed it explains why that net figure fell from USD 31.7 billion a year earlier — so segment scope and window account for the difference.

D1 reports an equity-segment FPI outflow in October 2024; D2's USD 31.7 billion is total net FPI inflow in April-December 2023, used only as a prior-year benchmark. Different segment coverage and non-overlapping periods — the pair is a false match.

D1's 3.3% is the Gross Fiscal Deficit of state governments as % of GDP for 2025-26 (BE), a budgetary flow measure; D2's 1.2% is India's current account deficit as % of GDP in Q2 FY25, an external-sector measure. Different attribute and different entity (states vs national balance of payments), so the numeric similarity is a false match.

State governments' Gross Fiscal Deficit (3.3% of GDP, 2025-26 BE) and India's current account deficit (1.3% of GDP, Q2 FY24) are different attributes for different subjects — a fiscal balance versus an external balance — and cover different periods. No comparison is meaningful.

D1 reports states' Primary Deficit of 1.8% of GDP for 2024-25 (RE); D2 reports the national current account deficit of 1.3% of GDP for Q2 FY24. Fiscal primary deficit and balance-of-payments CAD are distinct attributes with distinct subjects; the shared '% of GDP' unit is the only overlap.

States' Primary Deficit (1.8% of GDP, 2024-25 RE) versus India's current account deficit (1.2% of GDP, Q2 FY25): different measures (fiscal vs external), different subjects (state governments vs the national economy) and different periods. False match.

D1's 8.8% is the general government (Centre + States) Gross Fiscal Deficit as % of GDP for 2023-24 (RE); D2's 1.3% is the current account deficit as % of GDP in Q2 FY24. Fiscal deficit and current account deficit are different attributes and are not comparable despite both being ratios to GDP.

General government GFD of 8.8% of GDP (2023-24 RE) and CAD of 1.2% of GDP (Q2 FY25) measure different things over different periods — a consolidated fiscal balance versus an external current account balance. No corroboration or conflict is possible.

D1 states the general government GFD 'moderated to 7.6 per cent of GDP' for 2024-25 (BE); D2 reports CAD of 1.3% of GDP for Q2 FY24. These are distinct attributes (fiscal versus external deficit) with different periods and scopes.

General government Gross Fiscal Deficit (7.6% of GDP, 2024-25 BE) versus India's current account deficit (1.2% of GDP, Q2 FY25) are different measures entirely; the only commonality is expressing both as a share of GDP.

D1's +20 per cent is states' budgeted capital outlay for 2025-26 (BE) measured over 2024-25 (RE) — a forward-looking plan for a year that had not begun. D2's -5.6 per cent is actual states' capital-account expenditure during April-November FY25 versus the same months of FY24. Different periods and different bases (budget plan vs eight-month realised spend), so a planned increase and an in-year decline are not in conflict.

Both are IMF-based global growth projections for calendar 2025, but from different forecast rounds: D3 explicitly cites the IMF World Economic Outlook update of July 2024 ('hold steady at 3.3%'), while D1 (RBI Annual Report 2024-25, finalised around May 2025) says growth is 'expected to be even lower in 2025 (2.8 per cent)', reflecting the IMF's April 2025 downgrade. Same period, different forecast vintage.

D2 (published 31 Jan 2025) cites the IMF projection of 3.3 per cent for 2025; D1 (RBI Annual Report for FY2024-25, released after March 2025) puts 2025 global growth at 2.8 per cent. The period and scope are identical; the gap is the later IMF forecast round cutting the 2025 projection, i.e. a data-vintage difference rather than a disagreement. Verification would be the specific WEO editions cited.

D2 states the IMF 'has projected growth of ... 3.3 per cent for ... 2025' and D3 states 'global economic growth for 2025 will likely hold steady at 3.3%' on the IMF WEO update. Same subject (world GDP), same period (calendar 2025), same source and same value of 3.3 per cent.

Both cite 4.3 per cent for EMDE growth, but they refer to different years: D1 says EMDE output 'moderated to 4.3 per cent from 4.7 per cent' as a 2024 estimate, while D3 projects EMDE growth 'stable at 4.3%' for 2025 on the July 2024 IMF WEO. Identical values for different reference years, so neither confirms nor conflicts with the other.

Both cover calendar 2024 global growth: D2 (Jan 2025) reports the IMF's projection of 3.2 per cent, while D1 reports the outturn estimate that 'global economic growth moderated to 3.3 per cent in 2024'. The 0.1 pp gap is a forward projection made during 2024 versus the later realised estimate published in the RBI's FY2024-25 report.

Same subject, period and scope — world GDP growth in calendar 2023 — but D2 (31 Jan 2025) says 'The global economy grew by 3.3 per cent in 2023' while D1 says '3.5 per cent in 2023'. Neither document flags a revision, but the later RBI report reflects the IMF's upward revision of 2023 global growth in a subsequent WEO round; to confirm one would check which WEO edition each cites.

D1 reports merchandise imports 'expanded by 6.2 per cent (y-o-y) to US$ 720.2 billion during 2024-25' (full twelve months), whereas D2 reports 5.2 per cent growth for April-December 2024, only the first nine months of the same fiscal year. The higher full-year growth is consistent with faster import growth in Q4 FY25; the periods differ, so the rates are not comparable directly.

Both describe merchandise import growth in FY25, but D2's 5.2 per cent covers April-December FY25 (nine months) while D1's 6.2 per cent covers the full year 2024-25 ending 31 March 2025. The difference is a partial-year versus full-year window, not a disagreement.

D1's US$ 720.2 billion is merchandise imports alone for the full year 2024-25; D2's USD 682.2 billion is total imports of merchandise plus services for April-December 2024. Different scope (goods only vs goods+services) and different length of period, so the two dollar totals measure different aggregates.

D2's USD 682.2 billion is 'total imports' for the first nine months of FY25, which in that document combines merchandise and services; D1's US$ 720.2 billion is merchandise imports for the full twelve months of 2024-25. The gap follows from both the wider commodity coverage in D2 and the shorter nine-month window.

D1 reports nominal merchandise import value up 6.2 per cent to US$ 720.2 billion over the full year 2024-25, while D2 reports imports of goods and services at constant prices contracting 2.9 per cent in Q2 FY25 'primarily driven by a decline in commodity prices'. Different measurement basis (nominal customs/BoP value vs national-accounts constant-price volumes), different coverage and a single quarter versus the year, so the signs can legitimately differ.

D1 reports food inflation of 6.7 per cent for the full year 2024-25 (Apr 2024-Mar 2025), while D2 reports CFPI food inflation of 8.4 per cent for FY25 April-December only. D1's own quote explains the gap: a 'sharp correction in vegetable prices in February-March 2025 led to a moderation in food inflation to 6.7 per cent' — those two low months are outside D2's April-December window. A secondary definitional wedge exists (CPI food group vs CFPI), but the window difference alone accounts for most of the 1.7pp.

D1's 6.7 per cent is food inflation for 2024-25; D2's 7.5 per cent CFPI figure is for FY24 (2023-04-01..2024-03-31) — different fiscal years, so they are not competing measurements. Both documents agree food inflation was lower in 2024-25 than in the prior year (D1: 6.7 vs 7.0; D2 measures the earlier year at 7.5 on the CFPI definition).

D1's 6.7 per cent is all-items food inflation for full-year 2024-25; D2's 4.3 per cent is explicitly food inflation with vegetables and pulses stripped out, for April-December FY25, and D2 says that exclusion is '4.1 per cent lower than the overall food inflation' (i.e. 8.4 per cent). The difference is a constructed sub-index plus a shorter window, not a disagreement about measured food inflation.

D1's 1.2 per cent is the CPI 'fuel and light' sub-group for 2023-24; D2's 5.4 per cent is all-items retail inflation for the same FY24. Same period, but a sub-group rate and the headline index are different attributes — a low fuel print is fully compatible with 5.4 per cent headline.

Fuel and light group inflation for 2023-24 (1.2 per cent) versus headline retail inflation for April-December FY25 (4.9 per cent): different attribute and different period, so the pair is a false match.

D1 gives core (CPI ex food and fuel) levels: 4.3 per cent in 2023-24 easing to 3.5 per cent in 2024-25, a 0.8pp fall over the full year. D2 states a '0.9 percentage point reduction in core (non-food, non-fuel) inflation between FY24 and April-December 2024', implying roughly 3.4 per cent for April-December. The 0.1pp gap is explained by D2's shorter April-December window versus D1's full April-March year; the two are consistent statements about the same series.

Both values are 4.3 per cent, but that is coincidence: D1's is core CPI excluding food and fuel for 2023-24, D2's is food inflation excluding vegetables and pulses for April-December FY25. Different attribute (core vs a food sub-index) and different period.

D1's 4.3 per cent is core CPI (ex food and fuel) for 2023-24; D2's 3.2 per cent is headline CPI recomputed excluding only vegetables and pulses for April-December FY25. Different exclusion sets and different periods — these are not two readings of one series.

Core CPI ex food and fuel for 2023-24 (4.3 per cent) versus food inflation excluding tomato, onion and potato for April-December FY25 (6.5 per cent): different attribute (core versus a food sub-aggregate) and different period.

D1's core inflation excludes all food and fuel; D2's 4.2 per cent is headline inflation excluding only the TOP vegetables, for April-December FY25. Different constructed measures over different windows, so the pair is a false match.

Both cover the identical period 2023-24/FY24 but use different food indices: D1 quotes 7.0 per cent for the CPI food group (food and beverages, which includes prepared meals, snacks and non-alcoholic beverages), while D2 quotes 7.5 per cent for the Consumer Food Price Index, whose narrower basket excludes those items. The 0.5pp wedge is the standard CFPI-vs-food-and-beverages difference, not a disagreement on the data.

D1's 7.0 per cent is for 2023-24; D2's 8.4 per cent is CFPI for April-December of FY25 — consecutive, non-overlapping periods, plus the food-group vs CFPI definitional difference. Both documents agree food inflation rose into FY25 before the Feb-Mar 2025 vegetable correction pulled the full-year 2024-25 figure down to 6.7 per cent (D1).

D1's 7.0 per cent is all-items food inflation for 2023-24; D2's 4.3 per cent is food inflation for April-December FY25 with vegetables and pulses excluded — a different year and a deliberately stripped-down index that D2 says runs 4.1pp below overall food inflation. Neither figure purports to measure the other.

D1 reports 7.4 per cent average for the full CPI food and beverages group over April 2024-January 2025; D2's 4.3 per cent for April-December FY25 explicitly removes vegetables and pulses, which D2 says accounts for 4.1pp of overall food inflation. Once the excluded high-inflation items are added back (D2's implied overall 8.4 per cent), the two are consistent readings differing by index definition and by one extra month in D1's window.
D1's 7.4 per cent is the food and beverages group averaged over April 2024-January 2025; D2's 5.4 per cent is headline retail inflation for FY24. Different attribute and non-overlapping periods.

Overlapping windows (Apr 2024 onward) but different attributes: D1 measures the CPI food and beverages group (7.4 per cent), D2 measures all-items headline retail inflation (4.9 per cent). Food above headline is the expected relationship, not a contradiction.

D1's 7.4 per cent is an inflation rate for the food and beverages group; D2's 32.3 per cent is a contribution share of vegetables and pulses to overall inflation. Rate versus contribution weight — different attributes with incomparable units.

D1 states vegetables carry a 13.2 per cent weight within the food and beverages group; D2 states vegetables and pulses together carry 8.42 per cent of the whole CPI basket. Different denominators and different item sets: 13.2 per cent of the ~45.9 per cent food-and-beverages share is about 6.0 per cent of the full basket, and adding pulses (~2.4 per cent) gives ~8.4 per cent, matching D2.

D1's 19.4 per cent is the vegetables inflation rate for 2024-25; D2's 32.3 per cent is the share of overall inflation contributed by vegetables and pulses in April-December FY25. A price-change rate and a contribution share are different attributes measured in different terms.

D1 measures vegetables inflation (19.4 per cent); D2's 4.3 per cent is food inflation with vegetables and pulses removed. The two series are constructed to exclude each other, so they measure different things by design.

D1's fact is a vegetables inflation rate of 19.4 per cent (with an incidental 13.2 per cent within-food weight); D2's fact is that food items are about two-fifths of the CPI basket. Different subjects (vegetables rate vs food's basket share), so this is a false match on the word 'weight'.

D1's 7.2 per cent is the cereals and products sub-group (21 per cent of CPI food and beverages) for 2024-25; D2's 8.4 per cent is aggregate CFPI food inflation for April-December FY25. A single sub-group rate and the overall food aggregate are different attributes, and the periods differ as well.

Cereals and products inflation for 2024-25 (7.2 per cent) versus aggregate CFPI inflation for FY24 (7.5 per cent): a component versus the whole food basket, and different fiscal years. The near-equal numbers are coincidental.
D1 reports a food sub-group (cereals and products, 7.2 per cent, 2024-25); D2 reports all-items retail inflation (5.4 per cent, FY24). Different attribute and different period.

Cereals and products inflation (7.2 per cent, full-year 2024-25) is a sub-group of the food basket, whereas D2's 4.9 per cent is headline retail inflation for April-December FY25 — different attributes over different windows.

D1 reports the full-year 2024-25 merchandise trade balance as -282.8 US$ bn (last entry of the annual series -191.0, -264.9, -241.1, -282.8), while D2 reports USD 210.8 bn for April-December 2024 only. D2 was tabled 31 Jan 2025 and could only cover nine months of FY25; the implied Q4 (Jan-Mar 2025) deficit of about USD 72 bn is consistent with the quarterly run-rate. Same measure, different window.

D1's -282.8 US$ bn covers FY2024-25 in full; D2's USD 64.5 bn is Q2 of FY24 (Jul-Sep 2023), a single quarter of the prior fiscal year, quoted only as the year-earlier comparator for the 75.3 bn Q2 FY25 figure. The two refer to non-overlapping periods of different years.

D1's -282.8 US$ bn is the merchandise-only trade balance for FY2024-25; D2's USD 69.7 bn is the overall deficit including services for April-December 2023. Services surplus offsets a large part of the goods deficit, so the overall figure is necessarily much smaller; the periods also differ (full FY25 vs nine months of FY24). Both scope and period explain the gap.

D1's 26.7 per cent is engineering goods' share of total merchandise exports in 2024-25; D2's 9.9 per cent is the year-on-year growth rate of engineering goods exports in April-December 2024. Same sector, but a share-of-total and a growth rate are different attributes and cannot corroborate or conflict with each other.

D1 states a percentage share (engineering goods = 26.7 per cent of merchandise exports, FY2024-25); D2 states an absolute dollar level for total exports of goods and services (USD 602.6 bn, Apr-Dec FY25). Different attributes at different aggregation levels; the pair is a false match on the word 'exports'.

As above: D1's 26.7 per cent engineering-goods share of merchandise exports is not comparable with D2's USD 602.6 bn total merchandise-plus-services export value for April-December FY25. Different attribute (share vs level) and different scope (one sector vs all exports).

Both report year-on-year growth of engineering goods exports, but D1's 6.7 per cent covers the full year 2024-25 while D2's 9.9 per cent covers only April-December 2024. D2 was published 31 Jan 2025 and could not include Q4 FY25; a weaker Jan-Mar 2025 quarter pulls the full-year rate below the nine-month rate. Same series, different windows.

D1's 6.7 per cent is growth of the engineering goods segment alone (FY2024-25); D2's 1.6 per cent is growth of total merchandise exports (Apr-Dec 2024). A segment growing faster than the aggregate is expected, especially with petroleum exports contracting (D1 reports -24.7 per cent). Segment-vs-total scope, plus differing windows.

Same relationship as the other merchandise-total figure: D1's 6.7 per cent applies to engineering goods only in FY2024-25, D2's 1.6 per cent to all merchandise exports in April-December 2024. A single strong sector can outpace the overall basket without contradiction; the reporting windows also differ.

D1's 6.7 per cent is engineering-goods merchandise export growth for FY2024-25; D2's 6 per cent is growth of total exports including services for April-December FY25. The near-equal values are coincidental — one is a goods sub-sector, the other an all-exports aggregate that includes the fast-growing services component.

D1's 6.7 per cent is nominal dollar growth of engineering goods exports over full FY2024-25; D2's 5.6 per cent is national-accounts growth of exports of goods and non-factor services at constant prices for H1 FY25. Different scope (one sector vs all goods and NFS), different valuation (nominal USD vs constant prices) and different window.

D1's 54.3 per cent applies specifically to mobile phone exports (to US$ 21.0 bn) over full FY2024-25; D2's 28.6 per cent applies to the whole electronic goods basket over April-December 2024. Mobile phones are the fastest-growing component within electronics, so the sub-segment rate exceeding the basket rate is expected; the windows also differ.

D1's 6.4 per cent is agricultural exports growth for 2024-25 up to February 2025; D2's 6 per cent is growth of total exports of merchandise and services (USD 602.6 bn) over April-December FY25. Agriculture is a small slice of the export basket, so the similar values are coincidental rather than the same measurement; windows differ too (11 months vs 9 months).

D1 measures agricultural exports only (+6.4 per cent, Apr 2024-Feb 2025); D2 measures all merchandise exports (+1.6 per cent, Apr-Dec 2024). A sector outperforming the total basket is not a conflict — D1's own text attributes the aggregate drag to petroleum products. Scope and window both differ.

Same pairing as above with D2's page-51 statement of the same aggregate: agricultural exports +6.4 per cent (D1, up to Feb 2025) against total merchandise exports +1.6 per cent (D2, Apr-Dec 2024). Segment-vs-total scope, plus an 11-month vs 9-month window difference.

D1's 6.4 per cent covers agricultural merchandise exports through February 2025; D2's 6 per cent covers merchandise plus services exports for April-December FY25. Different baskets entirely — the closeness of the two rates is incidental, and the periods do not match.

D1's 6.4 per cent is nominal growth of agricultural exports (Apr 2024-Feb 2025); D2's 5.6 per cent is constant-price growth of exports of goods and non-factor services in H1 FY25 from the national accounts. Different scope (one commodity group vs all goods and NFS), different price basis, and different window.

D1's 19.7 per cent is cumulative year-on-year growth of rice exports alone in 2024-25; D2's 6 per cent is growth of total exports of merchandise and services (USD 602.6 bn) in the first nine months of FY25. A single commodity rebounding strongly (after export restrictions eased) sits comfortably inside a 6 per cent aggregate; periods also differ.

Both measure year-on-year growth of drugs and pharmaceuticals exports, but D1's 9.4 per cent is for full FY2024-25 while D2's 6.4 per cent covers only April-December 2024. D2, tabled 31 Jan 2025, excludes Q4 FY25; a stronger Jan-Mar 2025 quarter lifts the full-year rate above the nine-month rate. Same series, different windows.

D1's 9.4 per cent refers to drugs and pharmaceuticals exports; D2's 5 per cent in the same sentence refers to the chemicals sector, a different item in the Survey's list ('6.4, 28.6, 9.9, and 5 per cent respectively'). Different commodity groups, so the figures are not measuring the same thing.

D1 gives POL imports of US$ 185.8 bn for FY2024-25, explicitly 25.8 per cent of total merchandise imports; D2 gives total imports of USD 682.2 bn for April-December FY25. One is a component, the other the aggregate (and D2's aggregate covers only nine months), so the two are consistent rather than competing figures.

D1 reports petroleum products exports contracting 24.7 per cent in FY2024-25; D2 reports non-petroleum exports rising 7.1 per cent in April-December 2024. These are complementary, mutually exclusive baskets — D2 explicitly strips petroleum out — so the opposite signs are expected, not contradictory. Windows also differ.

Same complementary split restated on D2 page 29: non-petroleum merchandise exports +7.1 per cent (Apr-Dec 2024) against D1's petroleum products exports -24.7 per cent (FY2024-25). The petroleum contraction is precisely what the Survey excludes to obtain its 7.1 per cent, so the two reinforce rather than conflict.

D1's -24.7 per cent covers petroleum products exports only (FY2024-25); D2's +1.6 per cent covers the total merchandise basket (Apr-Dec 2024). D2 itself notes that stripping petroleum out raises the rate to 7.1 per cent, which shows the petroleum decline is the drag inside the 1.6 per cent aggregate. Component vs total, plus differing windows.

D1's petroleum products exports fell 24.7 per cent in FY2024-25, while D2's aggregate merchandise exports grew 1.6 per cent in April-December 2024. The negative component is contained within the modestly positive total; D2's paired 7.1 per cent non-petroleum figure confirms the decomposition. No disagreement on any shared measure.

D1's -24.7 per cent is petroleum products export growth; D2's 9.9 per cent is engineering goods export growth. These are two distinct commodity groups with no overlap, so the values neither confirm nor conflict with one another.

D1's 10.7 per cent is cereals-and-products inflation in 2023-24 ('albeit lower than 10.7 per cent in the previous year'); D2's 5.4 per cent is all-items retail CPI inflation in FY24. Same period (Apr 2023-Mar 2024) but different attributes: a food sub-group index versus the headline index, so 10.7 vs 5.4 is not a disagreement.

Both cover FY24, but D1 measures only cereals and products (10.7 per cent) while D2 measures the whole Consumer Food Price Index (7.5 per cent). Cereals are one component of the CFPI basket, so a component running hotter than the aggregate is arithmetically normal, not a conflicting claim about the same attribute.

D1's 10.7 per cent is cereals inflation for 2023-24; D2's 8.4 per cent is total CFPI food inflation for Apr-Dec FY25. Both the attribute (cereals sub-group vs full food index) and the period (FY24 vs the first nine months of FY25) differ, so the figures were never measuring the same thing.

Cereals-and-products inflation of 10.7 per cent in 2023-24 (D1) and headline retail inflation of 4.9 per cent in Apr-Dec FY25 (D2) share neither attribute nor period. No comparison of values is meaningful.

D1 reports milk-and-products inflation 'range bound at 2.9 per cent during 2024-25' (full April 2024-March 2025); D2 reports headline retail inflation of 4.9 per cent for FY25 April-December. A single food sub-group averaging below headline is expected; the two are different attributes over different windows.

Milk-and-products inflation of 2.9 per cent in 2024-25 (D1) versus headline retail inflation of 5.4 per cent in FY24 (D2): different index (sub-group vs all-items) and different fiscal years, so the 2.9 vs 5.4 gap carries no consistency signal.

D1's 28 per cent is moong (pulses) output growth per the 2nd Advance Estimate of 2024-25 over 2023-24; D2's 6 per cent is industrial-sector GVA growth in H1 FY25. Different sectors and different measured quantities (crop tonnage vs industrial value added) — a false match on 'growth, per cent, India'.

Moong production growth of 28 per cent (2nd AE 2024-25, D1) has no relationship to industrial-sector growth of 8.3 per cent in Q1 FY25 (D2). Different sector, different variable, different reference window.

D1 gives pulses inflation of (-) 2.7 per cent for the single month of March 2025; D2 gives headline retail inflation of 4.9 per cent averaged over April-December FY25. A deflating sub-group in one month versus a nine-month all-items average are different attributes on different periods.

Pulses prices at (-) 2.7 per cent in March 2025 (D1, weight 5.2 per cent of CPI-food) versus headline CPI at 4.9 per cent for April-December 2024 (D2). One is a monthly component reading outside D2's window entirely, the other a headline nine-month average.

D1 reports a rate (pulses inflation of -2.7 per cent in March 2025); D2 reports a contribution share (vegetables and pulses accounting for 32.3 per cent of overall inflation in April-December FY25). D1 reports net outward FDI of US$29.2 bn for 2024-25 while D2 reports net FDI (to India) of US$10.1 bn for FY24 as a whole — a different BoP aggregate and a different year. D1's own series shows outward FDI of 16.7 in the prior year, not 10.1.

Both are net FPI flows into Indian equities, but D1's US$25.3 bn covers the whole of 2023-24 while D2's US$3.1 bn is a single month, December 2024. A full prior fiscal year and one month of the following year cannot be compared directly.

D1's US$25.3 bn is the equity segment only, for full 2023-24; D2's US$31.7 bn is total net FPI (equity plus debt) for April–December 2023. The larger D2 number is consistent with equity-only being a subset — debt inflows were substantial that year — and the windows also differ (9 months vs 12).

D1 gives equity-segment FPI net inflows of US$25.3 bn for 2023-24; D2's US$10.6 bn is all-segment net FPI for April–December 2024, a different fiscal year and a broader instrument scope. D1's US$25.3 bn equity FPI inflow is for 2023-24; D2's US$11.5 bn equity outflow is for October 2024 alone. Different fiscal years and a single month versus a full year, so the sign reversal reflects timing rather than a data disagreement.

D1 reports US$17.4 bn of debt-segment FPI inflows for the whole of 2024-25; D2's ₹62,431 crore covers only July–November 2024 (five months) and is in rupees — roughly US$7.4 bn at ~₹84/US$. A five-month sub-window worth under half the annual total is consistent with D1.

D1's US$17.4 bn is debt FPI for 2024-25 (Apr 2024–Mar 2025); D2's ₹1.1 lakh crore (~US$13 bn) spans October 2023 to June 2024, straddling the previous fiscal year and only the first quarter of 2024-25. D1's US$17.4 bn is the debt segment only, for 2024-25; D2's US$31.7 bn is total net FPI (all segments) for April–December 2023. Different instrument scope and a different, shorter period in the prior fiscal year.

Both are total net FPI inflows, but D1's US$1.7 bn is full-year 2024-25 while D2's US$31.7 bn covers April–December 2023, in the prior fiscal year. D1 separately puts 2023-24 at US$41.6 bn, which sits consistently above D2's nine-month 31.7.

Same measure and same fiscal year, different windows: D2's US$10.6 bn is April–December 2024 (nine months of FY25), D1's US$1.7 bn is the full twelve months to March 2025. The full year being ~US$8.9 bn lower implies net outflows in Jan–Mar 2025, consistent with the risk-off tone D1 describes.

D1's US$1.7 bn is total (equity plus debt) FPI for all of 2024-25; D2's US$3.1 bn is equity-only for the single month of December 2024. A one-month equity inflow larger than the annual all-segment net is unremarkable given the heavy October–November equity outflows D2 reports.

Same measure (total net FPI inflows): D2's US$31.7 bn covers April–December 2023, the first nine months of the year for which D1 reports US$41.6 bn. The ~US$9.9 bn difference is the Jan–Mar 2024 quarter, so the figures are consistent.

D1's US$41.6 bn is total net FPI for 2023-24; D2's US$10.6 bn is April–December 2024, i.e. the following fiscal year and only nine months of it. D2 explicitly contrasts it with US$31.7 bn in the year-earlier window, matching D1's much larger 2023-24 total.
D1's US$41.6 bn is all-segment net FPI for 2023-24; D2's US$3.1 bn is equity-only for December 2024. Different segment, different fiscal year and a month versus a year.

Both cover the same window (April-December 2024): D1 reports software services exports of US$118,129 million (~US$118.1 bn) as a BoP invisibles line, while D2 reports total merchandise-plus-services exports of US$602.6 bn. D1's US$135.5 billion covers services exports only for April-December 2024; D2's US$602.6 billion is merchandise and services combined for the identical nine months. The services figure is a component of the combined total, so no conflict. Note the D1 level also looks to be on a net (BoP) basis: D2's combined total less merchandise exports of roughly US$320 billion leaves gross services near US$280 billion, well above US$135.5 billion — worth confirming against the BoP tables.

D2's US$602.6 billion is explicitly 'total exports (merchandise and services)' for the first nine months of FY25, the same window as D1's US$135.5 billion services-export figure for April-December 2024. Services are nested inside the combined total, so the values differ by scope; as with the page-50 statement of the same US$602.6 billion, the D1 level appears to be net services rather than gross.

D1 reports a level (US$135.5 billion of services exports in April-December 2024); D2 reports a growth rate (11.6 per cent in the first nine months of FY25). Level and growth rate are different attributes, and without the prior-year base D2 does not state, neither figure can confirm or refute the other. The growth-rate comparison belongs with D1's own 12.9 per cent.

D1 gives India's services exports in dollars (US$135.5 billion, April-December 2024); D2 gives India's share of global services exports (around 4.3 per cent in calendar 2023). Different attribute (absolute value vs world-market share) and different period.

D1's US$135.5 billion is a nine-month 2024 services-export level; D2's 1.9 per cent is India's share of global services exports in 2005, quoted as the historical base for the doubling to 4.3 per cent. Different attribute and a period two decades apart.

Both cover the same window — D1's 'April-December 2024' is D2's 'first nine months of FY25' — yet D1 says services exports grew 12.9 per cent and D2 says 11.6 per cent. The likely cause is basis, not disagreement: D1 pairs its 12.9 per cent with a level of US$135.5 billion, whereas D2's combined merchandise-plus-services total of US$602.6 billion implies gross services exports nearer US$280 billion, so D1 appears to be growing a net (BoP) services series and D2 a gross one. To settle it, check whether D1's US$135.5 billion is net services receipts; if both series are gross, the 1.3pp gap would instead be a vintage effect between the 31 Jan 2025 Survey (December data provisional) and the later RBI report.

D1's 12.9 per cent is services exports alone for April-December 2024; D2's 6 per cent is total exports, merchandise and services combined, for the same nine months. D2 elsewhere puts merchandise export growth at just 1.6 per cent over that period, so a services rate near 12-13 per cent blended with weak merchandise growth is exactly what produces a combined 6 per cent. Scope, not disagreement.

D1's 12.9 per cent is nominal US-dollar services exports over April-December 2024; D2's 5.6 per cent is exports of goods AND non-factor services at constant prices over H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024). Three differences stack up: the D2 basket includes goods, it is measured at constant prices in the national accounts rather than in nominal dollars, and it covers six months rather than nine. Each pushes the aggregate rate below the services-only dollar rate.

D1 reports a growth rate for India's services exports (12.9 per cent y-o-y, April-December 2024); D2 reports India's share of global services exports (around 4.3 per cent in 2023). A growth rate and a market share are different attributes measured over different periods.

D1's 12.9 per cent is growth in services EXPORTS (external sector, April-December 2024); D2's 7.1 per cent is growth of the domestic services SECTOR output in H1 FY25. Domestic sectoral GVA and cross-border services receipts are different attributes, so the figures neither corroborate nor conflict.

D1's 14.5 per cent applies to software and business services, which it says account for around 74 per cent of India's services exports, over April-December 2024; D2's 11.6 per cent is all services exports over the same first nine months of FY25. A 74 per cent weight growing 14.5 per cent implies the remaining quarter grew roughly 3 per cent to average about 11.6 per cent — arithmetically coherent, so the sub-basket versus total scope explains the gap.

D1's 14.5 per cent covers only software and business services exports; D2's 6 per cent covers total exports, merchandise and services combined, for the same April-December FY25 window. The sub-component sits inside the total, and D2's own merchandise growth of 1.6 per cent over that period explains why the combined rate is far below the software line.

D1's 14.5 per cent is nominal dollar growth in software and business services exports over nine months to December 2024; D2's 5.6 per cent is constant-price growth of goods and non-factor services exports over H1 FY25. The D2 measure is a much broader basket including goods, is deflated to constant prices, and covers a shorter window, all of which pull the rate below a fast-growing services sub-component.

D1's 14.5 per cent is growth in software and business services exports; D2's 1.6 per cent is growth in merchandise exports, both for April-December 2024. Merchandise excludes services entirely, so these measure disjoint baskets rather than the same quantity — the contrast is informative narratively but neither figure corroborates or contradicts the other.

D1's 14.5 per cent covers software and business services exports; D2's 9.9 per cent covers engineering goods exports, one of several merchandise lines D2 lists for April-December 2024. These are two disjoint export baskets — a services category and a goods category — so despite the shared period they are different attributes.

Both give GFCF growth for the same year (RBI's "2024-25" = ES's "FY25", Apr 2024-Mar 2025) at constant 2011-12 prices, but from different NSO estimate rounds: D2 (published 31 Jan 2025) cites the First Advance Estimates at 6.4 per cent, while D1's appendix table carries the Second Advance Estimate at 6.1 per cent. The 0.3 pp gap is a standard SAE revision of the FAE, not a disagreement.

D1's 6.1 per cent is full-year 2024-25 GFCF growth (second advance estimate); D2's 6.4 per cent is for H1 FY25 only (Apr-Sep 2024) actuals. A half-year outturn and a full-year estimate for the same metric are different periods, so 6.4 vs 6.1 is not a conflict — the implied H2 growth is simply softer.

D2's 10.1 per cent is GFCF growth in H1 FY24 (Apr-Sep 2023), whereas D1's 6.1 per cent is full-year 2024-25. D2 itself frames the comparison as "a softening ... from 10.1 per cent in H1 FY24 to 6.4 per cent in H1 FY25", so the higher number belongs to an earlier period on a higher-investment base.

D1's 6.1 per cent is Gross Fixed Capital Formation growth for 2024-25; D3's 8.2 per cent is headline GDP growth for FY24. Different attribute (investment aggregate vs total output) and different fiscal year, so the resemblance of the two percentages is coincidental.

D2's 6.7 per cent is a single quarter (Q1 FY25, Apr-Jun 2024) at constant 2011-12 prices, alongside 5.4 per cent in Q2; D1's 6.5 per cent is the full-year 2024-25 second advance estimate. Quarterly outturns straddling the annual figure are consistent with it.

D3 (Delhivery FY24 report) cites 8.2 per cent GDP growth for FY24 (Apr 2023-Mar 2024); D1's 6.5 per cent is for 2024-25. Different fiscal years — indeed D1's own row shows 9.2 for the preceding year, the later revised FY24 figure — so no contradiction on the 2024-25 value.

Both are agriculture GVA growth for April 2024-March 2025: D2 gives 3.8 per cent from the First Advance Estimates (published 31 Jan 2025), D1 gives 4.6 per cent from the Second Advance Estimate at 2011-12 prices. The upward revision between estimate rounds — consistent with the strong kharif/rabi outturn — accounts for the 0.8 pp gap.

D2's 3.5 per cent is agriculture GVA growth in Q2 FY25 (Jul-Sep 2024) only; D1's 4.6 per cent is the full-year 2024-25 second advance estimate. D2 notes Q2 was itself "an improvement over the previous four quarters", so a stronger full-year figure driven by H2 is consistent.

D1's 4.6 per cent is the agriculture, forestry and fishing sub-sector's GVA growth; D2's 6.4 per cent is economy-wide real GVA growth for the same FY25. A sector with roughly 14-15 per cent weight (per D1's own share columns: 15.5/14.7/14.4) growing slower than the aggregate is expected, not contradictory.

D2's 6.2 per cent is total real GVA growth for H1 FY25, while D1's 4.6 per cent is agriculture-only GVA for full-year 2024-25. Both scope (one sector vs all sectors) and period (half-year vs full year) differ, so the figures are not measuring the same quantity.

D1's 30.3 per cent is gross savings for the whole economy expressed as a share of GNDI in 2023-24; D2's ~14 per cent is only the private corporate component, expressed as a share of GDP. A component measured against a different denominator sits inside the aggregate, so the two numbers are compatible rather than competing.

D1's 3.5 per cent is CPI-Combined inflation excluding food and fuel (core) for full-year 2024-25; D2's 3.2 per cent is headline CPI recomputed excluding only vegetables and pulses, for April-December FY25. The exclusion baskets and the periods both differ, so the near-identical magnitudes are different constructs, not a check on each other.

D1's 3.5 per cent measures CPI inflation excluding food and fuel — i.e. explicitly stripping food out. D2's 4.3 per cent is a food-inflation (CFPI) series excluding vegetables and pulses. The two indices cover disjoint parts of the basket, so they are not comparable attributes.

D1 reports core CPI (excluding food and fuel) at 3.5 per cent for 2024-25; D2's 6.5 per cent is food inflation excluding tomato, onion and potato for April-December FY25. One excludes food entirely and the other is a food-only index, so they measure different things.

D2's -0.7 per cent is WPI inflation for FY24 (Apr 2023-Mar 2024); D1's 2.3 per cent (provisional, 2011-12=100) is for 2024-25. D1's own series ends "... -0.7 2.3", i.e. it carries the identical -0.7 for the prior year and then 2.3 for the current one, confirming the two documents agree and differ only by period.

D1's USD 325,540 million is BoP merchandise exports f.o.b. for April-December 2024; D2's USD 602.6 billion for the same nine months is merchandise plus services combined. The residual, 602.6 - 325.5 = USD 277.1 billion, is a plausible services-export figure for the period, so the two are consistent at different scopes.

Same nine-month window (Apr-Dec 2024): D2 states total exports of merchandise and services at USD 602.6 billion, while D1's appendix reports goods exports f.o.b. alone at USD 325,540 million (USD 325.5 billion). Goods-only versus goods-plus-services explains the entire difference.

D2's USD 4-5 billion is an estimate of e-commerce exports in FY23, a narrow channel-specific subset of an earlier year. D1's USD 325,540 million is total BoP merchandise exports for April-December 2024. Different period and vastly different scope; no meaningful comparison.

D1's USD 552,767 million is BoP merchandise imports c.i.f. for April-December 2024; D2's USD 682.2 billion for the first nine months of FY25 covers merchandise plus services. The gap, 682.2 - 552.8 = USD 129.4 billion, is a reasonable services-import total for nine months, so the scopes explain the difference.

Both cover April-December 2024. D2's USD 682.2 billion is explicitly "merchandise and services combined", whereas D1's USD 552,767 million is goods imports c.i.f. on the BoP. Same period, different aggregation (and c.i.f. goods valuation), so the figures are compatible.

D2's USD 352.1 billion is non-oil, non-gold imports for the first nine months of FY25 — a subset of D1's USD 552,767 million total merchandise imports c.i.f. for the same April-December 2024 window. The USD ~200 billion residual corresponds to petroleum and gold/silver imports, so the two nest consistently.

D2's USD 340.5 billion is non-oil, non-gold imports for April-December FY24 (2023), while D1's USD 552,767 million is all merchandise imports c.i.f. for April-December 2024. Both the commodity coverage and the year differ, so the values are not expected to match.

D2's 5.2 per cent is a YoY growth rate for merchandise imports over April-December FY25; D1's USD 552,767 million is a level. Different attribute (rate vs value), so they cannot corroborate or contradict each other directly.

D1's -USD 227,227 million is the BoP merchandise trade balance for April-December 2024 (552,767 imports less 325,540 exports = 227,227 deficit). D2's USD 79.5 billion is the overall deficit including services (682.2 - 602.6 = 79.6, matching within rounding). Goods-only versus goods-plus-services fully explains the gap; the services surplus of roughly USD 148 billion bridges them.

D2's USD 69.7 billion is the overall (merchandise plus services) trade deficit for April-December 2023, while D1's -USD 227,227 million is the merchandise-only deficit for April-December 2024. Both period and scope differ, so the figures are not alternative measurements of the same quantity.

D2's USD 704.9 billion is a stock of foreign exchange reserves as of September 2024; D1's -USD 227,227 million is a flow, the merchandise trade balance over April-December 2024. Different attributes (reserve stock vs trade flow), matched only by both being USD BoP-adjacent figures.
Same attribute key 'real_gdp_growth', same period 2024-04-01..2025-03-31, same unit %; values 6.5 percent (none) and 6.5 per cent (none) agree within 0.00% after scale normalisation.
Same attribute key 'real_gdp_growth', same period 2024-04-01..2025-03-31, same unit %; values 6.5 (none) and 6.5 per cent (none) agree within 0.00% after scale normalisation.
Same attribute key 'foreign_exchange_reserves', same period 2025-03-31..2025-03-31, same unit USD; values 668 (billion) and US$ 668.3 billion (billion) agree within 0.04% after scale normalisation.

Both report the same figure for the same period and definition: D3 says core inflation was a "3.5 percent FY2024/25 average" and D1 says core (CPI excluding food and fuel) inflation moderated "to 3.5 per cent" in 2024-25. FY2024/25 in the IMF's notation and 2024-25 in the RBI's are the identical April 2024–March 2025 year.

The values differ (3.5% vs 4.3%) only because the periods differ: D3's 3.5% is the FY2024/25 average, while D1's 4.3% is explicitly the prior year, 2023-24. D1's own sentence links them — core "eased to 3.5 per cent during 2024-25 from 4.3 per cent a year ago" — so the two are consecutive points on the same series, not a disagreement.

Different attributes of the CPI basket: D3's 3.5% is core inflation (CPI excluding food and fuel), whereas D1's 6.7% is CPI food-group inflation for 2024-25. Core inflation by construction excludes the food component, so the two figures are not comparable measures.

D3 reports core CPI inflation (3.5%, FY2024/25); D1's 7.0% is CPI food-group inflation for the earlier year 2023-24. Both the attribute (core vs food) and the period differ, so this is a false match rather than a comparable pair.

D3's 3.5% is aggregate core CPI inflation over FY2024/25; D1's (-)2.7% is a single-month (March 2025) reading for pulses, a sub-item weighting 5.2% of CPI food and beverages — which core inflation excludes entirely. Different attribute and different period.

D3's 5.2 percent is a single month (September 2025) from the monthly PLFS, which measures unemployment on the current weekly status; D2's 3.2 per cent is the annual PLFS unemployment rate for persons aged 15+ on usual (principal plus subsidiary) status for 2023-24. Usual status consistently yields a lower rate than weekly status, and the periods are more than a year apart, so the gap is definitional and temporal rather than a disagreement.

D2's 6 per cent is the 2017-18 PLFS usual-status rate for ages 15+, quoted as the start of a declining series ending at 3.2 per cent in 2023-24; D3's 5.2 percent is a September 2025 monthly reading on a different (current weekly status) basis. Seven years and a different survey basis separate them, so they are not competing measurements of the same quantity.

Both cover general government (Centre plus States) for 2024-25, but D1's 7.6 per cent is explicitly a budget-estimate basis ("2024-25 (BE)") while D3, written in November 2025, says the deficit "is estimated to have fallen to 7.9 percent of GDP" using IMF staff's own definition of the general government balance. The 0.3 pp gap reflects a budgeted target versus a later staff estimate of the outturn on a staff definition; to confirm, one would check the RBI/IMF definitional bridge (off-budget items, coverage of UTs).

Same period (2024-25) but different level of government: D3's 7.9 percent of GDP is the general government (Centre plus States) deficit, whereas D1's 4.7 per cent is the Centre alone on revised estimates. Adding D1's state GFD of about 3.6 per cent to the Centre's 4.7 per cent and netting intergovernmental flows lands close to the ~7.9 per cent general-government figure.

D1's 3.6 per cent of GDP is the gross fiscal deficit of 28 states and 3 UTs only, while D3's 7.9 percent of GDP for the same 2024-25 year covers the general government, i.e. states plus the Centre. The state figure is a component of, not an alternative to, the general-government total.

Both refer to 2024-25, but D1's 4.7 per cent is the Centre's GFD on Revised Estimates while D3's 7.9 percent is general government (Centre plus States). The two are different coverage levels of the same fiscal year, and the state deficit of roughly 3.6 per cent bridges most of the difference.

D1's 4.4 per cent is the Centre's Budget Estimate for 2025-26, a different government level and a later fiscal year than D3's 7.9 percent general-government estimate for FY2024/25. Both scope (Centre vs Centre plus States) and period differ, so the values are not in conflict.

Both are general-government (Centre plus States) fiscal deficit ratios, but D3's 8.1 percent of GDP is for FY2023/24 while D1's 7.6 per cent is for 2024-25 (BE). D3's own sentence describes the deficit falling from 8.1 percent in FY2023/24, so the lower 2024-25 number is the consecutive year, not a competing estimate.

D3's 8.1 percent of GDP is the general-government deficit for FY2023/24; D1's 4.7 per cent is the Central Government's GFD on revised estimates for the following year, 2024-25. Both the coverage (general government vs Centre only) and the fiscal year differ.

D1's 4.7 per cent is Centre-only GFD on Revised Estimates for 2024-25; D3's 8.1 percent covers general government (Centre plus States) for the earlier year FY2023/24. Different coverage and different year, so the figures measure different quantities.

D1's 3.6 per cent is the combined GFD of 28 states and 3 UTs in 2024-25; D3's 8.1 percent is the whole general government (states plus Centre) in FY2023/24. The state figure is one component of the general-government aggregate and refers to a different year.

D1's 4.4 per cent is the Centre's 2025-26 Budget Estimate, two fiscal years after the FY2023/24 general-government figure of 8.1 percent in D3, and covers only the central government rather than Centre plus States.

Both are the central government deficit for 2024-25, but D3 explicitly flags a definitional wedge: "4.9 percent of GDP (4.8 percent of GDP per the authorities' definition)". D1's 4.7 per cent is the RBI's reporting of the authorities' Revised Estimate, so the 0.2 pp gap combines the IMF staff adjustment (4.9 vs 4.8) with the RE-versus-outturn vintage difference.

D1's 4.7 per cent is the GFD in 2024-25 (RE) on the authorities' definition; D3's 4.9 percent is the same year on IMF staff's definition, which the same sentence contrasts with "4.8 percent of GDP per the authorities' definition". The difference is therefore an explicitly stated definitional adjustment plus the revised-estimate vintage, not a disagreement about the fiscal outturn.

D1's table gives the Centre's GFD as 4.7 per cent of GDP for 2024-25 (RE); D3 reports 4.9 percent on the staff definition while itself noting the authorities' figure is 4.8 percent. The gap is the staff-versus-authorities definitional adjustment layered on the RE-versus-actual vintage.

D3's 4.9 percent of GDP is the central government deficit for FY2024/25; D1's 4.4 per cent is the Centre's Budget Estimate for the following year, 2025-26. Consecutive fiscal years on a declining consolidation path, so the lower figure is not a contradiction.

D1's ₹2,473 thousand crore is a level figure for the combined Centre and State governments in 2024-25 (BE), while D3's 4.9 percent is a GDP ratio for the central government alone. Against 2024-25 nominal GDP of roughly ₹324 lakh crore, ₹2,473 thousand crore is about 7.6 per cent — the combined/general-government ratio, not the Centre's.

Both are the central government deficit for 2024-25 on the authorities' own definition: D3 gives 4.8 percent of GDP, D1 gives 4.7 per cent from the Revised Estimates. D3 was completed in November 2025, after the provisional actuals were available, so 4.8 reflects the outturn against the earlier 4.7 per cent RE.

D1 states the GFD was "4.7 per cent in 2024-25 (RE)" — a revised estimate published with the FY26 budget — while D3, finalised 6 November 2025, cites 4.8 percent of GDP "per the authorities' definition" for the same year. The 0.1 pp difference is the RE versus later provisional actual, on the same definition.

D1's appendix row "2024-25 (RE)" carries a Centre GFD of 4.7 per cent of GDP; D3 reports 4.8 percent for FY2024/25 on the authorities' definition. Same scope and definition, differing only because the IMF report post-dates the revised estimate and uses the settled outturn.

D3's 4.8 percent (authorities' definition) is FY2024/25; D1's 4.4 per cent is the Centre's 2025-26 Budget Estimate. The figures are consecutive years of the same series — D1 elsewhere describes "targeting the GFD at 4.4 per cent of GDP in 2025-26 (BE), down from 4.7 per cent in 2024-25 (RE)".

D1's ₹2,473 thousand crore is the combined Centre-plus-State gross fiscal deficit in rupee terms for 2024-25 (BE), whereas D3's 4.8 percent is a GDP ratio for the central government only. Different coverage and different units; the combined level corresponds to roughly 7.6 per cent of GDP, not 4.8 per cent.

Both cover central government capital spending in 2024-25, but D1's 4.0 per cent of GDP is explicitly "effective capital expenditure", which adds grants-in-aid to states for creation of capital assets to the Centre's own capital outlay, while D3's 3.2 percent of GDP is capital expenditure proper. The roughly 0.8 pp wedge is exactly the grants-in-aid component.

D1's 4.3 per cent of GDP is budgeted "effective capital expenditure" (capital outlay plus capital grants to states) for 2025-26, whereas D3's 3.2 percent is central capital expenditure proper in FY2024/25. Both the definition and the fiscal year differ, so the higher figure is not in conflict.

D3's 3.2 percent of GDP is central government capital expenditure in FY2024/25; D1's ₹1.5 lakh crore is a 2025-26 outlay for state governments' capital expenditure support. Different entity (Centre vs states), different year, and a rupee outlay rather than a GDP ratio.

D3's 6.5% is India's estimated *potential* growth rate 'over the medium term', a structural trend concept with no specific year; D1's 6.5% is the realised/estimated actual growth outturn for FY2024-25 (SAE). The numeric coincidence does not make them the same attribute or period.

Different attributes: D3 projects medium-term potential output growth ('returning to its potential rate of 6.5 percent'), whereas D1 states the actual 2024-25 outturn ('growth moderated to 6.5 per cent in 2024-25'). Same number, different concept and period.

D1's table row is measured expenditure-side GDP growth of 6.5% for 2024-25 (second advance estimate); D3's 6.5% is a medium-term potential-growth assumption, not an estimate of any particular fiscal year. Different attribute.

D1 reports the historical real GDP at market prices series ending 6.5% for 2024-25; D3 refers to potential (trend) growth of 6.5% over the medium term. Coincident values, different attributes and periods.

D2's 6.4% is the FY25 actual-year estimate (First Advance Estimates); D3's 6.5% is medium-term potential growth. Neither the attribute (actual vs potential) nor the period (FY25 vs medium term) matches, so the near-equal values are not evidence about each other.

D3 projects headline CPI inflation to average 2.8% in FY2025/26 (Apr 2025–Mar 2026); D1 reports the realised average of 4.6% for 2024-25 (Apr 2024–Mar 2025). Different fiscal years — a projected further disinflation, not a conflicting reading of the same year.
D1's 5.4% is the 2023-24 average headline CPI; D3's 2.8% is the projected FY2025/26 average. Two years apart on the same series, consistent with the declining path D1 itself describes (5.4% → 4.6%).

D1's 4.8% is a two-month CPI reading for April–May 2024; D3's 2.8% is a projected 12-month average for FY2025/26. Different (and non-overlapping) periods and different frequency, so the levels are not comparable as-is.
D1's 3.6% is the single-month July 2024 CPI print; D3's 2.8% is a projected annual average for FY2025/26. Monthly outturn vs forward annual average — different period and basis.

D1's 6.2% is the October 2024 monthly CPI spike (food-driven), while D3's 2.8% is an average projection for FY2025/26. A monthly peak inside 2024-25 does not contradict a lower average projected for a later year.

D3 expects headline inflation to converge to 4% in FY2026/27; D1 records a 4.6% average for 2024-25. Two different fiscal years on the same CPI-Combined series — a forward convergence projection versus a past-year average.

D1's 5.4% is the 2023-24 headline CPI average; D3's 4% is the projected FY2026/27 outcome. Three years apart, and D1's own 5.4% → 4.6% path is consistent with further convergence toward the 4% target.
D1's 4.8% covers April–May 2024 only; D3's 4% is a projected annual figure for FY2026/27. Different periods and frequencies (bi-monthly print vs projected annual convergence level).
D1's 3.6% is the July 2024 monthly reading; D3's 4% is the FY2026/27 projected convergence to target. Non-overlapping periods and different basis (monthly outturn vs annual projection).

D1's 6.2% is an October 2024 monthly print above the tolerance mid-point; D3's 4% is projected for FY2026/27. Different periods — a single 2024 month cannot conflict with a projected average two fiscal years later.

D3 projects a CAD of 1.0% of GDP for FY2025/26 (Apr 2025–Mar 2026); D1 reports an actual 1.3% of GDP for April–December 2024. Different periods (forward full-year projection vs a nine-month outturn inside 2024-25), and D3 attributes the change to weaker exports and REER under U.S. tariffs.

D1's 1.1% of GDP covers April–December 2023; D3's 1.0% of GDP is a projection for FY2025/26. Same ratio concept, but the periods are two years apart and one is an actual nine-month figure, the other a projected full year.

D1 gives the CAD in levels (US$37.1 billion) for April–December 2024, while D3 gives a ratio (1.0% of GDP) projected for FY2025/26. Different periods and different units (USD billions vs percent of GDP); D1's own parenthetical shows US$37.1bn = 1.3% of GDP for its window.

D1's US$30.7 billion is the April–December 2023 CAD level (1.1% of GDP); D3's 1.0% of GDP is a projected FY2025/26 ratio. Two years apart and expressed in different units, so the figures are not directly comparable.

D2 reports an actual CAD of 1.2% of GDP for Q2 FY25 (Jul–Sep 2024); D3 projects 1.0% of GDP for the full year FY2025/26. A single quarter of 2024-25 versus a projected annual ratio one fiscal year later.

D2's 1.2% of GDP is a single-quarter figure (Q2 FY25, Jul–Sep 2024); D1's 1.3% of GDP is the cumulative April–December 2024 ratio. The nine-month window contains but is wider than the quarter, so 1.2% and 1.3% are consistent readings of different aggregation periods.

D2's 1.2% of GDP refers to Q2 FY25 (Jul–Sep 2024); D1's 1.1% of GDP refers to April–December 2023. Different years and different aggregation windows, so the small gap reflects period, not disagreement.

D1 states the CAD level of US$37.1 billion for April–December 2024; D2 gives 1.2% of GDP for Q2 FY25 alone. Different units (level vs ratio) and different windows — the quarter is a subset of D1's nine-month period.
D1's US$30.7 billion (1.1% of GDP) covers April–December 2023; D2's 1.2% of GDP covers Q2 FY25 (Jul–Sep 2024). Different fiscal years, different window lengths and different units of expression.

Both state the central government deficit target for FY2025/26 (= 2025-26) as 4.4 percent of GDP: D3 'the central government's deficit target of 4.4 percent of GDP' and D1 'targeting the GFD at 4.4 per cent of GDP in 2025-26 (BE)'. D3 explicitly flags this as the authorities' definition, matching the Indian budget's GFD.

D1's appendix row for 2025-26 (BE) shows Gross Fiscal Deficit of 4.4 per cent of GDP for the Centre, the same figure and period as D3's 'deficit target of 4.4 percent of GDP' on the authorities' definition for FY2025/26.

D3's 4.4% is the FY2025/26 target; D1's 4.7% is the 2024-25 Revised Estimate. These are consecutive years on the same measure, and D1's own sentence spells out the path: 4.4% in 2025-26 (BE), 'down from 4.7 per cent in 2024-25 (RE)'.

D4's 9.7 is the table entry for real GDP at market prices in 2021/22 (the post-COVID rebound year); D2's 6.4 per cent is FY25. Different fiscal years four years apart.

9.7 percent refers to FY2021/22 in the IMF's selected-indicators row ('9.7 7.6 9.2 6.5 6.6 6.2'), whose FY2024/25 slot is 6.5; D2's 6.4 per cent is the FY25 advance estimate. The 9.7 figure simply belongs to a different year.
D4's 9.7 is full-year 2021/22 growth; D2's 6.0 per cent is H1 FY25 (Apr–Sep 2024). Different years and different spans.

Both describe the same disinflation in India: D4 says 'Headline inflation has declined markedly, driven by subdued food prices' and D2 says 'retail inflation eased in FY25'. Headline CPI and retail inflation are the same series, and both attribute the easing to food/policy factors.
Both state 6.5 per cent real GDP growth for the year ended 31 March 2025 — D4 as an outturn, D1 on Second Advance Estimates. Identical value, identical period.
D1 says the economy 'grown by 6.5 per cent in 2024-25' at constant prices and D4 cites 'economic growth of 6.5 percent in FY2024/25'. Same period (Apr 2024–Mar 2025) and same number.

D4's 6.5 percent is FY2024/25; D1's 9.2 per cent is explicitly the prior-year comparator, 2023-24 ('9.2 per cent a year ago'). Consistent with D4's own indicator row, which shows 9.2 for 2023/24 followed by 6.5 for 2024/25.
D4's 7.8 percent covers Q1 FY2025/26 (Apr–Jun 2025); D1's 6.5 per cent covers full-year 2024-25. A single quarter of the following year versus the prior full year.
7.8 percent is a Q1 FY2025/26 y/y outturn; 6.5 per cent is the Second Advance Estimate for full-year 2024-25. Different periods and different aggregation, so both can hold.

Both are projections for the same year (Apr 2025–Mar 2026): RBI's Annual Report puts it at 6.5 per cent 'with risks evenly balanced', the IMF at 6.6 percent under a baseline of prolonged 50% U.S. tariffs. The forecasts were made by different institutions at different times (RBI's FY25 Annual Report vs an IMF staff report completed 6 Nov 2025), and 0.1pp is within normal forecast revision.

D4's 6.2 percent is for FY2026/27 (Apr 2026–Mar 2027); D1's 6.5 per cent projection is for 2025-26 (Apr 2025–Mar 2026). D4's own sentence shows 6.6 for FY2025/26 'before moderating to 6.2 percent in FY2026/27', so the years differ.
D4's 9.7 is the 2021/22 entry in the real GDP (market prices) series; D1's 6.5 per cent is 2024-25. Different fiscal years — indeed D4's same row lists 6.5 in the FY2024/25 position, matching D1.
9.7 percent belongs to FY2021/22 in D4's indicator table; D1's 6.5 per cent (SAE) is FY2024-25. The values refer to years three fiscal years apart.

Both assess the same condition over roughly the same window: D4 says the financial and corporate sectors 'remained resilient, supported by adequate capital buffers and multi-year low non-performing assets'; D1 says the financial sector 'remained resilient and robust' on 'improved asset quality and capital buffers'. Same claim about capital buffers and asset quality.

D4's statement concerns the financial and corporate sectors (capital buffers, NPAs); D1's concerns the external sector (current account deficit, forex reserves, capital-flow volatility). Different attributes of the economy, matched only by the shared word 'resilience'.

Both point the same direction on monetary policy: D1 records the MPC changing 'the stance from neutral to accommodative' in April 2025, and D4's Directors judged there 'would likely be scope for further monetary easing amid benign inflation dynamics'. D4's word 'further' is consistent with the easing already begun in D1; strictly they describe an action versus a Board view, so this is directional agreement rather than an identical datum.

D3 cites an RBI projection of 7.2% for FY25 (Apr 2024–Mar 2025), made around Delhivery's FY24 annual report; D4 projects 6.6 percent for FY2025/26. Different target years and different forecasters, and the FY25 outturn later came in at 6.5%.
D3's 7.2% is an RBI forecast for FY25; D4's 6.2 percent is an IMF projection for FY2026/27 — two fiscal years apart, by different institutions and vintages.

Both cite RBI projections, but for different years and vintages: 7.2% for FY25 (as quoted in Delhivery's FY24 annual report, i.e. an RBI forecast made during 2024) versus 6.5 per cent for 2025-26 in the RBI's own FY25 Annual Report.

Both concern FY25 (Apr 2024–Mar 2025): D3 quotes an RBI forecast of 7.2% made during 2024, while D2's 6.4 per cent is the First Advance Estimate of 31 Jan 2025 based on actual data through the year. A mid-year forecast versus a later official estimate explains the gap.

The 7.2% figure is an RBI projection for FY25 cited in Delhivery's FY24 report; the 6.4 per cent is the FAE for the same FY25 at constant prices. Forecast versus subsequent estimate of the same period — growth undershot the earlier RBI projection (final outturn 6.5%).

D3's 7.2% is a full-year FY25 RBI projection; D2's 6.0 per cent is the realized H1 FY25 (Apr–Sep 2024) growth. Different spans and different vintages — the weaker first half is precisely why the 7.2% forecast was not met.

Both describe the aggregate/consolidated state-government fiscal deficit for FY2025-26 (Apr 2025-Mar 2026). D3 says deficits are "expected to return to about 3 percent of GDP on aggregate in FY2025/26"; D1 says the "consolidated GFD budgeted at 3.3 per cent of GDP" for 2025-26. The IMF's deliberately approximate "about 3 percent" is consistent with the states' budgeted 3.3 per cent, so these agree within the looseness of the IMF phrasing.

Same subject and scope (consolidated state governments' GFD as % of GDP) but different fiscal years: D3's "about 3 percent of GDP" is for FY2025/26, while D1's 3.2 per cent budget estimate is for 2024-25. The values are also mutually consistent as a small year-on-year path, so the gap is purely the period.

D3 projects state GFD of about 3 percent of GDP for FY2025/26; D1's 3.6 per cent (28 states + 3 UTs) is a 2024-25 figure from the appendix series "2.7 2.3 2.8 2.7 3.0 3.6". Different years, and D1 itself shows the 2025-26 budgeted level lower (3.3 per cent), so the difference is the reference period rather than a disagreement.

Both refer to the aggregate state fiscal deficit, but D3 gives about 3 percent of GDP for FY2025/26 while D1's Table II.6.2 gives ₹10.4 lakh crore for 2024-25 (BE) — a different year and a different unit (rupee level vs share of GDP). At roughly ₹324 lakh crore nominal GDP, ₹10.4 lakh crore is about 3.2 per cent, which is in the same range once converted.

D3's "about 3 percent of GDP" is the aggregate of state governments only for FY2025/26. D1's ₹2,473 thousand crore is the combined central-plus-state gross fiscal deficit for 2024-25 (BE), a different entity coverage, a different year, and a rupee level rather than a ratio. The apparent match is only on the words "fiscal deficit".

D3's 9.0 percent of GDP is central-government total revenues projected for FY2025/26. D1's ₹9,650 thousand crore is Total Receipts of the combined central and state governments for 2024-25 (BE) — roughly 30 per cent of GDP once converted. Different entity coverage, different year and different measure; the pair matches only on the word "total".

Both cover 2024-25, but D3's 9.2 percent of GDP is central-government total revenues on the IMF's presentation, whereas D1's ₹9,650 thousand crore is combined central + state Total Receipts (≈30 per cent of GDP at ~₹324 lakh crore nominal GDP). Different entity coverage and a different aggregate, not two readings of one figure.

D3's 2.9 is a level — GST revenue as a percent of GDP projected for FY2025/26. D1's 10.4 is a year-on-year growth rate of GST revenue in Q4 of 2024-25 (from the series "11.6 10.6 12.9 11.5 10.1 8.9 8.3 10.4"). Different attributes (share of GDP vs growth) and different periods.

D3's 13.4 percent of GDP is central-government total expenditure projected for FY2025/26; D1's 30.0 per cent is general-government (Centre plus states) total expenditure for 2024-25 (BE), described as a "moderation in total expenditure to 30.0 per cent of GDP from 30.2 per cent". Adding state spending roughly doubles the ratio, so the gap is coverage (plus a one-year difference), not a conflict.

D3 reports central-government total expenditure (13.4 percent of GDP, FY2025/26 projection); D1 reports combined central+state Total Receipts of ₹9,650 thousand crore for 2024-25 (BE). Expenditure versus receipts is a different attribute, on a different entity coverage, in a different unit and year.

D3's figure is fiscal — central-government total expenditure at 13.4 percent of GDP for FY2025/26. D2's USD 682.2 billion is merchandise/total imports in the first nine months of FY25, an external-sector flow. The only shared word is "total".

D3 gives a fiscal ratio (total central expenditure, 13.4 percent of GDP, FY2025/26 projection); D2 gives the 6.9 per cent year-on-year growth of India's total imports in April-December FY25. Different attribute, different sector, different period.

D1's ₹9,650 thousand crore is combined government Total Receipts for 2024-25 (BE); D2's USD 682.2 billion is India's total imports over April-December 2024. Government revenue and merchandise imports are unrelated attributes that merely share the label "total".

Both concern 2025-26 capital spending but on different entities and different aggregates: D3's 3.0 percent of GDP is total central-government capital expenditure (≈₹11 lakh crore), while D1's ₹1.5 lakh crore is a specific state-directed capex outlay ("continued in 2025-26, with total outlay of ₹1.5 lakh crore"). One is not a restatement of the other.

D3's 3.0 percent of GDP is budgetary capital expenditure by the central government in FY2025/26. D2's USD 30.5 billion is net capital inflows in the balance of payments for Q2 FY25. "Capital" is the only overlap; the attributes, units and periods all differ.

D3 measures central-government capital expenditure (3.0 percent of GDP, FY2025/26 projection); D2's USD 12.8 billion is net capital inflows in Q2 FY24 (Jul-Sep 2023). Fiscal spending versus balance-of-payments inflows, in different units and different years.

D1's ₹1.5 lakh crore is a 2025-26 capital-expenditure outlay for states; D2's USD 30.5 billion is net capital inflows into India in Q2 FY25 (Jul-Sep 2024). Different attribute (fiscal outlay vs external financing flow), different unit and different period.

D3's 5.5 percent is the central-government fiscal deficit for FY2023/24 (actual); D1's 4.7 per cent is the 2024-25 Revised Estimate. Notably D1's own series "3.7 5.4 3.7 6.5 5.5 4.7" carries 5.5 in the column immediately preceding 4.7, i.e. it also puts 2023-24 at 5.5 — so the two agree once the years are aligned.

Different fiscal years for the same measure: D3 reports 5.5 percent of GDP as the FY2023/24 outturn, while D1 states the GFD was "4.7 per cent in 2024-25 (RE)". The decline from 5.5 to 4.7 is the consolidation path both documents describe, not a disagreement.

D3's 5.5 percent refers to FY2023/24; D1's appendix row "2024-25 (RE)# 1.3 1.8 -1.6 4.7 55.3 56.0" gives 4.7 per cent for 2024-25 Revised Estimates. Same Centre-level GFD-to-GDP concept, one year apart.

D3's 5.5 percent is the FY2023/24 actual central fiscal deficit; D1's 4.4 per cent is the 2025-26 Budget Estimate ("2025-26 (BE) 0.8 1.5 -2.1 4.4 55.5 56.0"). Two years apart on a declining consolidation path, so the values are not comparable as a same-period claim.

D3's 5.5 percent of GDP is the central government's deficit in FY2023/24; D1's ₹2,473 thousand crore is the combined central-and-state gross fiscal deficit for 2024-25 (BE). Different entity coverage, different unit (rupee level vs ratio) and different year.

Both refer to the central-government fiscal deficit for 2024-25: D3 puts it at 4.9 percent of GDP (flagged as an estimate on the IMF definition), D1 at 4.7 per cent on the Indian Revised Estimates basis. IMF staff restate India's accounts on their own GFS-style coverage (and D3, completed November 2025, works from the later outturn rather than the RE), which accounts for the 0.2pp gap; to confirm one would check the IMF table's definitional footnote against the Budget's GFD definition.

Same year (2024-25), same nominal measure: D3's 4.9 percent (IMF definition, estimate) versus D1's "4.7 per cent in 2024-25 (RE)". The IMF presents the central deficit on its own coverage and from a later vintage (report completed 6 Nov 2025) than the Revised Estimates the RBI cites, which explains the 0.2 percentage point difference.

D3 reports 4.9 percent of GDP for FY2024/25 on the IMF definition; D1's appendix row "2024-25 (RE)# ... 4.7 ..." gives 4.7 per cent of GDP on the Budget's Revised Estimates. Identical period and entity, so the gap turns on the IMF's own fiscal coverage and its later data vintage rather than on a factual disagreement.

D3's 4.9 percent is the FY2024/25 estimate; D1's 4.4 per cent is the 2025-26 Budget Estimate. Consecutive years on a declining deficit path, so the values are not competing statements about the same period.

D3's 4.9 percent of GDP covers the central government only; D1's ₹2,473 thousand crore is the combined central-and-state gross fiscal deficit for 2024-25 (BE), a rupee level for a wider entity. Different coverage and different units, so the two numbers are not measuring the same quantity.

Both are forward-looking central-deficit figures for 2025-26: D3 projects 4.5 percent of GDP (IMF staff projection on the IMF definition, under a prolonged 50% U.S. tariff baseline), while D1 cites the government's own Budget Estimate of 4.4 per cent. A staff projection restated on IMF coverage sitting 0.1pp above the authorities' budget target is a definition/basis difference, not a conflicting claim.

D3's 4.5 percent is a projection for FY2025/26; D1's 4.7 per cent is the 2024-25 Revised Estimate. Different fiscal years on the same declining path (D1 itself notes the target falls from 4.7 per cent in 2024-25 to 4.4 per cent in 2025-26).

D3 projects 4.5 percent of GDP for FY2025/26, whereas D1's 4.7 per cent is explicitly "in 2024-25 (RE)" within the sentence that also targets 4.4 per cent for 2025-26. The two numbers belong to different years.

D3's 4.5 percent is the FY2025/26 staff projection; D1's appendix row labelled "2024-25 (RE)#" gives 4.7 per cent for the preceding year. Same Centre-level GFD ratio, one year apart, so no same-period disagreement.

D3's 4.5 percent of GDP is a central-government projection for FY2025/26; D1's ₹2,473 thousand crore is the combined central-and-state gross fiscal deficit for 2024-25 (BE). Different entity coverage, different unit and different year.

D3's $668bn is the March 2025 stock; D2's $704.9bn is the September 2024 peak, six months earlier. D3 in the same sentence describes exactly this move ("declined to $668 billion in March 2025, from $706 billion in September 2024"), so the two are consecutive points on one series, not competing values. The small gap between D3's $706bn and D2's $704.9bn for September 2024 is a rounding/reference-date nuance (peak weekly vs month-end reading), not a disagreement.

$668bn is dated March 2025 (D3); $640.3bn is dated end-December 2024 (D2, published 31 Jan 2025). The two dates are three months apart on a series both documents describe as falling from the Sept-2024 peak and then partly recovering, so the values differ only because the observation dates differ.

Same series, different observation dates: D3's $668bn is March 2025, D2's "moderated to USD 640.3 billion as of the end of December 2024" is a quarter earlier. D2 was published 31 Jan 2025 and could not have observed the March 2025 level; no conflict.

D2 reports $634.6bn on the weekly reference date 3 January 2025; D3 reports $668bn for March 2025, roughly three months later. Both sit on the same declining-then-recovering path D3 describes; the difference is the observation date, not the measure.
D2's $616.7bn is the end-January 2024 starting point of the run-up it describes; D3's $668bn is March 2025, fourteen months later. Different points on the same reserves series.

D3's $695bn is dated October 2025; D1's US$ 668.3bn is dated end-March 2025, seven months earlier. D3 (published Nov 2025) reports the later stock, and its own March-2025 figure ($668bn) matches D1's 668.3, confirming the two are consistent points on one series rather than rival estimates.
