$695bn is an October 2025 observation (D3, published Nov 2025); $640.3bn is end-December 2024 (D2, published Jan 2025). Ten months apart on the same series, and D2 predates the later reading entirely.

Same reserves series measured ten months apart: D2's $640.3bn is "as of the end of December 2024", D3's $695bn is "as of October" 2025. The gap is elapsed time (reserve accumulation through 2025), not a measurement dispute.

D2's $704.9bn is the September 2024 peak; D3's $695bn is October 2025, thirteen months later after the intervening drawdown to ~$668bn in March 2025 and partial rebuild. Different observation dates on one series.
D2's $634.6bn is the weekly reading for 3 January 2025; D3's $695bn is October 2025, some 22 months of series movement later. Values differ because the dates differ.
D2's $616.7bn is end-January 2024; D3's $695bn is October 2025, about 21 months later. Both are point-in-time stocks of the same headline reserves measure at widely separated dates.

D3's 0.2% of GDP is for 2025Q2 (Apr-Jun 2025, i.e. Q1 of FY2025/26); D1's 1.3% of GDP covers April-December 2024 of FY2024-25. Different, non-overlapping windows a year apart, and a single quarter versus a nine-month cumulative — both describe a contained CAD, so no dispute.

0.2% of GDP is D3's figure for Apr-Jun 2025; 1.1% is D1's prior-year comparator for April-December 2023. The windows are two years apart and of different length (one quarter vs nine months), so the levels are not comparable point estimates of the same thing.

D3 states the CAD as a ratio (0.2 percent of GDP, 2025Q2); D1 states it as a level (US$ 37.1 billion, April-December 2024, which it itself equates to 1.3 per cent of GDP). The figures differ in both denominator/unit (US$ bn vs % of GDP) and period (one quarter of FY2025/26 vs nine months of FY2024-25), so they measure different quantities rather than disagreeing.

D1's US$ 30.7 billion is a nine-month level for April-December 2023 (1.1 per cent of GDP in its own words); D3's 0.2 percent is a ratio for the single quarter Apr-Jun 2025. Different unit and different, non-overlapping period — not competing values.

Both are quarterly CAD-to-GDP ratios but for different quarters under different labelling conventions: D3's "2025Q2" is the calendar quarter Apr-Jun 2025 (Q1 of FY2025/26) at 0.2%, while D2's "Q2 of FY24" is Jul-Sep 2023 at 1.3%. Two years apart, so the gap is period, reinforced by a naming-convention difference (calendar vs Indian fiscal quarter).

D1 reports a level (US$ 37.1 billion for April-December 2024, equal to 1.3 per cent of GDP); D2 reports a ratio (1.3 per cent for Q2 FY24, Jul-Sep 2023). Different unit and different period — the coincident 1.3 per cent figures refer to different windows.

D1's US$ 30.7 billion is the April-December 2023 CAD level (1.1 per cent of GDP); D2's 1.3 per cent is the CAD/GDP ratio for the single quarter Jul-Sep 2023 within that window. Unit and aggregation window both differ, so the two are complementary rather than conflicting.

D3's 6.6 per cent is a staff projection for FY2025/26 (Apr 2025-Mar 2026), explicitly forward-looking and conditioned on the 2025Q2 outturn and GST reform; D2's 6.4 per cent is the First Advance Estimate for FY25 (Apr 2024-Mar 2025). Consecutive, non-overlapping fiscal years.

6.6 per cent is D3's FY2025/26 projection; 6.4 per cent is D2's first-advance-estimate growth for FY25 (year ended March 2025). The two refer to different fiscal years one apart, so the values are not comparable as rival estimates.

D2's 6.0 per cent is an actual for H1 FY25 only (Apr-Sep 2024); D3's 6.6 per cent is a full-year projection for FY2025/26. Different span (half-year vs full year) and different year, so the gap is period, not disagreement.

D1's 6.5 per cent is the outturn for 2024-25 ("growth moderated to 6.5 per cent in 2024-25"); D3's 6.6 per cent is a projection for the following year FY2025/26. Adjacent fiscal years, one actual and one forecast.

D1's 6.5 per cent is on a Second Advance Estimates basis for 2024-25; D3's 6.6 per cent is a baseline staff projection for FY2025/26. Different years and different bases (estimate of a completed year vs forecast of the next).

D1 records 6.5 per cent growth at constant prices for 2024-25; D3 projects 6.6 per cent for FY2025/26. The near-identical numbers refer to different fiscal years, so this is a period separation rather than corroboration.

D1's 9.2 per cent is the 2023-24 comparator (constant prices); D3's 6.6 per cent is the FY2025/26 projection. Two fiscal years apart, with the intervening moderation to ~6.5 per cent in 2024-25 documented in D1 itself.

D3's 6.2 per cent is a staff projection for FY2026/27 (Apr 2026-Mar 2027) under an assumption of persistent high U.S. tariffs; D2's 6.4 per cent is the First Advance Estimate for FY25. Two fiscal years apart and different basis (forecast vs advance estimate).
6.2 per cent is D3's FY2026/27 baseline projection; 6.4 per cent is D2's FY25 first advance estimate. Different fiscal years, so the values are not measuring the same quantity.
D2's 6.0 per cent covers only the first half of FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024) as an actual; D3's 6.2 per cent is a full-year projection for FY2026/27. Different span and different year.

D1's 6.5 per cent is the 2024-25 outturn; D3's 6.2 per cent is a projection two fiscal years later (FY2026/27), which D3 explains as a tariff-driven decline from its 6.6 per cent FY2025/26 forecast. Sequential periods, not a disputed value.

D1 reports 6.5 per cent for 2024-25 on Second Advance Estimates; D3 projects 6.2 per cent for FY2026/27. Different years and different bases (estimate of a completed year vs a conditional staff forecast).
D1's 6.5 per cent constant-price growth is for 2024-25; D3's 6.2 per cent is a FY2026/27 baseline projection. The two-year separation, plus D3's stated tariff assumption, accounts for the difference.
D1's 9.2 per cent is the 2023-24 comparator at constant prices; D3's 6.2 per cent is a projection for FY2026/27, three fiscal years later. Entirely different periods and one is a forecast.

D4 describes the policy framework ("the 4-percent target with ±2 percent band on headline inflation"), i.e. a target definition, while D1 reports an outturn ("Headline inflation moderated to an average of 4.6 per cent during 2024-25"). One is a mandated target, the other a realised average, so they are different attributes and cannot corroborate or conflict. The 4.6% outturn is in fact inside the 2-6% band, but that is consistency of a figure with a rule, not two documents reporting the same fact.

D4's "4-percent target with ±2 percent band" is the inflation-targeting mandate; D1's "6.2 per cent in October 2024" is a single monthly CPI print. Different attributes (target vs monthly outturn) and D4 gives no period, so no same-fact comparison is possible. Note the October print sits marginally above the 6% upper tolerance band, but neither document is asserting a conflicting value.

D4 states the framework parameter (4% target, ±2% band); D1 reports a realised monthly reading of "3.6 per cent in July 2024". Target definition versus a monthly CPI-Combined outturn are different attributes, so the pair is a false match.

D4's fact is the policy target band on headline inflation; D1's is the April-May 2024 CPI outturn of "4.8 per cent". A mandate and a two-month average print are different attributes measured over different (in D4's case, unspecified) periods.

D4 describes the 4% ±2% flexible inflation targeting framework; D1 reports that "Headline inflation eased to 3.3 per cent in March 2025". These are a target and an outturn respectively — different attributes, not competing measurements of the same quantity.

D4 (Staff Report completed Nov 2025) says "India remains the fastest-growing major economy" and D1 says for 2024-25 "India remained the fastest growing large economy". The claims are identical in substance, differing only in the wording "major" vs "large" economy, and D4's present-tense statement follows directly on its FY2024/25 outturn of 6.5 percent — the same year D1 is characterising.

D1 says India is "poised to remain the fastest-growing major economy in 2025-26"; D4, written in November 2025 (i.e. inside FY2025/26, projecting 6.6% for that year), asserts that "India remains the fastest-growing major economy". D4 therefore confirms in-year what D1 stated prospectively for the same fiscal year, with identical wording ("fastest-growing major economy").

The two describe opposite directions for net FDI: D2 (published 31 Jan 2025) says that over April-November 2024 "net FDI inflows declined relative to April-November 2023 due to a rise in repatriation/disinvestment", while D4 (Nov 2025) says "net inward FDI has shown signs of recovery as gross inflows picked up and repatriation/disinvestment edged down" in recent quarters. The windows do not overlap in substance — D2 covers the first eight months of FY25, D4 the quarters up to mid/late 2025 — and the stated driver flips in exactly the way the timing implies (repatriation rising in D2's window, edging down in D4's).

On the gross component both documents point the same way: D2 says "Gross foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows have shown signs of revival in the first eight months of FY25" and D4 says net FDI is recovering "as gross inflows picked up". The periods are adjacent rather than identical (Apr-Nov 2024 vs D4's unspecified recent quarters to 2025), so this is corroboration of a persisting direction, not of a single measured value.

D2 reports "Gross FDI inflows have shown a higher growth in the first eight months of FY25 compared to the corresponding period of the previous year", and D4 records that "gross inflows picked up" as part of the net FDI recovery. Same subject and same direction of movement in gross FDI; the difference is only that D4's window is later and unspecified.

D1 says "Inflation eased and moved below the target by the end of the year" (2024-25) while D4 says "Inflation has been generally within the target range". These are compatible once the two senses of "target" are separated: the point target is 4 percent, while the target range is the 2-6 percent tolerance band D4 itself describes elsewhere (4 percent ±2). D1's March 2025 print of 3.3 per cent is below 4 percent yet still inside the 2-6 band, so both statements hold simultaneously.

D2 states "retail inflation eased in FY25" and D4 states "Food prices have eased significantly, largely reflecting deflation in vegetable prices". They are not the same series — D2 refers to headline retail (CPI) inflation, D4 to the food component — but they point the same way and food is the dominant driver of Indian headline CPI, so D4's observation supports D2's. Confidence is limited because D4 gives no period and the component is narrower than D2's aggregate.

D4's claim is about the absolute volume of emissions ("India is the third largest emitter globally, while its per capital emissions are low"), whereas D1's is a composite policy-and-performance score ("Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI) 2025, which ranked India among the top 10 high performers"). Different metrics on different scales: being a large aggregate emitter and scoring well on the CCPI (which weights per-capita emissions, renewables and policy) are not competing statements about the same attribute.

D4 reports nominal GDP of USD 3,638 billion for FY2023/24 (year ended March 2024), while D3 cites the IMF for "India's GDP was US$3.9 trillion in 2024", which on the IMF's India convention is the year ended March 2025. A rise from ~USD 3.64 trillion to ~USD 3.9 trillion (about 7 percent in dollar terms) is consistent with one further year of nominal growth, so the gap is a period difference, not a disagreement.

D4's 3,638 is aggregate nominal GDP in USD billions; D3's US$2.73 thousand is GDP per head. Different attributes (level vs per-capita), so they cannot corroborate or conflict even though both derive from IMF data.

D4 gives a nominal GDP level (USD 3,638 billion for FY2023/24) and D3 gives a real growth rate (8.2% for FY24). A stock-style level in current dollars and a constant-price growth rate are different attributes, so the pair is a false match despite covering the same fiscal year.

D4's "GDP per capita (U.S. dollars) (IMF staff est.): 2,530" is tagged to FY2023/24, whereas D3 says "India's per capita GDP reached US$2.73 thousand in 2024", which on the IMF's India convention is the year ending March 2025. The USD 2,530 to USD 2,730 step is one year of nominal per-capita growth (~8%), consistent with the same source measured a year apart, so this is a period difference rather than a disagreement.

D4 reports GDP per capita in US dollars (2,530) and D3 reports a real GDP growth rate (8.2%). Different attributes — a per-head income level versus an aggregate growth rate — so no corroboration or conflict is possible.

D1's 6.5 per cent is a real growth rate for 2024-25; D3's US$3.9 trillion is a nominal GDP level in current dollars. Growth rate and level are different attributes and are not comparable as competing values.

The extracted D4 value 9.7 is the first entry of the row "Real GDP (at market prices) 9.7 7.6 9.2 6.5 6.6 6.2", i.e. FY2021/22, whereas D1 reports 6.5 per cent for 2024-25. Different years entirely; moreover the fourth entry in the same D4 row (6.5, corresponding to FY2024/25) matches D1's figure exactly, confirming the two sources agree once the columns are aligned to years.

D4's 9.7 belongs to FY2021/22 in the row "9.7 7.6 9.2 6.5 6.6 6.2", while D1's 9.2 per cent is the 2023-24 comparator ("with 9.2 per cent a year ago"). Different fiscal years; note the third entry of D4's row is itself 9.2, i.e. FY2023/24, so the two documents in fact agree on 2023-24 once the series is read positionally.

D4's 9.7 per cent is the FY2021/22 entry of its real GDP series, whereas D2's 6.4 per cent is the First Advance Estimate for FY25 (year ended March 2025). Three fiscal years apart, spanning the post-pandemic rebound year and a normalised year, so the values are not intended to describe the same period.

D4's 9.7 per cent refers to FY2021/22 (first column of "9.7 7.6 9.2 6.5 6.6 6.2"); D2's 6.0 per cent covers only H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024). The comparison spans both a different fiscal year and a half-year versus full-year basis, so the gap is fully explained by timing.

Both report state-government gross fiscal deficit as a share of GDP for 2024-25: IMF says 3.3% "estimated to have risen ... from 2.9 percent in FY2023/24", RBI's table shows 3.6% with 3.0% the year before. The near-identical prior-year values (3.0 vs 2.9) show the two series track each other, so the 3.6 vs 3.3 gap is the RBI table's budgeted/earlier vintage against the IMF's November-2025 estimate of the outturn (states habitually budget deficits above realised ones). To close it fully one would check whether the RBI row is Budget Estimates and which nominal-GDP denominator each uses.

D1 states the states/UT aggregate fiscal deficit as a level, ₹10.4 lakh crore for 2024-25 (BE); D3 states it as 3.3% of GDP for the same year. On FY2024-25 nominal GDP of roughly ₹330 lakh crore, ₹10.4 lakh crore is about 3.2%, so the two are the same magnitude expressed in different units (rupee level vs GDP ratio).

Both quote 3.3% of GDP for the consolidated states' GFD, but for different fiscal years: D3's 3.3% is the estimated FY2024/25 (Apr 2024–Mar 2025) outturn, while D1 says the GFD is "budgeted at 3.3 per cent of GDP" for 2025-26. The matching value is coincidental across adjacent years, not the same measurement.

D1's ₹2,473 thousand crore for 2024-25 BE is the combined central-plus-state gross fiscal deficit (row "3 Gross Fiscal Deficit [1 - (2.1 + 2.2)]"), whereas D3's 3.3% of GDP covers state governments only. On ~₹330 lakh crore nominal GDP the combined figure is roughly 7.5% of GDP, of which the states account for about 3.3% — consistent once the scope and unit differences are applied.

D1's 4.7% of GDP for 2024-25 (RE) is the Central Government's GFD ("down from 4.7 per cent in 2024-25 (RE)" in the context of the Union targeting 4.4% in 2025-26 BE), while D3's 3.3% is the combined state governments' deficit. Different fiscal entities, so the values are not comparable claims.

D1 reports scheduled commercial bank credit growth of 12.1% for the year 2024-25 (i.e. y-o-y to end-March 2025); D3 reports 10.4% y/y in September 2025 and notes it was "13 percent in September 2024". These are different observation dates on a decelerating series, so 12.1% (March 2025) sitting between 13% (Sep 2024) and 10.4% (Sep 2025) is consistent rather than conflicting.

D1's appendix series gives SCB bank credit growth of 12.1% for 2024-25 (y-o-y to end-March 2025); D3's 10.4% is the y/y rate in September 2025, six months later. The deceleration path 13% (Sep 2024) → 12.1% (Mar 2025) → 10.4% (Sep 2025) is internally coherent; the figures measure different reference dates.

D1's 11.8% is bank credit to the commercial sector for the full year 2024-25 (with 15.6% a year earlier); D3's 10.4% is gross bank credit growth y/y in September 2025. Both the reference date (Mar 2025 vs Sep 2025) and the aggregate (commercial-sector credit within M3 vs gross bank credit) differ, and both documents describe the same moderating trend.

D1's 11.2% is net bank credit to government — banks' holdings of government securities — for 2024-25, while D3's 10.4% is bank credit growth to borrowers (gross bank credit) in September 2025. Different attributes on opposite sides of the credit aggregate; the numerical proximity is coincidental.

D1's 6.4% is the y-o-y credit growth to the large-industry sub-sector as at end-March 2025 (a row in the sectoral deployment table), not aggregate bank credit. D3's 10.4% is total gross bank credit growth in September 2025, so the two measure a component and the whole at different dates.

D1's 3.3% is reserve money (M0) growth for 2024-25, a central-bank liability aggregate; D3's 10.4% is commercial bank credit growth in September 2025. Different attributes entirely — a monetary base measure versus a credit measure.

D3's 20.7% y/y in March 2025 is credit extended BY non-bank financial companies ("NBFC credit growth ... partly due to the reclassification of a housing finance company"). D1's 5.9% at end-March 2025 is banks' credit TO NBFCs, a services sub-sector row in the sectoral deployment table. Same date and similar wording, but opposite sides of the lending relationship.

D1's 11.8% covers bank credit to the commercial sector for 2024-25 as a driver of M3; D3's 20.7% is lending by NBFCs in March 2025. Different lender universes (banks vs non-banks), so the two growth rates are not measuring the same aggregate.
D1's 11.2% is net bank credit to government for 2024-25; D3's 20.7% is NBFC credit growth in March 2025. Neither the lender (banks vs NBFCs) nor the borrower (government vs general) matches.
Reserve money growth of 3.3% in 2024-25 (D1) is a monetary base aggregate; NBFC credit growth of 20.7% in March 2025 (D3) is non-bank lending. Different attributes with no shared measurement basis.

D1 reports CAD at 1.3% of GDP for April–December 2024 (first nine months of FY2024-25); D3 reports 0.6% of GDP for the full FY2024/25. The full-year ratio is lower because the January–March 2025 quarter recorded a current account surplus, so the nine-month and twelve-month figures are different windows of the same year, not conflicting estimates.

D1's US$37.1 billion (1.3% of GDP) covers April–December 2024 only; D3's 0.6% of GDP covers the whole of FY2024/25. Both the window (9 months vs 12) and the unit (USD level vs GDP ratio) differ; a Q4 surplus brings the full-year deficit below the nine-month total.

D1's 1.1% of GDP is April–December 2023, i.e. nine months of FY2023-24, while D3's 0.6% is the whole of FY2024/25 — a different fiscal year and a different window. D3 separately puts FY2023/24 at 0.7%, which is the comparable full-year counterpart to D1's 1.1% nine-month figure.

D1's US$30.7 billion is the April–December 2023 CAD; D3's 0.6% of GDP is the FY2024/25 CAD. Different fiscal years and different window lengths (9 months vs full year), plus a unit difference (USD level vs GDP share).

D2's 1.3% of GDP is a single quarter, Q2 FY24 (Jul–Sep 2023); D3's 0.6% is the full FY2024/25. A quarterly ratio in one fiscal year and an annual ratio in the next are different measurements, and D3 itself puts full-year FY2023/24 at 0.7%.

D3 gives 0.7% of GDP for the whole of FY2023/24; D1 gives 1.1% of GDP for April–December 2023, the first nine months of that same year. The Q4 FY2023-24 current account surplus pulls the annual ratio below the nine-month one, so 1.1% (9M) and 0.7% (12M) are consistent.

D1's US$30.7 billion (1.1% of GDP) is the April–December 2023 deficit; D3's 0.7% of GDP is the FY2023/24 full-year deficit (roughly US$23 billion on ~US$3.6 trillion GDP). The smaller annual figure reflects the January–March 2024 surplus, so the difference is window length plus units, not disagreement.

D2's 1.3% of GDP refers to Q2 FY24 (Jul–Sep 2023) alone, while D3's 0.7% is the full-year FY2023/24 average. A single seasonally heavy quarter can exceed the annual ratio, so the two are different aggregation windows of the same fiscal year.

D1's 1.3% of GDP covers April–December 2024 (FY2024-25), whereas D3's 0.7% covers full-year FY2023/24. Different fiscal years and different window lengths; D3's own FY2024/25 figure is 0.6%, the comparable annual number for D1's window.

D3 says "net FDI dropped to about zero in FY2024/25 amid elevated disinvestment and repatriation"; D2 says "net FDI inflows declined relative to April-November 2023 due to a rise in repatriation/disinvestment" for the first eight months of FY25. Same direction, same stated cause (repatriation/disinvestment), with D2's eight-month window contained inside D3's full fiscal year; D2's earlier vintage is qualitative while D3 quantifies the annual endpoint.

D1 reports net FPI inflows of US$1.7 billion in 2024-25; D3 reports net FPI at 0.1% of GDP in FY2024/25, which on roughly US$3.9 trillion nominal GDP is about US$3.9 billion (US$1.7bn would round to ~0.0%). Both agree FPI collapsed to near zero from the prior year, and the residual ~US$2 billion gap is a coverage/denominator difference in the balance-of-payments portfolio aggregate rather than a disagreement about the outcome; confirming would require the exact BoP line the IMF ratio uses.

The D3 fact's headline value (0.1% of GDP) is FY2024/25, while D1's US$41.6 billion is 2023-24 — different years. The same D3 sentence puts FY2023/24 at 1.2% of GDP, which on ~US$3.6 trillion GDP is ~US$42 billion, matching D1's US$41.6 billion for that year.

D2's US$10.6 billion covers April–December 2024 only, whereas D3's 0.1% of GDP (~US$4 billion or less) covers the full FY2024/25. Heavy Q4 FY2024-25 portfolio outflows reduce the annual total below the nine-month figure, so the two are different windows of the same year rather than conflicting values.

D2's US$31.7 billion is April–December 2023 (nine months of FY2023-24); the D3 fact's 0.1% of GDP is full-year FY2024/25. Different fiscal years and window lengths; D3's stated FY2023/24 figure of 1.2% of GDP (~US$42bn full year) is the comparable annual counterpart to D2's nine-month total.

D1's US$10,980 million is the BoP line "Foreign Investment, Net (a+b)" — direct plus portfolio investment combined — for April–December 2024 (provisional), while D3's 0.1% of GDP is portfolio investment alone for the full FY2024/25. Different aggregate and different window.

D2 (published Jan 2025) reports net FPI inflows of US$10.6 billion for April–December 2024; D1 reports US$1.7 billion for the full year 2024-25. The two are consistent if the January–March 2025 quarter saw roughly US$9 billion of net portfolio outflows — a nine-month figure versus a twelve-month one, not a revision of the same number.

D2's US$31.7 billion covers April–December 2023, while D1's US$41.6 billion covers the full year 2023-24. The ~US$10 billion difference is the January–March 2024 quarter, so the nine-month and full-year totals are compatible.

The values are nearly equal for the same window (D1: US$10,980 million; D2: US$10.6 billion, both April–December 2024), but they measure different things: D1's row is "Foreign Investment, Net (a+b)", combining direct and portfolio investment, whereas D2's figure is net FPI alone. The near-match reflects net FDI being close to zero in that period, so treating them as the same series would be a false match.

D4 reports 8.4 months of cover measured 'In months of next year's imports (goods and services)' at end-FY2024/25, while D1's vulnerability table gives 10.5 months at end-December 2024 'based on merchandise imports of latest four quarters'. A denominator that adds services imports and uses next year's (larger) import bill mechanically yields a lower cover than a merchandise-only, trailing-four-quarter base; the reference dates also differ by one quarter.

D4's 8.4 months is explicitly cover of next year's goods AND services imports at end-FY2024/25; D2 states import cover 'stood at 10.9 months as of December 2024' on the Indian convention of merchandise imports. The 2.5-month gap is the denominator definition plus a three-month difference in reference date, not a disagreement about the reserve stock.

Both refer to the same date: D4's end-period FY2024/25 is 31 March 2025 and D1 says reserves were 'covering 11 months of merchandise imports' at end-March 2025. D4 measures 8.4 months against next year's goods-and-services imports; D1 measures against merchandise imports only, so the broader IMF denominator explains 8.4 vs 11.

D2 claims 'an import cover of more than ten months' as on 3 January 2025 (merchandise basis); D4 reports 8.4 months on a goods-and-services, next-year-imports basis for FY2024/25. The two are not in conflict once the denominators are aligned — the IMF metric is always the smaller of the two.

D1's 30.3 per cent is Gross Savings as a share of GNDI for 2023-24; D2's 10.9 months is the import cover of foreign exchange reserves in December 2024. Different attribute, different unit and different period — the pair is a false match.

D1's 18.5 per cent external-debt-to-GDP is 'as at end-March 2024'; D4's 18.8 per cent is the end-period estimate for FY2024/25 (end-March 2025), one year later. D4's own series in the same row ('19.5 18.6 18.4 18.8 19.2 19.0') carries 18.4 for the FY2023/24 column, effectively the same figure as RBI's 18.5 within revision noise.

D1 reports 19.1 per cent (provisional) at end-December 2024; D4 estimates 18.8 per cent at end-March 2025. The dates differ by one quarter, and a quarter of nominal GDP accretion plus valuation effects readily accounts for a 0.3 pp decline between the two reference points.

D4's 50 per cent is a country-wide U.S. tariff applied to India's merchandise exports from 27 August 2025; D2's 11.3 per cent is the tariff faced on one product line, silk shawls and scarves, described in a January 2025 document written before the 2025 tariff actions. Different scope (single HS line vs all merchandise) and different dates — not competing measurements of the same rate.

D4 says merchandise exports to the U.S. were 2.2 per cent of GDP in FY2024/25; D1 gives total merchandise exports of US$ 437.4 billion in 2024-25 (up 0.1 per cent y-o-y). One is a US-bound subset scaled by GDP, the other the global total in dollars; at roughly US$ 3.9 trillion GDP, 2.2 per cent is about US$ 86 billion, i.e. around a fifth of the US$ 437.4 billion total — consistent rather than conflicting.

Both cover FY2024/25. D2 (published 31 Jan 2025) reports 6.4 per cent explicitly from the First Advance Estimates; D4 (Staff Report completed 6 Nov 2025) cites 6.5 per cent as an outturn. The 0.1 pp difference is the standard upward revision from advance estimate to later official estimate.

D2's overview repeats the First Advance Estimate of 6.4 per cent for FY25; D4 reports realised growth of 6.5 per cent for the same April 2024-March 2025 year, using data available in November 2025. Advance estimate versus later actual, so the 0.1 pp gap is data vintage.

D2's 6.0 per cent covers H1 FY25 only (April-September 2024); D4's 6.5 per cent is the full FY2024/25 year. A weaker first half followed by a stronger second half yields a full-year figure above the half-year one, so the two are compatible measurements of different windows.

D1 states real GDP growth 'moderated to 6.5 per cent in 2024-25' (Second Advance Estimates) and D4 states 'India's real GDP grew by 6.5 percent in FY2024/25'. Same period (April 2024-March 2025), same measure, identical value.
D1 page 23 records growth of 6.5 per cent in 2024-25 at constant prices; D4 reports 6.5 percent real GDP growth for FY2024/25. Same fiscal year, same constant-price concept, same number.

D1's 9.2 per cent is explicitly the prior-year comparator for 2023-24 ('as compared with 9.2 per cent a year ago'), whereas D4's 6.5 per cent is FY2024/25. Different fiscal years, and the deceleration from 9.2 to 6.5 is exactly the moderation D1 describes.

D4's 7.2 per cent private consumption growth is FY2024/25; D3 cites 6.8 per cent private final consumption expenditure growth for FY23 (April 2022-March 2023), two years earlier. Same concept, different fiscal years.

D3 records PFCE growth of 4.0 per cent in FY24 (April 2023-March 2024); D4 reports private consumption growth of 7.2 per cent in FY2024/25. Consecutive fiscal years — the rebound from 4.0 to about 7 per cent matches D4's description of 'increasing rural demand'.

Both cover 2024-25: D1's table gives 7.6 per cent PFCE growth explicitly on the Second Advance Estimates at 2011-12 prices (published mid-2025), while D4's 7.2 per cent is stated as an outturn in a staff report completed 6 November 2025. The 0.4 pp gap is the downward revision from advance to provisional/first-revised national accounts; confirming it requires the NSO release D4 relied on.
D3's 6.8 per cent PFCE growth is FY23; D1's 7.6 per cent is 2024-25 on Second Advance Estimates. Same national-accounts aggregate, two fiscal years apart.
D3 reports PFCE growth of 4.0 per cent for FY24 (year ended 31 March 2024); D1 reports 7.6 per cent for 2024-25. Adjacent but distinct years, so the difference is timing rather than conflict.

D2's 'around 14 per cent of GDP' measures private corporate savings as a stock-flow share of GDP with no period stated; D4's 7.2 per cent is the growth rate of private consumption in FY2024/25. Different attribute and different unit (share vs growth rate).

D2 reports private corporate savings at roughly 14 per cent of GDP; D1's 7.6 per cent is the growth rate of Private Final Consumption Expenditure in 2024-25. Savings share versus consumption growth are distinct attributes in different units.

D1's 6.5 per cent is aggregate real GDP growth in 2024-25; D4's 7.2 per cent is private consumption growth in the same year. Same period but different aggregates, so the numbers are not alternative measures of one quantity.

D4's 7.1 per cent is the growth rate of domestic gross investment in FY2024/25; D1's US$ 10,980 million is net foreign investment in the balance of payments capital account for April-December 2024. Different attribute (domestic capital formation growth vs cross-border financial flows) and different unit.

D1's 3.3 per cent is Reserve Money growth as at 28 March 2025, a monetary aggregate; D4's 7.1 per cent is real investment growth in FY2024/25. Same-sounding percentages, entirely different attributes.

D4's 7.1 per cent is investment (gross capital formation) growth; D2's 6.4 per cent is headline real GDP growth for FY25. Both are FY25 growth rates but of different aggregates, so they are not competing values for one measure.

D1's 6.5 per cent is total real GDP growth in 2024-25; D4's 7.1 per cent is investment growth in the same year. Different aggregates within the national accounts, so the pair is a false match rather than a disagreement.

D3's table row "Real GDP (at market prices) 9.7 7.6 9.2 6.5 6.6 6.2" places 9.2% at FY2023/24, and D1 states the economy grew "9.2 per cent a year ago" relative to 2024-25, i.e. 2023-24. Same value, same fiscal year, same real-GDP concept.

D3's 9.2% is tagged to FY2023/24 (1 Apr 2023-31 Mar 2024); D2's 6.4% is the First Advance Estimate for FY25 (1 Apr 2024-31 Mar 2025). Different fiscal years of the same series, so the gap is entirely a period difference.
D3's 9.2% covers full-year FY2023/24; D2's 6.0% is explicitly "the first half of the current fiscal", i.e. H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024). Neither the year nor the coverage window is the same.

D3 assigns 9.2% to FY2023/24 while D1 says growth "moderated to 6.5 per cent in 2024-25". The moderation from 9.2% to 6.5% is precisely the year-on-year change D1 describes; different periods, not conflicting values.
9.2% in D3 is the FY2023/24 column; D1's 6.5% is the Second Advance Estimate for 2024-25. Consecutive fiscal years of the same real-GDP series.
D3's 9.2% refers to FY2023/24; D2's "6.4 per cent in FY25" refers to 2024-25 first advance estimates. Different years, so the two numbers are not in competition.
D3 places 9.2% in FY2023/24; D1 says the economy "grown by 6.5 per cent in 2024-25". Adjacent fiscal years of the same constant-price series.
D3's row "9.7 7.6 9.2 6.5 6.6 6.2" puts 6.5% at FY2024/25, and D1 states growth "moderated to 6.5 per cent in 2024-25". Identical value, identical fiscal year, same market-price real GDP concept.
Both report 6.5% real GDP growth for 2024-25; D1 attributes it to the Second Advance Estimates and D3 (published Nov 2025) carries the same 6.5% outturn for FY2024/25. Same number, same period.
D1: the economy "grown by 6.5 per cent in 2024-25" at constant prices; D3's table shows 6.5% for FY2024/25 at market prices. Same period and same magnitude.

D2's 6.4% for FY25 is a First Advance Estimate published 31 Jan 2025, before the year ended; D3's 6.5% for FY2024/25 was compiled in November 2025 from the completed-year data. The 0.1pp gap is an advance-estimate-to-outturn revision.

"India's real GDP is estimated to grow by 6.4 per cent in FY25" (D2, first advance estimates, Jan 2025) versus D3's 6.5% for the same FY2024/25 reported as an outturn in Nov 2025. Same year, later data vintage.
D3's 6.5% is the full FY2024/25; D2's 6.0% covers only "the first half of the current fiscal" (Apr-Sep 2024). A softer H1 is consistent with a 6.5% full-year figure.
D3's 6.5% sits in the FY2024/25 column while D1's 9.2% is the 2023-24 comparator. The two figures are consecutive years of the same series, matching D1's description of moderation from 9.2% to 6.5%.
D3's 6.6% is a staff projection for FY2025/26 (1 Apr 2025-31 Mar 2026); D2's 6.4% is an estimate for FY25 (2024-25). Different fiscal years, and one is a forward projection.
6.6% in D3 is projected for FY2025/26; D2's 6.0% is actual growth for H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024). Different years and different coverage windows.
D3's 6.6% is the FY2025/26 projection; D1's 6.5% is the outturn for 2024-25. Adjacent years, so a modest projected pickup rather than a disagreement.
6.6% (D3) refers to FY2025/26 under staff projections; 6.5% (D1) is the Second Advance Estimate for 2024-25. Different periods of the same series.
D3 projects 6.6% for FY2025/26 while D2 estimates 6.4% for FY25 (2024-25). The years do not overlap, so the figures are not competing measurements.
D3's 6.6% is projected for 2025-26; D1's 6.5% is realised growth in 2024-25 at constant prices. Consecutive but distinct fiscal years.
D3's 6.6% is a FY2025/26 projection; D1's 9.2% is the 2023-24 comparator. Two years apart in the same real-GDP series.
D3's 6.2% is a staff projection for FY2026/27; D2's 6.4% is the first advance estimate for FY25 (2024-25). Two fiscal years apart, one projected and one estimated.
6.2% (D3) is projected for 2026-27; 6.0% (D2) is actual H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024) growth. Different years and different coverage, so proximity of the values is coincidental.
D3's 6.2% belongs to the FY2026/27 projection column; D1's 6.5% is realised 2024-25 growth. Distinct periods of the same series.
6.2% is D3's FY2026/27 baseline projection; 6.5% is D1's Second Advance Estimate for 2024-25. The periods differ by two years.
D3 projects 6.2% for FY2026/27 while D2 estimates 6.4% for FY25. Different fiscal years, and D3's figure is a forward projection made under a prolonged-tariff baseline.
D3's 6.2% is for 2026-27; D1's 6.5% is realised growth in 2024-25 at constant prices. No period overlap.
D3's 6.2% is a FY2026/27 projection; D1's 9.2% is the 2023-24 outturn used as a prior-year comparator. Three years apart in the same series.

D3's row "Consumer prices - Combined 5.5 6.7 5.4 4.6 2.8 4.0" gives 4.6% for FY2024/25 as a period average, and D1's appendix gives CPI Combined (average % change) of 4.6 as the last entry of "4.5 6.7 5.4 4.6", i.e. 2024-25. Identical value, period and definition.

D1's General Index (All Groups) CPI Combined figure for 2024-25 is 4.6% (last value of "6.7 5.4 4.6"), matching D3's 4.6% combined consumer price inflation for FY2024/25. Same headline all-groups index, same fiscal year.

D3's 4.6% is headline combined CPI (all groups) for 2024/25, whereas D1's 6.7% is the Food and Beverages sub-group of the same CPI Combined basket for the same year. A food sub-index running above the headline is the expected composition effect, not a conflicting measure of the same aggregate.
D1's 5.4% General Index figure is for 2023-24, and D3's own series lists 5.4 in the FY2023/24 slot before 4.6 for FY2024/25. The 4.6 vs 5.4 gap is purely the change of year.

D4's 7.8% is a single quarter, 2025Q2 (Apr–Jun 2025, i.e. Q1 of FY2025/26), on a y/y basis; D2's 6.4% is the full year FY25 (Apr 2024–Mar 2025). Different, non-overlapping periods in different fiscal years.
7.8% (D4) refers to the April–June 2025 quarter; 6.4% (D2) is the FY25 (Apr 2024–Mar 2025) annual estimate. The quarter falls in the following fiscal year, so the figures measure different periods.
D4's 7.8% is 2025Q2 (Apr–Jun 2025) y/y; D2's 6.0% is H1 FY25 (Apr–Sep 2024). Both are sub-annual real GDP growth rates, but for periods a year apart.

D1's 6.5% is annual growth for 2024-25 (year ended March 2025); D4's 7.8% is the single quarter Apr–Jun 2025, after that year ended. Quarterly acceleration in the next fiscal year does not contradict the prior annual outturn.
6.5% (D1, Second Advance Estimates) is the FY2024-25 annual rate; 7.8% (D4) is 2025Q2 y/y growth. Non-overlapping periods, so different values are expected.
D1 reports 6.5% constant-price growth for 2024-25; D4 reports 7.8% for the Apr–Jun 2025 quarter. The quarter lies outside the fiscal year D1 measures.
D1's 9.2% is the prior-year comparator for 2023-24; D4's 7.8% is quarterly y/y growth for Apr–Jun 2025. The periods are two years apart, so no direct comparison of values is meaningful.

D4's 8.8% is explicitly *nominal* GDP growth for 2025Q2 ('reflecting a low deflator'); D3's 8.2% is India's real GDP growth for FY24. Different measure (nominal vs real) and different period, so the closeness of the numbers is coincidental rather than like-for-like.
D4 reports nominal GDP growth of 8.8% for 2025Q2; D2 reports real (constant-price) GDP growth of 6.4% for FY25. Nominal includes the deflator and the periods differ, so the values are not comparable.
8.8% (D4) is nominal GDP growth for the Apr–Jun 2025 quarter; 6.4% (D2) is real GDP growth for FY25. The gap is the price deflator plus a period difference, not a factual conflict.
D4's 8.8% is nominal growth in 2025Q2; D2's 6.0% is real growth in H1 FY25 (Apr–Sep 2024). Both the price basis (nominal vs constant prices) and the period differ.
D4's 8.8% is nominal GDP growth for 2025Q2; D1's 6.5% is real GDP growth (Second Advance Estimates) for 2024-25. Different price basis and different period.

Both cover the same year — D4's FY2024/25 and D1's 2024-25 are both Apr 2024–Mar 2025 — but D4's 9.8% is nominal GDP growth while D1's 6.5% is real growth (SAE). The ~3.3pp wedge is the implied GDP deflator, consistent with D4's own remark about 'a low deflator'.

Same fiscal year (FY2024/25 = FY25), but D4 measures nominal GDP growth (9.8%) and D2 measures real growth at constant prices (6.4%, first advance estimates). The difference is the deflator, compounded slightly by the estimate vintage.
D4's 9.8% for FY2024/25 is nominal; D2's 6.4% for FY25 is real GDP growth. Identical period, different price basis — nominal less the deflator explains the gap.
D4's 9.8% is nominal growth for the full FY2024/25; D2's 6.0% is real growth for H1 FY25 only. Both the price basis and the coverage period differ.

D4's 9.8% is nominal GDP growth for FY2024/25, while D3's 8.2% is real GDP growth for FY24 (Apr 2023–Mar 2024). The two differ on both period (consecutive fiscal years) and price basis, so they measure different quantities.
D4's 1.5% is a single-month y/y reading for September 2025; D1's 5.4% is the annual average for 2023-24. Two years apart and monthly vs annual-average basis, so the values measure different things.

D4 itself frames the comparison: inflation 'declined to 1.5 percent in September 2025, down from 4.6 percent (FY2024/25 average)', which is exactly D1's 4.6% average for 2024-25. A monthly September 2025 reading versus an FY25 annual average — different periods, same series.
1.5% (D4) is September 2025; 4.8% (D1) is April–May 2024. Both are CPI-Combined headline readings but about 16 months apart, over which D4 documents a sustained decline.
D1's 6.2% is the October 2024 spike; D4's 1.5% is September 2025. Different months in different fiscal years of the same monthly CPI series.
3.6% (D1) is July 2024 and 1.5% (D4) is September 2025 — distinct monthly observations of the same headline CPI series, over a year apart.

D4 states '4.6 percent (FY2024/25 average)' and D1 states 'Headline inflation moderated to an average of 4.6 per cent during 2024-25'. Same series, same April–March year, same value on the same average basis.

D4's 4.6% is the FY2024/25 average; D1's 5.4% is explicitly the previous year's (2023-24) average. D1's own sentence links them — 'moderated to an average of 4.6 per cent during 2024-25 from 5.4 per cent in the previous year' — so the gap is purely the year.
4.6% (D4) is a 12-month FY2024/25 average, whereas 4.8% (D1) is the April–May 2024 reading within that year. A two-month print slightly above the annual mean is consistent, not contradictory.
D1's 6.2% is the October 2024 monthly peak inside 2024-25; D4's 4.6% is the average across the whole of FY2024/25. A within-year peak above the annual average is expected.
D1's 3.6% is the July 2024 trough inside 2024-25; D4's 4.6% is the FY2024/25 average. Monthly observation versus annual mean of the same series.

D4's 4.6% core reading is for September 2025 and it explicitly names D1's figure as the base — 'increased to 4.6 percent (from 3.5 percent FY2024/25 average)' — matching D1's core of 3.5% for 2024-25. Periods differ (single month vs FY25 average); the exclusion baskets differ slightly too (D4 excludes food, gold and silver; D1 excludes food and fuel).

D1's 4.3% core is the 2023-24 annual average ('eased to 3.5 per cent during 2024-25 from 4.3 per cent a year ago'); D4's 4.6% is a September 2025 monthly reading. Two years apart, and on slightly different exclusion definitions.

D4's 4.6% is core CPI inflation, which by construction excludes food; D1's 6.7% is CPI food-group inflation for 2024-25. Different attributes measuring different baskets, so the numbers were never comparable.
D1's 7.0% is food inflation for 2023-24; D4's 4.6% is core inflation (food excluded) for September 2025. Different attribute and different period — a false match on the word 'inflation'.

D1's (-)2.7% is pulses price inflation for March 2025, a single food sub-group with 5.2% weight in CPI food and beverages; D4's 4.6% is aggregate core inflation excluding food. Different attributes entirely.

Both cover the same full fiscal year (1 Apr 2024–31 Mar 2025) but on different measurement bases: D3 labels its US$729.0 bn as 'balance of payments basis', while D1's US$720.2 bn (with 6.2% y-o-y growth) is the customs/DGCI&S trade series used in the RBI's external-sector chapter. The ~US$8.8 bn gap is the usual BoP-vs-customs coverage/valuation adjustment, not a disagreement about the outturn.

D1 gives quarterly y-o-y import growth of 1.2 per cent for Q4 2024-25 (Jan–Mar 2025); D2 gives 5.2 per cent cumulatively for April–December 2024. The quarters do not overlap, so the values measure different things.

D3's current account balance of -US$23.3 bn is the full FY2024/25 (Apr 2024–Mar 2025) outturn; D1's -US$37,100 mn (-US$37.1 bn) row is flagged provisional with 'data pertain to April-December 2024', i.e. only the first nine months. The gap of US$13.8 bn is the Q4 FY25 current account surplus, so the nine-month deficit being larger than the full-year deficit is arithmetically coherent, not contradictory.

D3 states a current account level (-US$23.3 bn for FY2024/25); D1's -1.3 per cent is a memo item expressing the balance as a ratio to GDP for April–December 2024. Different attribute (absolute USD level vs share of GDP) and different window, so the two numbers are not measuring the same quantity.

Again a level-versus-ratio mismatch: D3 reports -US$23.3 bn for the full FY2024/25, D1 reports a Current Account Balance/GDP ratio of -1.3 per cent for the provisional April–December 2024 period. Different attribute and different coverage.

D1's -US$13,821 mn is the Overall Balance of Payments [A(5)+B(8)+C], which nets the capital and financial account against the current account; D3's -US$23.3 bn is the current account balance alone. Different BoP aggregates, and D1's is for April–December 2024 while D3's is the full year.

D3 reports gross reserves of US$668.3 bn as an end-period (31 Mar 2025) figure; D2 reports US$704.9 bn in September 2024, the peak before the late-2024 drawdown. Reserves are a stock at a point in time, and the two dates are six months apart, so the values are not comparable as-is.

US$640.3 bn in D2 is dated 'as of the end of December 2024'; D3's US$668.3 bn is explicitly end-period for FY2024/25, i.e. 31 March 2025. Three months apart on a stock series that was recovering after the Q3 FY25 decline, so both can be right.

Same stock measured on different dates: D2 puts reserves at US$640.3 bn at end-December 2024, D3 at US$668.3 bn at end-March 2025 (its stated end-period for FY2024/25). A quarter's difference on a point-in-time reserve stock.

D2's US$616.7 bn is dated end-January 2024, fourteen months before D3's end-March 2025 stock of US$668.3 bn. D2 itself describes reserves rising from that January 2024 level, so the two figures trace the same upward series at different points.

D1's 30.3 per cent is Gross Savings as a percentage of Gross National Disposable Income for 2023-24 — a domestic saving rate. D2's US$704.9 bn is the stock of foreign exchange reserves in September 2024. Different attributes entirely; the group match is spurious.

Duplicate orientation of the same spurious pairing: reserve stock in US$ billions versus a savings-to-GNDI percentage for a different fiscal year (2023-24). Retained only to flag that no comparison is possible.

D3's US$668.3 bn is gross foreign exchange reserves (an asset stock, end-March 2025); D1's US$717.9 bn is the external debt stock at end-December 2024 (a liability). Similar magnitudes but opposite sides of the external balance sheet.

D3 reports external debt at 18.8 per cent of GDP as an end-period figure for FY2024/25 (31 Mar 2025); D2 reports 19.4 per cent at end-September 2024 (and notes 18.8 per cent at end-June 2024). Different measurement dates on a ratio that moved within the year — the coincidence with the June 2024 value underlines that these are dated snapshots, not rival estimates of one date.

D1's 19.1 per cent is provisional and dated end-December 2024; D3's 18.8 per cent is the end-period FY2024/25 (end-March 2025) estimate. Three months apart, and the GDP denominator grows over the year, so a modest decline in the ratio between December and March is expected.

Both are full-year 2024-25 merchandise trade balances but on different bases: D3 states BPM6 balance-of-payments basis (-US$287.2 bn), while D1's annual series of -US$282.8 bn sits alongside its customs figures (exports US$437.4 bn, imports US$720.2 bn, which net to about -US$282.8 bn). The US$4.4 bn wedge is the same BoP-versus-customs adjustment seen in the import levels.

D1's -US$227,227 mn (-US$227.2 bn) is flagged provisional with 'data pertain to April-December 2024' — nine months — while D3's -US$287.2 bn is the full FY2024/25 BoP trade balance. The implied Q4 FY25 deficit of about US$60 bn is plausible, so the two are consistent parts of one year.

D2's US$75.3 bn is a single quarter (Q2 FY25, Jul–Sep 2024) merchandise trade deficit; D3's US$287.2 bn covers the whole of FY2024/25. A quarter cannot be compared to a year — four quarters of roughly this size sum to the annual figure.

D2's US$189.7 bn deficit is explicitly 'the same period last year', i.e. April–December 2023 (nine months of FY24); D3's US$287.2 bn is the full FY2024/25. Different fiscal year and different length of window.

Both are nine-month April–December figures but for different years: D1's -US$227.2 bn covers April–December 2024, D2's US$189.7 bn covers April–December 2023. The widening is consistent with D2's own statement that the FY25 nine-month deficit exceeded the year-earlier one (bases also differ: D1's row is the BoP trade balance, D2's the customs deficit).

D1's -US$227.2 bn is the cumulative April–December 2024 trade balance; D2's US$75.3 bn is only Q2 FY25 (Jul–Sep 2024), one of the three quarters inside that window. A component versus its cumulative total.
D1's -US$282.8 bn is the annual 2024-25 merchandise trade deficit; D2's US$75.3 bn is the Q2 FY25 deficit alone (up from US$64.5 bn a year earlier). Quarter versus full year on the same series.
D1 gives the full-year 2024-25 deficit of US$282.8 bn; D2's US$189.7 bn is the April–December 2023 (FY24 nine-month) comparator. Both a different fiscal year and a shorter window.
D1's US$437.4 bn is merchandise exports for 2024-25; D2's US$75.3 bn is the merchandise trade deficit for Q2 FY25. Gross flow versus net balance — different attributes, and different periods.

D3's US$188.8 bn is the services balance (net services exports) for FY2024/25; D1's -US$227,227 mn is the merchandise trade balance for April–December 2024. Different components of the current account, plus different periods — they are complements, not measures of the same thing.

D1's 6.6 per cent is the debt service ratio (debt service to current receipts) at end-December 2024; D3's US$188.8 bn is the FY2024/25 services balance. No shared attribute — the match appears to hinge on the word 'service'.

Both give gold imports of US$58.0 bn for the same fiscal year: D3 lists 58.0 for 2024/25 and D1 states value 'rose by 27.4 per cent (y-o-y) in 2024-25 to US$ 58.0 billion'. Identical value, identical period, identical unit — D3's estimate matches the RBI's reported figure exactly.

D2's US$352.1 bn is expressly non-oil, non-gold imports for the first nine months of FY25 — a category that excludes gold by construction — while D3's US$58.0 bn is gold imports for the full year. Mutually exclusive baskets and different windows.
D2's US$340.5 bn covers non-oil, non-gold imports in the first nine months of FY24, explicitly excluding gold; D3's US$58.0 bn is FY2024/25 gold imports. Different basket, different fiscal year.

D1's US$720.2 bn is total merchandise imports for the full year 2024-25; D2's US$352.1 bn is the non-oil, non-gold subset for the first nine months of FY25. The smaller figure is a component of a narrower basket over a shorter window, so it should be well below the total.

Gold imports of US$58.0 bn (D3) are one commodity line inside D1's total merchandise imports of US$720.2 bn for the same year 2024-25 — about 8 per cent of the total. Component versus aggregate, so the different magnitudes are expected rather than conflicting.

D4 gives 2.8% as a projected combined-CPI period average for FY2025/26 (Apr 2025-Mar 2026); D1 gives 4.6% as the average % change for 2024-25 (Apr 2024-Mar 2025). Different fiscal years, so the values need not match. D4's own series 'Consumer prices - Combined 5.5 6.7 5.4 4.6 2.8 4.0' carries 4.6 in the FY2024/25 slot, exactly matching D1's 4.6 for 2024-25.

2.8% is D4's FY2025/26 projection for combined CPI; 4.6% is D1's all-groups General Index outturn for 2024-25. The gap is a one-year period difference, and D4's series slot for FY2024/25 is itself 4.6, identical to D1's 4.6.

D4's 2.8% is projected for FY2025/26 while D1's 5.4% is the 2023-24 all-groups outturn — two years apart. D4's series ('...6.7 5.4 4.6 2.8 4.0') also shows 5.4 in the FY2023/24 slot, matching D1 exactly.

D4's 2.8% is headline combined CPI (all groups) projected for FY2025/26; D1's 6.7% is the Food and Beverages sub-group for 2024-25. Different index (sub-group vs headline) and different year — not the same attribute.
D4's 4.0% is a projection for FY2026/27; D1's 4.6% is the 2024-25 average % change. Two fiscal years apart. The FY2024/25 slot of D4's own series ('5.5 6.7 5.4 4.6 2.8 4.0') is 4.6, agreeing with D1.
4.0% is D4's FY2026/27 combined-CPI projection; 4.6% is D1's 2024-25 General Index (All Groups) outturn. Different periods explain the gap, and D4's FY2024/25 entry is itself 4.6.
D4 projects 4.0% for FY2026/27 while D1 reports 5.4% actual for 2023-24 — three fiscal years apart. D4's series carries 5.4 for FY2023/24, matching D1's actual.
D4's 4.0% is projected headline combined CPI for FY2026/27; D1's 6.7% is the Food and Beverages sub-index for 2024-25. Different sub-aggregate and different period — a false match.

D4 reports gross saving at 32.3 percent of GDP for FY2024/25; D1 reports gross savings at 30.3 per cent of GNDI for 2023-24. Two differences explain the gap: the denominator (GDP vs Gross National Disposable Income, which is the larger base) and the year. D4's own FY2023/24 entry is 32.6% of GDP against D1's 30.3% of GNDI for the same year, confirming the gap is denominator-driven rather than a disagreement.
D4's 32.3% is a gross saving ratio (percent of GDP) for FY2024/25; D3 cites the IMF's level of India's GDP as US$3.9 trillion in calendar 2024. A ratio and a level are different attributes.

D4's 32.9% is gross investment as a share of GDP for FY2024/25; D1's 30.3% is gross savings as a share of GNDI for 2023-24. Investment and saving are distinct aggregates (their gap is the current account), on different denominators and years.

D4's gross investment is a domestic capital formation ratio (32.9% of GDP, FY2024/25); D1's US$10,980 million is net foreign investment in the BoP capital account for Apr-Dec 2024. Different attributes.
Gross domestic investment as a share of GDP (D4, 32.9%) is not the same measure as gross FDI inflows in dollars (D2, USD 55.6 billion for Apr-Nov FY25).
D4's 32.9% of GDP is total gross domestic investment for FY2024/25; D2's USD 47.2 billion is gross FDI inflows over the first eight months of FY24. Different attribute and different period.
D4 measures aggregate gross investment as a percent of GDP; D1's US$ 81.0 billion is gross FDI inflows for 2024-25. FDI is one financing source, not the investment ratio.
D1's 30.3 per cent of GNDI is the domestic gross savings rate for 2023-24; D2's USD 55.6 billion is gross FDI inflows for Apr-Nov FY25. Different attributes and periods.
Domestic gross savings as a share of GNDI (D1, 30.3%, 2023-24) and gross FDI inflows in dollars (D2, USD 47.2 billion, Apr-Nov FY24) are unrelated measures.

D1's US$10,980 million is net foreign investment (FDI plus portfolio, net) for Apr-Dec 2024; D2's USD 47.2 billion is gross FDI inflows for Apr-Nov FY24 — a different year as well as a gross-versus-net definition. Both differences must be applied before the figures are comparable.

D4's -4.9 percent is the central government fiscal balance as a share of GDP for FY2024/25; D1's -13,821 million is the overall balance of payments (external account) for Apr-Dec 2024. A fiscal deficit and a BoP overall balance are entirely different accounts, in different units.

D4's -7.9 percent of GDP is the consolidated (Centre plus States) fiscal balance for FY2024/25; D1's -US$13,821 million is the balance of payments overall balance for Apr-Dec 2024. Different account, different unit, different coverage.

Both cover the same year and scope: D1 puts general government debt at 81.9 per cent of GDP in 2024-25 (BE) and D4 at 81.6 percent for FY2024/25. D1's figure rests on the 2024-25 Budget Estimates, while D4's is an IMF staff estimate completed 6 November 2025 with later outturn and nominal-GDP data. A 0.3pp gap between a budget-stage estimate and a post-year staff estimate is a vintage difference, not a disagreement.

D4's 81.6 percent is end-FY2024/25; D1's 81.8 per cent is 2023-24 (RE). Adjacent but different fiscal years, so the 0.2pp difference is a period effect. Note D4's own FY2023/24 slot in 'General government debt 4/ 83.5 82.2 80.7 81.6 81.1 80.7' reads 80.7, about 1.1pp below D1's 81.8 RE for that year — a separate coverage/GDP-base difference worth checking if the two series are used together.

D4's 81.6 percent of GDP is general government (public sector) debt; D2's USD 711.8 billion is India's total external debt as of September 2024, which is owed to non-residents by all sectors. Different attribute and unit.

General government debt as a percent of GDP (D4) and the stock of external debt in dollars as of September 2024 (D2) measure different liabilities — domestic-plus-external public debt versus all-sector cross-border debt.
D1's 81.9 per cent of GDP is Centre-plus-States government debt for 2024-25 (BE); D2's USD 711.8 billion is the September 2024 external debt stock. Different borrower universe and different unit.
D1's 81.8 per cent of GDP is general government debt for 2023-24 (RE); D2's USD 711.8 billion is external debt at end-September 2024. Different attribute, unit and reference date.
A government-debt-to-GDP ratio (D1, 2023-24 RE) and an external debt stock in dollars (D2, September 2024) are not the same measure.

D4 lists broad money growth of 9.4 percent y/y end-period for FY2024/25 as an estimate; D1 reports M3 growth of 9.6 per cent as on March 21, 2025, the last reporting Friday of that year. Same concept and same year-end, differing by 0.2pp because D4 carries a staff estimate on a March-31 end-period convention while D1 uses the actual reporting-Friday observation.

Both are FY2024-25 broad-money growth: D4's 9.4 percent (estimate, end-period) against D1's 9.6 per cent (y-o-y as of March 21, 2025). The 0.2pp gap reflects the estimate versus the actual reporting-date observation, not a substantive disagreement.

D1's appendix records M3 change of 9.6 per cent for 2024-25 with the explicit note that data relate to March 21, 2025; D4's estimate for the same year is 9.4 percent end-period. Same series, 0.2pp apart on estimate-vs-actual and end-date convention.

D4's 9.4 percent refers to FY2024/25; D1's 11.2 per cent is the year-ago comparison as on March 22, 2024, i.e. FY2023-24. Different years — and D4's own series ('8.8 9.0 11.6 9.4 9.3 9.6') shows 11.6 in the FY2023/24 slot, close to D1's 11.2 on a slightly different end-date convention.

D4's 9.4 percent is a growth rate; D1's 272.1 lakh crore (INR trillion) is the outstanding stock of M3 as on March 21, 2025. A level and a growth rate are different attributes, though the same D1 line also carries the 9.6 growth figure.

D4 reports merchandise exports of US$441.8 billion for FY2024/25 explicitly on a balance of payments basis; D1 reports US$ 437.4 billion for 2024-25, the customs/DGCI&S trade figure tied to its 0.1 per cent y-o-y statement. The US$4.4 billion gap is the standard BoP-versus-customs coverage and valuation adjustment, not a conflict.
D4's 441.8 is a dollar level of exports for FY2024/25; D1's 0.1 per cent is the growth rate for the same year. Level and growth are different attributes (they are consistent, but not the same claim).
D4 gives a full-year export level in dollars; D1's -4.4 per cent is a Q4 2024-25 y-o-y growth rate. Different attribute and different period.
A full-year dollar level of exports (D4, 441.8 billion) is not comparable to a growth rate for April-December 2024 (D2, 1.6 per cent YoY).
D4 reports an export level for FY2024/25; D2 reports 1.6 per cent YoY growth for April-December 2024. Different attribute and period span.
D1's US$ 437.4 billion is a full-year export level; D2's 1.6 per cent is an April-December 2024 growth rate. Different attributes.
An export value in dollars for 2024-25 (D1) and a YoY growth rate for April-December FY25 (D2) are different measures.

D1's -4.4 per cent is Q4 2024-25 (Jan-Mar 2025) export growth; D2's +1.6 per cent covers April-December 2024. Non-overlapping quarters of the same fiscal year, so opposite signs are expected rather than contradictory — together they yield the 0.1 per cent full-year figure D1 reports.

D4's 6.6% is a staff projection for FY2025/26 (1 Apr 2025-31 Mar 2026); D2's 6.4% is the First Advance Estimate for FY25 (1 Apr 2024-31 Mar 2025). Different fiscal years, so the 0.2pp gap is not a disagreement. D4's own row shows 6.5 for FY2024/25 immediately before the 6.6.

Same attribute (India real GDP growth) but different years: D4 projects 6.6% for FY2025/26, while D2 estimates 6.4% for FY25 (2024-04-01..2025-03-31). Successive fiscal years cannot contradict each other.
D2's 6.0% is a half-year outturn (H1 FY25, Apr-Sep 2024); D4's 6.6% is a full-year projection for FY2025/26. Neither the period nor the horizon match, so the values are not comparable.
D1 reports 6.5% actual growth for 2024-25; D4 projects 6.6% for FY2025/26, the following year. D4's table row ("...9.2 6.5 6.6 6.2...") itself carries 6.5 for FY2024/25, consistent with D1.
D1's 6.5% is the Second Advance Estimate for 2024-25; D4's 6.6% is a projection for FY2025/26. Different fiscal years; D4's same row shows 6.5 for FY2024/25, matching D1.
D1 states the economy grew 6.5% in 2024-25 (constant prices); D4's 6.6% covers FY2025/26. The years differ, and D4's table lists 6.5 for FY2024/25.

D1's 9.2% is the 2023-24 comparator; D4's 6.6% is a FY2025/26 projection — three fiscal years apart. D4's row ("9.7 7.6 9.2 6.5 6.6 6.2") independently carries 9.2 in the FY2023/24 slot, so the series agree.
D4's 6.2% is a staff projection for FY2026/27 (Apr 2026-Mar 2027); D2's 6.4% is the First Advance Estimate for FY25 (Apr 2024-Mar 2025). Two years apart, so the values are not in competition.
Same attribute, different years: 6.2% projected for FY2026/27 in D4 versus 6.4% estimated for FY25 in D2. A projection two years ahead cannot contradict a current-year estimate.
D2's 6.0% is a half-year outturn for Apr-Sep 2024; D4's 6.2% is a full-year FY2026/27 projection. Neither period nor basis coincide.
D1 reports 6.5% actual for 2024-25; D4 projects 6.2% for FY2026/27, two fiscal years later. D4's own series carries 6.5 in the FY2024/25 slot, matching D1.
D1's 6.5% is the Second Advance Estimate for 2024-25; D4's 6.2% is a projection for FY2026/27. Different years, and D4's table shows 6.5 for FY2024/25, agreeing with D1.
6.5% in D1 refers to 2024-25 at constant prices; 6.2% in D4 is the FY2026/27 baseline projection made under prolonged 50% U.S. tariffs. Different periods and forward-looking basis.
D1's 9.2% is the 2023-24 outturn; D4's 6.2% is a FY2026/27 projection — three years apart. D4's row independently shows 9.2 for FY2023/24, so the underlying series agree.

Both are CPI headline inflation for FY2024-25, but D2 (published 31 Jan 2025) reports 4.9% for April-December 2024 only, while D4 gives 4.6% as the full-year FY2024/25 period average. The sharp disinflation in Jan-Mar 2025 pulls the 12-month average below the 9-month figure, so 4.9% (9M) and 4.6% (12M) are consistent.
D2's 5.4% is FY24 (2023-24) retail inflation; D4's 4.6% is FY2024/25. Different years — and D4's row ("5.5 6.7 5.4 4.6 2.8...") carries 5.4 in the FY2023/24 slot, exactly matching D2's FY24 figure.

Same year (2024-25) but different indices: D4's 4.6% is all-groups consumer price inflation, while D1's 6.7% is the CPI food group alone. Food is a sub-index that ran well above headline in 2024-25, which is why headline sits lower.

D1's 6.7% average for 2024-25 is food inflation specifically ("food inflation remained elevated"); D4's 4.6% is the headline consumer price index for the same FY2024/25. Sub-index versus aggregate, not a conflicting measurement.
D1's 7.0% is CPI food-group inflation in 2023-24; D4's 4.6% is headline consumer prices in FY2024/25. Both the index (food vs all-groups) and the year differ.
D4's 2.8% is a projected FY2025/26 average; D2's 4.9% covers Apr-Dec of FY25 (2024-25). Different fiscal years, and D4's figure is forward-looking.
5.4% in D2 is FY24 retail inflation; 2.8% in D4 is the FY2025/26 projection — two years apart. D4's own series shows 5.4 for FY2023/24, matching D2.
D1's 6.7% is CPI food-group inflation for 2024-25; D4's 2.8% is projected all-groups consumer price inflation for FY2025/26. Different index and different year.
Food inflation of 6.7% in 2024-25 (D1) is a sub-index of a prior year; D4's 2.8% is headline CPI projected for FY2025/26. Neither scope nor period coincides.
D1's 7.0% food inflation is for 2023-24; D4's 2.8% is a headline CPI projection for FY2025/26 — different index and three fiscal years apart.

D4's 4.0% is a medium-term projection for FY2026/27 (the anchor value repeated across its forecast horizon); D2's 4.9% is the actual Apr-Dec 2024 outturn within FY25. Different periods and estimate-vs-projection basis.
5.4% is D2's FY24 retail inflation outturn; 4.0% is D4's FY2026/27 projection, three fiscal years later. D4's row separately carries 5.4 in the FY2023/24 position.
D1's 6.7% measures the CPI food group in 2024-25; D4's 4.0% is projected all-groups consumer price inflation for FY2026/27. Different index and different year.
D1 reports food inflation averaging 6.7% in 2024-25; D4's 4.0% is headline CPI projected for FY2026/27. Sub-index versus headline, plus a two-year period gap.
D1's 7.0% is food-group CPI inflation in 2023-24; D4's 4.0% is a headline consumer price projection for FY2026/27 — different measure and different period.

D2's 4.9% is headline retail (all-groups CPI) inflation for Apr-Dec of FY25; D1's 6.7% is the CPI food group average for the full 2024-25. D2 itself notes the headline moderation came "despite challenging food price dynamics", i.e. food ran above headline.

Headline retail inflation of 4.9% (D2, Apr-Dec FY25) versus food inflation of 6.7% (D1, full 2024-25). Food is a component that stayed elevated above the all-groups index, and the periods also differ (9 months vs 12).
D2's 4.9% is all-groups retail inflation for Apr-Dec 2024 (within FY25); D1's 7.0% is food-group inflation for 2023-24. Different index and different year.

Both cover 2023-24 (FY24), but D2's 5.4% is headline retail inflation across all groups while D1's 7.0% is the CPI food group. The food sub-index running ~1.6pp above headline in FY24 is the well-documented pattern, not a contradiction.
D2's 5.4% is FY24 headline retail inflation; D1's 6.7% is FY2024-25 food-group inflation. Different index and different fiscal year.
Headline CPI of 5.4% in FY24 (D2) versus food inflation of 6.7% in 2024-25 (D1) — a sub-index for the following year, so neither scope nor period matches.

The denominators differ: D4 reports gross saving at 32.3 percent of GDP for FY2024/25, while D1's appendix reports gross savings at 30.3 per cent of GNDI for 2023-24. GNDI exceeds GDP (net factor income and transfers), so the same saving flow yields a lower ratio; the years also differ, and D4's series shows 32.6 (of GDP) for FY2023/24.

D4's 32.3 percent is a gross saving rate as a share of GDP for FY2024/25; D3 cites the IMF's estimate of India's GDP level of US$3.9 trillion in calendar 2024. A ratio and a currency level are different attributes with nothing to reconcile.

D1's figure is a savings rate (30.3 per cent of GNDI, 2023-24); D3's is the absolute size of India's economy (US$3.9 trillion, calendar 2024, per the IMF). Different attributes, different units, no shared claim.

D3's 32.9% is gross investment as a percent of GDP for FY2024/25; D1's 30.3% is gross savings as a percent of GNDI for 2023-24. Different attribute (investment vs savings), different denominator (GDP vs GNDI) and different year — the pair was matched only on the word 'gross'.

D3's 32.9 percent of GDP is domestic gross investment (capital formation); D1's US$81.0 billion is gross FDI inflows, a cross-border financing flow measured in dollars. Different attributes and different units — no common quantity to compare.

Both refer to the central government deficit for 2024-25, but D3 reports -4.9% of GDP on the IMF definition, whose own footnote states divestment and license proceeds are treated as financing (below the line), while D1's 4.7% is the Indian budget's Gross Fiscal Deficit (revised estimates), which nets those receipts above the line. Reclassifying those receipts as financing raises the measured deficit, which accounts for the ~0.2pp gap.

D1 states the GFD at 4.7 per cent of GDP in 2024-25 (RE); D3 shows -4.9 percent of GDP for FY2024/25. Same period and same government, but D3's series footnote treats divestment/license proceeds as financing rather than revenue, which mechanically widens the deficit relative to India's budget GFD concept.

D1's appendix row '2024-25 (RE)# ... 4.7' is the Centre's GFD on the budget definition; D3's -4.9 for FY2024/25 is the IMF staff measure that treats divestment and license proceeds as financing. Identical period and scope (Centre), so the 0.2pp difference is a coverage-of-receipts definition difference, not a disagreement on the fiscal outturn.

D3's -4.9% is FY2024/25 (year ended March 2025); D1's 4.4% is the 2025-26 Budget Estimate (Apr 2025-Mar 2026). Different fiscal years on a declining consolidation path — D3's own series shows -4.5 for the following year — so the two figures are not in conflict.

Both cover FY2025-26: D3 projects a central government balance of -4.5% of GDP, D1 cites the Budget Estimate GFD of 4.4%. The 0.1pp gap follows from D3's stated treatment of divestment/license proceeds as financing rather than receipts, plus D3 being a November 2025 staff projection against a February 2025 budget target.

D3's -4.5% is the FY2025/26 projection while D1's 4.7% is the 2024-25 Revised Estimate — consecutive but distinct fiscal years. D1 itself frames 4.4% in 2025-26 (BE) as 'down from 4.7 per cent in 2024-25 (RE)', confirming the decline is a period effect.

D3's -4.5% refers to FY2025/26 (Apr 2025-Mar 2026); D1's 4.7 per cent refers to 2024-25 (RE). The consolidation path in D1's own sentence ('4.4 per cent in 2025-26 (BE), down from 4.7 per cent in 2024-25 (RE)') explains the difference as year-to-year change.

D3's -4.5% is a FY2025/26 projection; D1's 4.7% is the 2024-25 revised-estimate GFD. Different years, with the deficit budgeted to fall between them, so the values are consistent rather than conflicting.

D3's 56.3% of GDP is central government debt, a stock; D1's 4.7% of GDP is the gross fiscal deficit, an annual flow. Same government and same year, but different attributes entirely — a debt level cannot corroborate or contradict a deficit.

Both give general government debt for 2024-25: D1 says 81.9 per cent of GDP on Budget Estimates, D3 estimates 81.6 percent. D3's figure was produced in November 2025 using outturn GDP and fiscal data rather than the budget projections D1 relied on, and D3's footnote defines the aggregate as combined domestic liabilities of centre and states plus sovereign external debt. A 0.3pp gap between a budget estimate and a later staff estimate on a slightly different perimeter is a vintage/definition difference, not a disagreement.

D1's 81.8 per cent is 2023-24 (RE); D3's 81.6 percent is FY2024/25. Different fiscal years — D3's own series carries 80.7 for the preceding year — so the figures describe different points on the debt path rather than conflicting readings of one year.

D3's 81.6 percent of GDP is general government (centre plus states) debt, overwhelmingly domestic public liabilities. D2's USD 711.8 billion as of September 2024 is India's total external debt, which is mostly private/corporate borrowing from abroad. Different perimeter, different units and different reference date.

D1's 81.9 per cent of GDP measures general government debt for 2024-25 (BE); D2's USD 711.8 billion is the stock of external debt at end-September 2024, cited in the context of reserve cover. Public-sector domestic debt versus economy-wide external liabilities — different attributes with no shared basis.

D3 reports merchandise export growth of 0.1 percent in U.S. dollar terms for FY2024/25 and D1 states exports 'grew marginally by 0.1 per cent in 2024-25'. Identical period (Apr 2024-Mar 2025), identical measure and identical value.

D3's 0.1 percent FY2024/25 merchandise export growth matches D1 page 77: 'merchandise exports increased marginally by 0.1 per cent year-on-year'. Same fiscal year, same dollar-denominated y-o-y basis, same figure.

D3's 0.1 percent covers the full FY2024/25; D2's 1.6 per cent YoY covers only April-December 2024, nine months of that year. The full-year figure is lower because exports contracted in the final quarter — D1 records -4.4 per cent y-o-y in Q4 2024-25 — pulling the annual rate down from the nine-month pace.

D2's 'modest growth of 1.6 per cent (YoY basis)' is for April-December 2024, whereas D3's 0.1 percent is the whole of FY2024/25. The Jan-Mar 2025 quarter, which D1 shows at -4.4 per cent y-o-y, drags the twelve-month rate below the nine-month one.

D1's -4.4 per cent is a single quarter (Q4 2024-25, Jan-Mar 2025) on a y-o-y basis; D3's 0.1 percent is the full FY2024/25 average. A weak closing quarter is consistent with a flat full year given the positive earlier quarters (D1's series shows 5.9 and 3.0 in intervening quarters).

D1's 0.1 per cent is full-year 2024-25; D2's 1.6 per cent YoY is April-December 2024 only. D2 was published 31 January 2025, before the year ended, so it could only report nine months; the weaker Jan-Mar quarter reduces the annual figure to 0.1 per cent.

Same series, different windows: D2 reports 1.6 per cent YoY for April-December 2024 while D1 reports 0.1 per cent for the complete 2024-25 fiscal year. The three months D2 could not observe (Jan-Mar 2025) were negative, which reconciles the two rates.

D1's 0.1 per cent y-o-y is for all of 2024-25; D2's 1.6 per cent YoY covers April-December 2024. The nine-month figure predates the Q4 contraction (-4.4 per cent y-o-y per D1), so the two are consistent readings of different windows.

Both measure y-o-y merchandise export growth, but D2's 1.6 per cent spans April-December 2024 and D1's 0.1 per cent spans the full 2024-25 year. Adding the negative January-March quarter to D2's window produces D1's near-flat annual rate.

D1's -4.4 per cent is Q4 of 2024-25 (Jan-Mar 2025) alone; D2's 1.6 per cent is the cumulative April-December 2024 growth. Non-overlapping windows within the same fiscal year — the quarterly contraction is exactly what brings the full-year rate down to 0.1 per cent.

D3 reports merchandise import growth of 6.2 percent in U.S. dollar terms for FY2024/25; D1 states 'merchandise imports grew by 6.2 per cent during this period' for 2024-25. Identical period, measure and value.

D3's 6.2 percent is the full FY2024/25 outturn; D2's 5.2 per cent YoY covers only April-December FY25. D2 was published 31 January 2025 and could not include Jan-Mar 2025, so the nine-month pace differs from the twelve-month one.

D2 reports imports growing 5.2 per cent during April-December 2024, while D3 reports 6.2 percent for the whole of FY2024/25. Nine months versus twelve months of the same year; D1's quarterly series (9.7 and 6.5 per cent in the middle quarters) shows the later months lifting the annual average above the nine-month rate.

D1's 1.2 per cent is a single quarter (Q4 2024-25, Jan-Mar 2025) y-o-y; D3's 6.2 percent is the full FY2024/25. A soft final quarter is compatible with a 6.2 per cent annual rate given the stronger preceding quarters D1 lists (7.6, 9.7, 6.5).

D1's -5.3 per cent refers explicitly to 2023-24 ('the previous year'), whereas D3's 6.2 percent is FY2024/25. Different fiscal years; D3's own series carries -4.9 for FY2023/24, so a swing from contraction to growth across the year boundary is expected.

D1's 6.2 per cent is full-year 2024-25 import growth; D2's 5.2 per cent YoY is April-December FY25 only. The two describe the same series over different windows, with the January-March 2025 months (absent from D2, published 31 January 2025) accounting for the difference.
D2 measures April-December 2024 (5.2 per cent) and D1 the complete 2024-25 year (6.2 per cent). Same measure, different length of window; D2 simply had no Q4 data at its 31 January 2025 publication.

D1's 1.2 per cent covers only Q4 2024-25 (Jan-Mar 2025) while D2's 5.2 per cent is cumulative April-December 2024. The windows do not overlap, so the slower closing quarter does not contradict the stronger nine-month cumulative rate.

D1's -5.3 per cent is the 2023-24 full-year import contraction; D2's 5.2 per cent is growth during April-December 2024 (FY25). Different fiscal years, and the FY25 growth is measured against that contracted FY24 base.

D3 (p.79) states "India's R&D expenditure represented only 0.6 percent of GDP in 2020" (UNESCO); D1 (p.17) states "India's relatively low share of research & development (R&D) expenditure in GDP (0.6 per cent)". Same subject, same attribute, identical value of 0.6 per cent. D1 gives no explicit year, but its comparator framing matches the same low-share point, so the two agree.

D3 reports India's gross domestic R&D expenditure at "0.6 percent of GDP in 2020" on UNESCO data; D1 (p.35) says "the ratio of R&D expenditure in GDP rose marginally from 0.61 per cent to 0.64 per cent ... between 1995-96 and 2020-21". 0.64 rounds to 0.6 at one decimal, and the reference periods differ only by the calendar-2020 versus April 2020-March 2021 convention (plus UNESCO versus Indian DST source), so the values are consistent rather than conflicting.

D3's 0.6 percent of GDP is explicitly for 2020; D1's 0.61 per cent is the start point of a series "between 1995-96 and 2020-21", i.e. the 1995-96 value. The near-identical numbers refer to different years 25 years apart, and D1 itself notes the ratio "rose marginally" over that span, which explains why the two figures look alike without being the same observation.

D3 measures India's R&D expenditure as a share of its own GDP (0.6 percent in 2020); D1 (p.35) measures India's share of world R&D expenditure ("rose from 2.1 per cent in 2000 to 2.6 per cent in 2023", WIPO). Different denominators and different attributes, so the percentages are not comparable.

D3's 0.6 percent refers to India; D1's 2.4 per cent refers to China ("such as China (2.4 per cent), Korea (4.8 per cent) and Malaysia (1 per cent)"). Same attribute but different countries, so no agreement or conflict is implied.
