D3's figure is India's R&D/GDP ratio (0.6 percent, 2020); D1's 4.8 per cent is Korea's. Different entities in the same comparator sentence, so the pair is a false match on subject.
D3 gives India 0.6 percent of GDP for R&D; D1's 1 per cent is Malaysia's figure in the comparator list. Different countries, so the values are not in the same comparison.

D3's 0.9 percent of GDP is the "G20 emerging market average", a group aggregate; D1's 0.6 per cent is India's own R&D/GDP share. A country value and a peer-group average are different subjects, so the gap between 0.6 and 0.9 is not a disagreement.

D3 reports a G20 emerging-market average of 0.9 percent of GDP; D1 reports China individually at 2.4 per cent. One is a multi-country average, the other a single country within (or alongside) that group, so they measure different things.

D3's 0.9 percent is a G20 emerging-market average; D1's 4.8 per cent is Korea's national R&D/GDP ratio. Different subjects (group average versus one advanced-economy country), so no corroboration or conflict.
D3's 0.9 percent of GDP is an emerging-market group average; D1's 1 per cent is Malaysia alone. Similar magnitudes but different subjects, so this is a false match rather than agreement.

D3's 2.2 percent of GDP is "the advanced economies average"; D1's 0.6 per cent is India's own ratio. Different subjects — a group average versus a single emerging-market country — so the difference is by construction, not a discrepancy.

D3 gives an advanced-economy average of 2.2 percent of GDP; D1 gives China at 2.4 per cent. A group average and an individual country are different subjects, so the near values neither corroborate nor contradict.

D3's 2.2 percent is the advanced-economy mean; D1's 4.8 per cent is Korea specifically. Korea may be one component of that average, but a component and an aggregate are distinct measurements, so the pair is a false match.
D3's 2.2 percent of GDP is an advanced-economy average; D1's 1 per cent is Malaysia. Different entities entirely, with no shared subject to compare.

D3's 2.2 percent of GDP for 2020 is an advanced-economy average; D1's 0.64 per cent for 2020-21 is India's ratio. Same attribute and near-identical period, but different subjects, so the gap reflects India's position relative to the AE benchmark rather than conflicting data.

D3 (p.80) reports the higher-education sector's share of India's total R&D spending ("only 10 percent", DST 2023); D1 (p.35) reports India's share of global R&D expenditure (2.6 per cent in 2023, WIPO). Both are 2023 percentages but of entirely different bases — performer split within India versus India's weight in the world total.

D3's 10 percent is the higher-education share of India's own R&D spending in 2023; D1's 2.1 per cent is India's share of global R&D expenditure in 2000. Different attribute and different year, so there is nothing to reconcile.

D3 (p.87) ranks India's stock market — "now the fourth largest globally" — while D2 (p.34) ranks India's economy: "Currently the fifth-largest economy in the world". Different ranked quantities (equity market capitalisation versus GDP), so fourth versus fifth is not a conflict.

D3 states a current stock-market ranking (fourth largest globally); D2 makes a forward-looking claim about economic size, "likely to be among the top three economic powers in the world by 2035". Different attribute (market versus economy) and different horizon (current versus 2035 projection).

D3 reports the composition of India's corporate bond stock by rating — "AAA (86 percent), AA (10 percent)" — a share of outstanding issuance. D1's 7.62 per cent is the March 2025 monthly-average yield on AAA-rated 3-year corporate bonds (Table II.5.2). Both mention AAA but measure different quantities (share versus yield), so they are not comparable.

D4's 7.9% is a quarterly, not-seasonally-adjusted y-o-y GDP growth forecast for the July-September 2025 quarter (September 2025 vintage), whereas D3 quotes an RBI projection of 7.2% for the full fiscal year FY25 (Apr 2024-Mar 2025). Different reference periods (one quarter of FY26 vs all of FY25) and different forecasters, so the 0.7pp gap is not a disagreement about the same number.

D4 forecasts 7.9% y-o-y growth for a single quarter (2025Q3, i.e. Q2 of FY2025/26), while D2 gives a full-year FY26 range of 'between 6.3 and 6.8 per cent'. A single quarter's y-o-y rate can exceed the annual average; the periods (one quarter vs twelve months) differ, so the figures are not comparable point estimates.

D3 cites an RBI projection of 7.2% for FY25 (Apr 2024-Mar 2025); D2 projects 6.3-6.8% for FY26 (Apr 2025-Mar 2026). Different forecast years and different forecasters (RBI vs Economic Survey), so the values are not in conflict.

D4's 81.6 is general government public (domestic plus external) debt expressed as a percent of GDP for FY2024/25; D2's 711.8 is India's external debt stock in USD billion at end-September 2024. Different attributes, units and reference dates - a false match on the word 'debt'.

D4 reports public debt of 81.6 percent of GDP (general government, FY2024/25); D2 reports external debt of USD 711.8 billion as of September 2024. Different concepts (public vs external debt) and different units (% of GDP vs USD billion).

81.6 percent of GDP of general government public debt (D4, FY2024/25) and USD 717.9 billion of external debt stock (D1, end-December 2024) measure different things in different units; they are not competing estimates of one quantity.

D4's 81.1 is a projected general government public debt ratio (percent of GDP) for FY2025/26; D2's USD 711.8 billion is the external debt stock at September 2024. Different attribute, unit and period - a false match.
Public debt as a share of GDP projected for FY2025/26 (81.1%) has no common attribute with an external debt stock of USD 711.8 billion at September 2024; the units and the debt concepts differ.

D4's 81.1 percent-of-GDP public debt projection for FY2025/26 and D1's USD 717.9 billion external debt stock at end-December 2024 are different indicators in different units; no comparison is possible.
D4 projects general government public debt of 80.7 percent of GDP for FY2026/27; D2 states external debt of USD 711.8 billion at September 2024. Different attributes and units.
A projected public-debt-to-GDP ratio of 80.7% for FY2026/27 (D4) is not the same measure as a USD 711.8 billion external debt stock at September 2024 (D2); the pair is a false match on 'debt'.
D4's 80.7 percent of GDP public debt projection (FY2026/27) and D1's USD 717.9 billion external debt at end-December 2024 differ in concept, unit and period.

D4's 71.0 is an extended projection of general government public debt as a percent of GDP for FY2034/35; D2's USD 711.8 billion is the September 2024 external debt stock. No shared attribute, unit or period.
A FY2034/35 public-debt-to-GDP projection of 71.0% (D4) cannot be compared with an external debt level of USD 711.8 billion at September 2024 (D2); different measures entirely.
D4's 71.0 percent of GDP public debt projection for FY2034/35 and D1's USD 717.9 billion external debt stock at end-December 2024 measure different concepts in different units and periods.

D4 lists real GDP growth of 6.5 percent for FY2024/25 as an actual outturn; D1 states 'real GDP growth moderated to 6.5 per cent in 2024-25'. Same subject, same April 2024-March 2025 period, same value.
Both report 6.5 per cent real GDP growth for FY2024-25: D4 as an actual in its DSA memo line, D1 on the basis of the Second Advance Estimates. Identical value and identical fiscal year.
D1 says the economy 'grown by 6.5 per cent in 2024-25' at constant prices, matching D4's 6.5 percent real GDP growth for FY2024/25. Same period and same figure.

D2 (published 31 Jan 2025) gives 6.4 per cent for FY25 from the First Advance Estimates, while D4 (staff report completed Nov 2025) cites 6.5 percent for FY2024/25 as an actual outturn. The 0.1pp gap is the standard advance-estimate-to-actual revision, not a disagreement.

D2's 6.4 per cent for FY25 is explicitly an estimate ('is estimated to grow') from the First Advance Estimates published January 2025; D4's 6.5 percent for the same FY2024/25 is a later actual. Data vintage explains the 0.1pp difference.

D2's 6.0 per cent covers only H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024), whereas D4's 6.5 percent is full-year FY2024/25 growth. Stronger second-half growth lifts the annual figure above the half-year rate; the periods differ.

D1's 9.2 per cent is explicitly the prior-year comparator for 2023-24, while D4's 6.5 percent is FY2024/25 growth. Different fiscal years; D1 itself contrasts 6.5 per cent in 2024-25 'with 9.2 per cent a year ago'.
D4's 6.6 percent is a staff projection for FY2025/26 (Apr 2025-Mar 2026), while D2's 6.4 per cent is the First Advance Estimate for FY25 (Apr 2024-Mar 2025). Consecutive but different fiscal years.
D2 estimates 6.4 per cent growth for FY25; D4 projects 6.6 percent for the following year FY2025/26. Different reference years and different bases (advance estimate vs staff projection).
D2's 6.0 per cent covers H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024) actuals; D4's 6.6 percent is a full-year projection for FY2025/26. Neither the year nor the period length coincides.
D1 reports actual growth of 6.5 per cent for 2024-25; D4's 6.6 percent is a baseline projection for the next year, FY2025/26. Different fiscal years, so no conflict.
D1's 6.5 per cent is the Second Advance Estimate for 2024-25; D4's 6.6 percent is a projection for FY2025/26. The periods differ by one full fiscal year.
D1 records 6.5 per cent constant-price growth for 2024-25, while D4 projects 6.6 percent for FY2025/26 under its DSA baseline. Adjacent but distinct years.
D1's 9.2 per cent is the 2023-24 outturn used as the prior-year comparator; D4's 6.6 percent is a projection for FY2025/26, two fiscal years later. Different periods and bases (actual vs projection).

D6's table column for FY2024/25 gives external debt at 18.8% of GDP 'end-period', i.e. as at 31 March 2025, while D3 states '18.5 per cent as at end-March 2024'. The reference dates are a full year apart, so the 0.3pp gap is a period difference, not a disagreement; D6's own series (19.2, 19.0, 18.8...) shows the ratio moving year to year.

D3 reports the external-debt-to-GDP ratio 'remained modest at 19.1 per cent as at end-December 2024' (provisional), whereas D6's 18.8% is the FY2024/25 end-period figure, i.e. as at end-March 2025. Different measurement dates three months apart, plus D3's figure is provisional, so 19.1% vs 18.8% is a period/vintage difference rather than a contradiction.

D6 expresses external debt as a ratio (18.8% of GDP, end-March 2025) while D4 gives the stock level ('external debt of USD 711.8 billion as of September 2024'). They are the same series in different units and at different dates; against D6's own FY2024/25 GDP of US$3,910bn, USD 711.8bn is ~18.2%, consistent with an 18.8% end-March 2025 ratio.

Same relationship as the other D4 mention: D4 quotes the stock ('USD 711.8 billion as of September 2024') and D6 quotes the ratio (18.8% of GDP at FY2024/25 end-period). Level vs percent-of-GDP, and September 2024 vs March 2025; the two are arithmetically compatible (711.8/3,910 ≈ 18.2%).

D3's appendix gives the external debt stock as US$717.9bn at end-December 2024; D6 gives 18.8% of GDP at FY2024/25 end-period (end-March 2025). Different units (US$ billion vs percent of GDP) and different dates; 717.9 against a ~US$3.8–3.9tn GDP is roughly 18–19%, consistent with both D6's 18.8% and D3's own 19.1% ratio.

D6's staff table shows 'GDP in billions of U.S. dollars ... 3,910' for FY2024/25; D5 says 'According to the IMF, India's GDP was US$3.9 trillion in 2024'. US$3,910bn rounds to US$3.9tn, and D5 explicitly attributes the figure to the IMF, whose India series is reported on the April–March fiscal year — the same period D6 labels FY2024/25.

D6's 3,910 is aggregate GDP in US$ billion; D5's US$2.73 thousand is GDP per capita. Different attributes (total vs per-head), so they are not competing measurements — though they are mutually consistent, since 3,910bn over ~1.43bn people is about US$2.7 thousand per person.

D6's 4,125 is the projected GDP level for FY2025/26, the column after the 3,910 FY2024/25 estimate; D5 reports IMF GDP of US$3.9 trillion for 2024. The gap is one fiscal year of nominal growth (3,910 → 4,125, ~5.5%), and D6's figure is a forward projection while D5 cites the 2024 level.

D6's 4,125 US$ billion is aggregate GDP projected for FY2025/26; D5's US$2.73 thousand is per-capita GDP for 2024. Different attribute (aggregate vs per capita) and different period, so the pair is a false match rather than a value disagreement.

Both measure regulatory capital for scheduled commercial banks under the same definition (CAR/CRAR). D4 pins its 16.7% to 'as of September 2024', while D6's 17.4% is the FY2024/25 column, i.e. the position at end-March 2025 — and D6's own series (16.3, 16.8, 17.2, 16.8, 17.4) shows the ratio moving between reporting dates, so the 0.7pp gap is a six-month period difference.

D6's 0.5% is 'Net nonperforming assets (percent of outstanding net advances)'; D3's 79.1% is the Credit-Deposit Ratio. These are entirely different banking indicators for the same sector and period, so there is nothing to corroborate or contradict.

D6 reports asset quality (net NPAs at 0.5% of net advances); D4 reports capital adequacy (CRAR of 16.7%). Same sector, different attributes measuring different things (bad loans vs regulatory capital), so the pair is a false match.

D3's 79.1% is the Credit-Deposit Ratio for scheduled commercial banks in 2024-25; D4's 16.7% is the capital-to-risk-weighted-assets ratio as of September 2024. Different attributes with different denominators — lending vs deposits against capital vs risk-weighted assets.

D6's 2.2% is 'Gross nonperforming assets (percent of outstanding advances)'; D3's 79.1% is the Credit-Deposit Ratio. Both describe scheduled commercial banks in 2024-25 but measure different quantities, so no corroboration or conflict is possible.

D6's gross NPA ratio (2.2% of outstanding advances) and D4's CRAR (16.7% as of September 2024) are distinct indicators — asset quality versus capital adequacy — for the same bank population. Different attribute, so the apparent pairing is spurious.

D6's 1.4% is return on assets (net profit as a percent of total assets); D3's 12.1% is y-o-y bank credit growth. Profitability versus credit expansion are different attributes, so the two 2024-25 figures are not comparable measurements.

D6's 1.4% return on assets and D3's 10.6% growth in aggregate deposits describe unrelated attributes (bank profitability vs deposit growth) even though both cover scheduled commercial banks in 2024-25.

D2 shows 'Total assets 11,213 11,453' (INR crore) at 31 March 2024 and D5's consolidated balance sheet shows 'Total Assets 114,530.20 112,134.30' in INR million at 31 March 2024. 114,530.20 million = 11,453.02 crore, and the prior-year columns match too (112,134.30 million = 11,213.4 crore) — the same figure in two scales.

D2's 11,453 crore is the 31 March 2024 balance; D5's 112,134.30 million (= 11,213.4 crore) is the 31 March 2023 comparative. The values differ because the dates differ by a year — and D2's own line carries 11,213 as its prior-year column, matching D5's FY23 figure exactly.

D5 reports consolidated total assets of INR 114,530.20 million as at 31 March 2024; D1's restated consolidated statement reports INR 84,294.83 million as at 31 December 2021. Same entity, same basis (consolidated) and same unit, but balance-sheet dates over two years apart, so the growth in the asset base explains the gap.

INR 45,977.98 million in D1 is the restated consolidated total assets as at 31 March 2021, while D5's INR 114,530.20 million is as at 31 March 2024. Three fiscal years apart (and D1 pre-dates the IPO and the Spoton acquisition), so these are successive point-in-time balances, not conflicting values.

D1's INR 43,573.08 million is total assets as at 31 March 2020 on a restated consolidated basis; D5's INR 114,530.20 million is as at 31 March 2024. Identical metric, entity and unit at balance-sheet dates four years apart, so the difference is purely period.

D2 gives total assets of 11,453 crore (= 114,530 million) at 31 March 2024; D1 gives 84,294.83 million at 31 December 2021. Both are Delhivery total assets but differ in scale convention and, decisively, in balance-sheet date — a nine-month interim close in 2021 versus a full-year close in 2024.

D5's INR 112,134.30 million is consolidated total assets at 31 March 2023; D1's INR 84,294.83 million is the restated consolidated figure at 31 December 2021. Same measure and unit, roughly fifteen months apart, so the increase reflects the intervening period rather than a discrepancy.

D1's INR 5,167.75 million relates to Spoton Logistics Private Limited (special purpose consolidated, 31 March 2021), a separate acquired entity, while D5's INR 114,530.20 million is Delhivery Limited's consolidated total assets at 31 March 2024. Different reporting entities, so the figures are not alternative measurements of the same thing.

Spoton Logistics' total assets of INR 5,167.75 million (D1, at 31 March 2021) and Delhivery Limited's 11,453 crore (D2, at 31 March 2024) belong to different legal entities and different dates; D1's line presents Spoton alongside Delhivery precisely because they are separate balance sheets.

D6's 20.7% is the aggregate total assets of India's non-banking financial companies expressed as a percent of GDP; D5's 114,530.20 million is Delhivery Limited's balance-sheet total. Different entity (a whole sector vs one logistics company) and different unit, so the label 'total assets' is the only thing they share.

D6 measures NBFC sector assets at 20.7% of GDP for FY2024/25; D2 reports Delhivery's company total assets of 11,453 crore at 31 March 2024. Different subjects and incommensurable units — a sector ratio versus a single firm's rupee balance.

D6 states 'India's NIIP improved to −9.6 percent of GDP in 2024, from −10.5 percent in 2023'; D3's table gives NIIP of −US$364.5 billion at end-December 2024. Same concept at essentially the same date, expressed as a ratio versus a level: −364.5 against a ~US$3.8tn 2024 GDP is about −9.6%, so the two are arithmetically consistent.

D3 states NIIP was −10.5% of GDP in calendar 2023 and improved to −9.6% of GDP in 2024; D1's appendix reports NIIP of −US$364.5 billion at end-December 2024. The two facts refer to different reference dates (end-2023 vs end-December 2024) and different units (% of GDP vs US$ billion). They are consistent: −$364.5bn against India's ~$3.8–3.9trn 2024 GDP is roughly −9.3 to −9.6%, matching D3's 2024 figure rather than its 2023 −10.5%.

D3's 27.9% is India's gross foreign assets as a percent of GDP in calendar 2024 (external IIP concept). D1's 30.3% is Gross Savings as a percent of Gross National Disposable Income for FY2023-24 (domestic saving concept). Different attribute, different denominator, different period — the only similarity is that both are percentages near 30.

D3's 37.5% measures gross foreign liabilities as a share of GDP in 2024 (external balance sheet); D1's 30.3% measures Gross Savings as a share of GNDI in 2023-24 (national accounts). Different attributes and denominators; no comparable claim.

D3's 27.9% of GDP is a stock measure (gross foreign assets outstanding in 2024); D1's US$81.0 billion is a flow measure (gross FDI inflows during 2024-25). Different attribute and different unit basis (stock share of GDP vs annual inflow in US$).

Both report gross FDI inflows, but over different windows: D1 gives US$81.0 billion for the full year 2024-25 (Apr 2024–Mar 2025, +13.7% y-o-y), while D2 gives US$55.6 billion for only the first eight months of FY25 (Apr–Nov 2024, +17.9% y-o-y). The eight-month figure annualises to roughly US$83 billion, close to D1's full-year US$81.0 billion, so the values agree once the period difference is applied.

D2's US$47.2 billion covers gross FDI inflows in the first eight months of FY24 (Apr–Nov 2023); D1's US$81.0 billion covers the full year 2024-25. These are different years and different lengths of window, so the gap is entirely period-driven; D1's stated +13.7% y-o-y for full-year FY25 and D2's +17.9% y-o-y for the eight-month window are consistent in sign and rough magnitude.

D1's US$10,980 million is net Foreign Investment in the BoP capital account for April–December 2024 (provisional), which nets outward FDI, repatriation/disinvestment and portfolio flows. D2's US$55.6 billion is gross FDI inflows only, for April–November 2024. The much smaller net figure is the expected result of subtracting repatriation and outward investment from gross inflows, not a disagreement about the same quantity; the windows also differ (9 months vs 8 months).

D3 reports a full-year FY2024/25 current account deficit of 0.6% of GDP; D1 reports 1.3% of GDP for April–December 2024 only. The nine-month figure excludes Q4 FY25, in which India recorded a current account surplus, pulling the full-year ratio down to ~0.6%. Same measure, different window.

D1's US$37.1 billion (1.3% of GDP) is the April–December 2024 CAD; D3's 0.6% of GDP is the CAD for the whole of FY2024/25. A US$37.1bn nine-month deficit reduces to roughly 0.6% of GDP for the full year only because the March 2025 quarter ran a surplus, so the difference is a period/coverage difference, not a conflicting estimate.

D1's 1.1% of GDP is the April–December 2023 CAD (nine months of FY24); D3's comparator for the prior year is 0.7% of GDP for the full FY2023/24, alongside 0.6% for FY2024/25. The lower annual ratio reflects inclusion of the Jan–Mar 2024 quarter, so the two are the same series over different windows.

D1 gives US$30.7 billion (1.1% of GDP) for April–December 2023; D3 characterises the full previous year (FY2023/24) CA deficit as 0.7% of GDP against 0.6% in FY2024/25. Different window (nine months vs full fiscal year) and different unit (US$ vs % of GDP) explain the gap; the direction of narrowing is common to both.

D2's 1.3% of GDP is a single quarter (Q2 FY24, Jul–Sep 2023); D3's 0.6% of GDP is the full-year FY2024/25 outturn. Quarterly CAD ratios are volatile and routinely exceed the annual average, so a 1.3% quarter in FY24 is not in conflict with a 0.6% annual deficit a year later.

D3's 1.0% of GDP is a staff projection for FY2025/26 (Apr 2025–Mar 2026), made in the November 2025 staff report; D1's 1.3% is an actual for April–December 2024. Different years and different status (projection vs outturn), so the values are not competing measurements.

D1's US$37.1 billion (1.3% of GDP) is the realised April–December 2024 CAD; D3's 1.0% of GDP is a forward projection for FY2025/26. Different reference years and different vintage (actual vs baseline projection under prolonged 50% U.S. tariffs), so no disagreement is implied.

D2 cites 1.3% of GDP for Q2 FY24 (Jul–Sep 2023), an actual quarterly ratio; D3 projects 1.0% of GDP for the full FY2025/26. Different periods, different frequency (quarter vs year) and different vintage (historical vs projection).

D1 reports 1.1% of GDP for April–December 2023; D2 reports 1.3% of GDP for Q2 FY24 (Jul–Sep 2023), a single quarter falling inside D1's nine-month window. A quarter above the nine-month average is arithmetically ordinary, so the two figures are the same series measured over different spans.

Both quote 1.3% of GDP, but for entirely different windows: D1's is April–December 2024 (nine months of FY25) and D2's is Q2 FY24 (Jul–Sep 2023). The numerical equality is coincidental, so this is not corroboration of a single figure; the periods must be kept distinct.

D1 reports the 40-currency REER appreciated 1.5% y-o-y in 2024-25, a comparison of fiscal-year averages. D3 says that as of March 2025 the REER stood about 2.6% below its 2024 calendar-year average, a point-in-time deviation from a calendar-year mean on the IMF's own REER measure. An FY average that is higher than the previous FY average is fully compatible with a March 2025 month-end reading below the 2024 average, given the rupee's depreciation from December 2024 onward.

D2 gives an index level (107.2 in December 2024 on the RBI 40-currency, 2015-16=100 basis); D3 gives a percentage deviation of the March 2025 REER from its 2024 average on the IMF's measure. Different index construction, different reference concept (level vs deviation) and different dates; the REER peaking around December 2024 and then falling below the 2024 average by March 2025 is consistent with both.

D1 states the 40-currency REER appreciated 1.5% y-o-y over 2024-25 (fiscal-year average change); D2 gives the December 2024 level of 107.2 on the same 40-currency index. A level reading and an annual-average percentage change are different quantities, but both point to appreciation through 2024, so they are compatible rather than conflicting.

D2's 103.2 is the April 2024 level of the 40-currency REER (2015-16=100); D1's 1.5% is the y-o-y change in the average of that index for 2024-25. The within-year rise D2 describes (103.2 in April to 107.2 in December, about +3.9%) is a monthly-level move, whereas D1's 1.5% averages the whole fiscal year against the prior year — different constructions of the same underlying index, same direction.

D3's −9% is a model-based REER *gap* (estimated misalignment implied by the staff CA gap, range −12.8 to −5 with semi-elasticity 0.18), not an observed exchange-rate movement. D1's 1.5% is the actual y-o-y appreciation of the 40-currency REER in 2024-25. Different attributes: assessed undervaluation versus realised change.

D3's −9% is an estimated REER misalignment gap from the IMF's external balance assessment; D2's 107.2 is an observed December 2024 index level of the RBI 40-currency REER. One is a normative gap estimate, the other a measured index — not the same attribute.

D3 says net FDI inflows fell to an almost zero balance in FY2024/25 while gross inflows stayed steady; D2 says net FDI inflows declined relative to April–November 2023 because of a rise in repatriation/disinvestment. Same direction, same mechanism (gross holding up, net collapsing on repatriation), with D2's eight-month FY25 window falling inside D3's full FY2024/25.

D2's claim is about gross FDI inflows reviving in the first eight months of FY25; D3's is about net FDI falling to near zero in FY2024/25. These are the two sides of the same story — D3's own quote attributes the near-zero net balance to 'steady gross' inflows offset by repatriation — so the apparent tension is a gross-versus-net scope difference, not a disagreement.

D2 reports higher growth in gross FDI inflows in Apr–Nov FY25 versus the same period a year earlier; D3 reports net FDI inflows falling to an almost zero balance in FY2024/25. Gross rising and net collapsing are simultaneously true when repatriation and outward FDI rise, which D2 states elsewhere; the difference is gross versus net scope (and a full-year versus eight-month window).

IMF reports a full-year FY2024/25 current account balance of -23.3 US$ bn (1 Apr 2024-31 Mar 2025), while the RBI figure of -37,100 US$ million is flagged '2024-25 (P)' with data pertaining only to April-December 2024. The nine-month deficit exceeding the full-year one implies a Q4 (Jan-Mar 2025) surplus of about +13.8 US$ bn, which is consistent rather than contradictory. Same series, different coverage window and vintage.

The IMF fact is a level (-23.3 US$ bn current account balance for FY2024/25); the RBI fact is a ratio (-1.3% of GDP for April-December 2024). Different measure and different coverage window, so they are not directly comparable values of the same attribute.

IMF's -23.3 US$ bn is a currency-denominated full-year balance; RBI's -1.3% is the CAB/GDP ratio as at end-December 2024 from the external vulnerability indicators table. Different attribute (level vs ratio) and different period, so no direct comparison.

IMF reports the current account balance as a US$ level (-23.3 bn, FY2024/25); the RBI memo item -1.3% is a ratio to GDP for April-December 2024. Different attribute and window; not a like-for-like value pair.

The IMF -23.3 US$ bn is the current account balance; the RBI -13,821 US$ million is the overall balance of payments ('D. Overall Balance [A(5)+B(8)+C]'), which also includes the capital/financial account and errors and omissions. Different attributes entirely.

The IMF's -41.4 US$ bn is a staff projection for FY2025/26 (1 Apr 2025-31 Mar 2026), whereas the RBI's -37,100 US$ million is provisional data for April-December 2024 within FY2024-25. Different fiscal years and different bases (forward projection vs part-year outturn), so the gap is explained by period.
IMF's -41.4 US$ bn is a US-dollar level projected for FY2025/26; the RBI's -1.3% is a CAB/GDP ratio for April-December 2024. Different attribute and different fiscal year.
A projected FY2025/26 dollar level (-41.4 bn) versus an end-December 2024 CAB/GDP ratio (-1.3%): different measure and different period, so the pair is not a genuine value comparison.
IMF -41.4 US$ bn (FY2025/26 projection) is a level; RBI -1.3% is the memo-item ratio to GDP for April-December 2024. Different attribute and different fiscal year.

Current account balance projection (-41.4 US$ bn, FY2025/26) versus the RBI's overall balance of payments (-13,821 US$ million, Apr-Dec 2024), which nets in the capital and financial account. Different attributes and different periods.

IMF puts the current account deficit at 0.6% of GDP for full-year FY2024/25; RBI's -1.3% covers only April-December 2024 (marked provisional). The full-year ratio is smaller because the January-March 2025 quarter was in surplus (RBI 9-month deficit US$37.1 bn vs IMF full-year US$23.3 bn). Same indicator, different coverage window.

RBI's CAB/GDP ratio of -1.3% is dated end-December 2024 (cumulative April-December 2024), while the IMF's -0.6% is the full FY2024/25 outturn to 31 March 2025. The Q4 FY25 current account surplus narrows the annual ratio, so the two are sequential readings of the same series.

Both are current account balance as a percent of GDP, but the RBI memo item (-1.3%) is explicitly '2024-25 (P)' with data pertaining to April-December 2024, whereas the IMF's -0.6% is the full April 2024-March 2025 year. Nine-month vs twelve-month coverage, plus the Q4 surplus, accounts for the difference.

IMF's -0.6% is a ratio to GDP; RBI's -37,100 US$ million is an absolute dollar balance for April-December 2024. Different attribute (ratio vs level) as well as different coverage, so they are not two readings of the same quantity.
The IMF -0.6% of GDP refers to the current account; the RBI -13,821 US$ million is the overall balance of payments including capital and financial flows. Different attribute and different unit.

The IMF's -1.0% of GDP is a staff projection for FY2025/26 (Apr 2025-Mar 2026), while the RBI's -1.3% is provisional April-December 2024 data inside FY2024-25. Different fiscal years and different bases (projection vs part-year provisional), so the values are not in conflict.
RBI's -1.3% CAB/GDP is dated end-December 2024; the IMF's -1.0% is a projection for the later year FY2025/26. Same indicator measured for different years, one an outturn-to-date and one a forecast.

Both express the current account balance as a share of GDP, but the RBI memo item (-1.3%) is provisional April-December 2024 data and the IMF value (-1.0%) is a projection for FY2025/26. The difference is a year and a basis apart, not a disagreement on the same period.
A projected ratio (-1.0% of GDP, FY2025/26) versus an absolute provisional balance (-37,100 US$ million, Apr-Dec 2024): different attribute and different fiscal year.

Current account balance as percent of GDP (IMF projection) versus the RBI's overall balance of payments in US$ million. Different attributes; the overall balance includes financial account flows and reserve changes.

IMF reports gross reserves of US$668.3 billion end-period FY2024/25, i.e. as at 31 March 2025; RBI states 'ample forex reserves at US$ 668.3 billion (as at end-March 2025)'. Identical figure, identical reference date and scope.

IMF's US$668.3 bn is the end-March 2025 stock; the Economic Survey's US$640.3 bn is 'as of the end of December 2024'. Reserves are a point-in-time stock, so the US$28 bn gap reflects three additional months of accretion, not a conflicting measurement.

The Survey's US$634.6 bn is dated 3 January 2025 while the IMF's US$668.3 bn is the end-March 2025 (end-FY2024/25) stock. Different observation dates on the same weekly reserves series; reserves rebuilt over Jan-Mar 2025.

US$704.9 bn is the September 2024 peak reported by the Economic Survey; US$668.3 bn is the IMF's end-March 2025 stock. The Survey itself notes reserves moderating after September 2024, so the lower end-March level is a later point on the same series.

US$616.7 bn is dated end-January 2024, over a year before the IMF's end-March 2025 stock of US$668.3 bn. Point-in-time stocks at different dates on a rising series; the Survey documents the intervening rise to US$704.9 bn.

IMF reports external debt of US$736.3 bn end-period FY2024/25 (31 March 2025); RBI's external vulnerability table shows US$717.9 bn at end-December 2024. Both are end-period stocks one quarter apart, and the RBI series itself runs 623.9 -> 668.8 -> 717.9, consistent with 736.3 by March 2025.

The Economic Survey's US$711.8 bn is dated September 2024; the IMF's US$736.3 bn is the end-March 2025 stock. Two quarters of accumulation separate them, and the intermediate RBI reading of US$717.9 bn at end-December 2024 fits the same upward path.

Same US$711.8 bn September 2024 external debt stock cited in the Survey versus the IMF's US$736.3 bn as at end-March 2025. Point-in-time stocks six months apart on a rising series, so the difference is period, not a conflicting estimate.

US$711.8 bn (Economic Survey, September 2024) and US$717.9 bn (RBI, end-December 2024) are consecutive quarter-end external debt stocks; a US$6.1 bn increase over one quarter is ordinary accretion. Different reference dates on the same series.

The Survey's US$711.8 bn is as at September 2024 and RBI's US$717.9 bn is end-December 2024 - successive quarter-ends of the same external debt stock, differing by one quarter of net borrowing and valuation change.

IMF's US$736.3 bn is an external debt level at end-March 2025; RBI's 18.5 per cent is the external-debt-to-GDP ratio at end-March 2024. Different attribute (stock vs ratio) and a year apart, so not a comparable value pair.

The IMF figure is a dollar stock (US$736.3 bn, end-March 2025); the RBI figure is the debt-to-GDP ratio (19.1 per cent, end-December 2024). Different measures, so they cannot corroborate or contradict each other directly.
US$711.8 bn (September 2024) is an external debt level from the Economic Survey; 18.5 per cent (end-March 2024) is RBI's external debt to GDP ratio. Different attribute and different reference date.
A dollar stock of external debt (US$711.8 bn, September 2024) versus a ratio to GDP (19.1 per cent, end-December 2024). Different measures of related but distinct quantities.
The Survey states an external debt level of US$711.8 bn as of September 2024; the RBI states an external-debt-to-GDP ratio of 18.5 per cent at end-March 2024. Different attribute and period.
Level (US$711.8 bn, September 2024) versus ratio to GDP (19.1 per cent, end-December 2024, provisional). Not the same attribute, so no corroboration or contradiction can be drawn.

D4's 6.2% is an IMF DSA baseline projection for FY2026/27 (Apr 2026-Mar 2027), while D2's 6.4% is the First Advance Estimate for FY25 (Apr 2024-Mar 2025). Two fiscal years apart, and one is a projection versus an estimate of a current year; the numbers are not in competition.
D4 projects 6.2% for the full year FY2026/27; D2 reports 6.0% actual for H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024). Different fiscal years and different coverage (half-year vs full-year), so no disagreement.
D4's 6.2% is a projection for FY2026/27; D1's 6.5% is the actual outturn for 2024-25 ('growth moderated to 6.5 per cent in 2024-25'). Two years apart, projection vs actual.
D4's 6.2% covers FY2026/27 as a DSA baseline projection; D1's 6.5% is the Second Advance Estimate for 2024-25. Different reference years entirely.
D4 projects 6.2% for FY2026/27; D2 estimates 6.4% for FY25 on First Advance Estimates. Periods differ by two fiscal years.
D4's 6.2% is for FY2026/27 (projection); D1's 6.5% is measured growth for 2024-25 at constant prices. Different years.
D4's 6.2% projection is for FY2026/27; D1's 9.2% is the prior-year comparator for 2023-24 at constant prices. Three fiscal years apart.

The values coincide at 6.4% but the periods do not: D4's figure is an IMF DSA baseline projection for FY2027/28, while D2's 6.4% is the First Advance Estimate for FY25 (Apr 2024-Mar 2025). Matching digits three years apart are not corroboration.
Both read 6.4%, but D4's is a projection for FY2027/28 in the DSA baseline row, and D2's is the FY25 First Advance Estimate. Same number, different fiscal years and bases.
D4 projects 6.4% for the full year FY2027/28; D2 reports 6.0% actual for H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024). Different years and different coverage.
D4's 6.4% is a FY2027/28 projection; D1's 6.5% is the 2024-25 actual outturn. Three fiscal years apart, projection vs actual.
D4's 6.4% belongs to the FY2027/28 column of the DSA baseline; D1's 6.5% is the Second Advance Estimate for 2024-25. Different reference years.
D4 projects 6.4% for FY2027/28; D1 records 6.5% growth for 2024-25 at constant prices. Distinct periods.
D4's 6.4% is a FY2027/28 projection; D1's 9.2% is the 2023-24 prior-year comparator. Four fiscal years apart.

D4 reports GDP deflator inflation of 3.1% for the full FY2024/25 (Apr 2024-Mar 2025); D1 reports 3.0% for April-December 2024 only, i.e. the first nine months of that same year. A 0.1 pp difference between a 9-month figure and the annual figure is exactly what a slightly firmer Q4 would produce — consistent, not conflicting.

D4's 1.8% is a projection for FY2025/26 (Apr 2025-Mar 2026) in the DSA baseline; D1's 3.0% is realised deflator inflation for April-December 2024. Different years and projection vs outturn, so the lower projected deflator does not contradict the 2024 reading.

D4's 4.0% is a long-run assumption for 2030 in the large-amortization risk scenario; D1's 3.0% is measured deflator inflation for April-December 2024. A modelled steady-state value roughly five years out versus a current-period actual.

Both cover FY2024/25, but D4's 9.8% is NOMINAL GDP growth while D2's 6.4% is REAL growth at constant prices. The arithmetic ties out against D4's own deflator row of 3.1% for the same year (about 6.5 real + 3.1 deflator = 9.8 nominal).

D4's 9.8% for FY2024/25 is nominal GDP growth; D2's 6.4% for FY25 is real GDP growth on First Advance Estimates. Same year, different price basis — the wedge is the ~3.1% GDP deflator D4 reports alongside.

Same fiscal year (2024-25) but different measures: D4 gives nominal GDP growth of 9.8%, D1 gives real GDP growth of 6.5% (Second Advance Estimates). Nominal minus real equals roughly the 3.1% deflator D4 lists in the adjacent row.
D4's 9.8% is nominal, full-year FY2024/25; D2's 6.0% is real growth for H1 FY25 only. Both the price basis (nominal vs constant-price) and the coverage (full year vs half year) differ.

D4's 9.8% is nominal GDP growth for FY2024/25; D3's 8.2% is India's real GDP growth for FY24 (year ended 31 March 2024), cited as 'the highest among the major economies'. Both the year and the price basis differ, so the figures measure different things.

D3's 8.2% is India's growth in FY24 (1 Apr 2023-31 Mar 2024), the year its annual report covers; D2's 6.4% is the First Advance Estimate for FY25 (1 Apr 2024-31 Mar 2025). Consecutive but different fiscal years.

D3's 8.2% is FY24 growth (year ended 31 Mar 2024); D1's 6.5% is the Second Advance Estimate for 2024-25. Adjacent fiscal years, so the 1.7 pp gap reflects the moderation D1 itself describes ('moderated to 6.5 per cent').

Both figures describe India's real GDP growth for the same year 2023-24: D3's annual report (FY24) cites 8.2%, the estimate available at the time, while D1 cites 9.2% for 2023-24 as the prior-year comparator at constant prices. The gap is the NSO's later upward revision of FY24 growth, i.e. a data-vintage difference, though I would want the specific NSO release dates to confirm.

Both read 6.5%, but they are not the same claim: D4's is a long-term risk-assessment scenario assumption for 2030, while D1 projects 6.5% specifically 'for 2025-26, with risks evenly balanced'. Identical values five years apart under different modelling bases, so this is period alignment rather than corroboration.
D4's 6.5% is a 2030 long-term scenario value; D2's 6.4% is the FY25 First Advance Estimate. Roughly five fiscal years apart, scenario assumption vs current-year estimate.
The 6.5% in D4 is a custom long-term (2030) scenario projection in the large-amortization risk assessment; D2's 6.4% is the FY25 constant-price First Advance Estimate. Different periods and bases.
D4's 6.5% applies to 2030 under a long-term scenario; D2's 6.0% is actual H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024) growth. Neither year nor coverage matches.

Both values are 6.5%, but D4's is a 2030 long-term scenario assumption while D1's is the Second Advance Estimate for 2024-25. Same number, roughly five years apart and on different bases (scenario vs official estimate).

D1 projects 6.5% for 2025-26 ('projected at 6.5 per cent, with risks evenly balanced'), whereas D2 estimates 6.4% for FY25 (2024-25). Consecutive fiscal years, and one is a forward projection versus a current-year estimate.
D1's 6.5% is the forward projection for 2025-26; D2's 6.4% is the First Advance Estimate for FY25. Different years, projection vs estimate.
D1 projects 6.5% for the full year 2025-26; D2 reports 6.0% actual for H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024). Different years and different coverage.

These are different attributes despite both being ratios to GDP with negative signs: D4's -1.6% is the fiscal PRIMARY BALANCE-to-GDP ratio in a 2030 long-term scenario, while D1's -1.3% is the external CURRENT ACCOUNT balance as a ratio to GDP for 2024-25 (P), a Balance of Payments memo item. Different accounts and different periods — a false match.

D4's fact measures the TIMELINESS of BoP data releases ('improved from around 90 to 60 days after the reference quarter'), a publication-lag statistic in days. D1's fact is the current account balance value of -US$37,100 million for 2024-25 (P). Same broad topic (Balance of Payments) but entirely different attributes and units.

Both describe portfolio flows for the same year ended March 2025: the IMF says flows were "almost evenly balanced at 0.1 percent of GDP" (≈$4bn on a ~$3.9trn GDP), while the RBI reports "FPI recorded net inflows of US$ 1.7 billion during 2024-25". Both convey a near-zero net portfolio position, but the magnitudes differ because the IMF measures BoP net portfolio investment (a broader instrument set, expressed to one decimal of GDP) whereas the RBI figure is the domestic-market FPI series. To close the gap one would compare the BoP portfolio-investment line in the RBI's own balance-of-payments table.

The IMF's 0.1 percent-of-GDP figure covers the full FY2024/25 and explicitly attributes the near-balance to "large equity outflows in late 2024"; the RBI's US$18.5 billion is a net outflow for the sub-period October 2024 to March 2025. The half-year outflow is a component of, not a rival to, the full-year near-balance.

The IMF's balanced portfolio flows of 0.1 percent of GDP are for FY2024/25, whereas the RBI's US$41.6 billion net FPI inflow is for 2023-24 ("a year ago"). Different fiscal years, so the large gap is a genuine year-on-year swing rather than a disagreement.

D2's USD 30.5 billion is total net capital inflows for Q2 FY25 (Jul-Sep 2024), covering FDI, portfolio, loans and banking capital; D1's US$1.7 billion is net foreign portfolio investment for the whole of 2024-25. Different attribute (capital account aggregate vs one component) and different period, so the apparent similarity is a false match.

USD 12.8 billion is D2's total net capital inflows for Q2 FY24 (Jul-Sep 2023); US$41.6 billion is D1's full-year 2023-24 net FPI inflow. Different aggregates (whole capital account vs portfolio only) and different windows (one quarter vs full year).

The IMF's $646.4 billion is the stock at end-FY2023/24 (31 March 2024); the RBI's US$668.3 billion is the stock at end-March 2025. Different measurement dates one year apart, and the IMF sentence itself states reserves rose from $646.4bn to $668.3bn over that year.

$646.4 billion is a 31 March 2024 stock; USD 616.7 billion is the end-January 2024 stock. Reserves are a point-in-time level and rose over those two months, so the difference is a dating difference, not a conflict.

$646.4 billion (31 March 2024) versus USD 704.9 billion (September 2024) are stocks six months apart; D2 explicitly describes reserves rising through September 2024 before moderating, so the higher September peak is consistent with the lower March level.

$646.4 billion is the end-March 2024 stock, while USD 640.3 billion is the end-December 2024 stock after the post-September moderation. Nine months apart, so the two levels describe different points on the same series.
Same series, different dates: $646.4 billion at 31 March 2024 versus USD 640.3 billion "as of the end of December 2024" after reserves moderated from their September 2024 peak.
$646.4 billion is the end-FY2023/24 stock (31 March 2024); USD 634.6 billion is a weekly reading "as on 3 January 2025". Nine months apart on a point-in-time series.

The IMF reports reserves of $668.3 billion at end-FY2024/25 and the RBI reports US$668.3 billion "as at end-March 2025" — the same date under the April-March convention and an identical figure to the decimal.

$668.3 billion is the 31 March 2025 stock; USD 640.3 billion is the 31 December 2024 stock. Three months apart, with reserves rebuilding over Q4 FY25, so the levels are successive points on one series.
Same reserves series measured at different dates: USD 640.3 billion at end-December 2024 (after moderating) versus $668.3 billion at end-March 2025.
USD 634.6 billion is a 3 January 2025 weekly reading, the trough referenced in D2; $668.3 billion is the 31 March 2025 fiscal-year-end stock. Different dates on a volatile point-in-time series.
USD 704.9 billion is the September 2024 peak; $668.3 billion is the end-March 2025 level after the late-2024 moderation the IMF also describes. Different measurement dates, same series.
USD 616.7 billion (end-January 2024) and $668.3 billion (end-March 2025) are stocks fourteen months apart; both documents describe reserves accumulating over that span.
RBI's US$668.3 billion is at end-March 2025; the Survey's USD 640.3 billion is at end-December 2024, published 31 January 2025 before the Q4 rebuild. Three-month dating difference on the same series.
Same attribute, different measurement dates: USD 640.3 billion at end-December 2024 versus US$668.3 billion at end-March 2025.
USD 634.6 billion is the 3 January 2025 weekly level cited in the pre-Budget Survey; US$668.3 billion is the 31 March 2025 fiscal-year-end level in the RBI report, roughly three months later.

USD 704.9 billion is the September 2024 high point; US$668.3 billion is the end-March 2025 level. The intervening moderation (to USD 640.3bn by end-December 2024, per D2) explains the lower later figure.
USD 616.7 billion at end-January 2024 versus US$668.3 billion at end-March 2025 — stocks fourteen months apart on the same reserves series.

Both are reserve-adequacy ratios but against different denominators: the IMF's 209 percent is reserves over short-term debt on residual maturity at end-March 2025, while the Survey's ~90 per cent is reserves over total external debt of USD 711.8 billion at September 2024. Reserves of roughly $650-670bn against ~$712bn total debt gives ~90%, and against a short-term residual-maturity stock of roughly $320bn gives ~209%, so the two are arithmetically compatible; the dates also differ by six months.

The IMF's 209 percent is reserves expressed as a share of short-term debt; the RBI's 42.4 per cent is short-term debt (residual maturity) as a share of total external debt. Different numerators and denominators entirely — the shared phrase "short-term debt (residual maturity)" is the only overlap.

42.4 per cent is the composition ratio of short-term debt within total external debt at end-December 2024; ~90 per cent is reserves as a share of total external debt at September 2024. Different attributes (debt composition vs reserve cover).

Both refer to reserve import cover at end-March 2025 but on different import bases: the IMF cites "over eight months of import coverage" (its standard measure includes services imports), while the RBI cites "11 months of merchandise imports". The RBI's narrower denominator mechanically yields a longer cover, and 11 does not falsify "over eight". Confirming would require the IMF's import denominator (goods vs goods-and-services).

Same date and same concept, different denominators: the RBI states reserves at end-March 2025 gave "a cover of 11 months of merchandise imports (on BoP basis) for 2024-25", while the IMF reports "over eight months of import coverage" at end-FY2024/25, its measure conventionally including services imports. The lower IMF figure is consistent with a wider import base.

The IMF's "over eight months" is at end-March 2025; the RBI table's 10.5 months is at end-December 2024 and is explicitly "based on merchandise imports of latest four quarters". Both the reference date and the import denominator differ, and a merchandise-only base gives the longer cover.

10.9 months (December 2024, Economic Survey) versus "over eight months" (end-March 2025, IMF): different measurement dates and different import bases, with the IMF's broader import denominator producing the shorter cover. Neither figure contradicts the other's direction.

Both are lower-bound statements — "more than ten months" (3 January 2025, Survey) and "over eight months" (end-March 2025, IMF). They are compatible as bounds; the gap in the implied level reflects different import denominators (merchandise-based Indian convention vs the IMF's broader import coverage) and dates three months apart.

The Survey's 10.9 months is at December 2024; the RBI's 11 months is at end-March 2025. Reserves rose from USD 640.3bn (end-December 2024) to US$668.3bn (end-March 2025), so cover edging up from 10.9 to 11 months over the quarter is a period difference on the same measure.

D2 says import cover was "more than ten months" as on 3 January 2025; D1 says 11 months at end-March 2025. The RBI's point estimate satisfies the Survey's bound, and the two readings are about three months apart on a rising reserves series.

Both give import cover at end-December 2024 but differ: 10.5 months (RBI, explicitly "based on merchandise imports of latest four quarters") versus 10.9 months (Economic Survey). On reserves of USD 640.3bn the two imply monthly imports of ~$61.0bn and ~$58.7bn respectively, so the gap is a denominator choice (trailing four-quarter BoP merchandise imports vs the Survey's import base). To settle it one would need the Survey's stated import denominator and reserve reference date.

D1's 10.5 months at end-December 2024 satisfies D2's statement of "an import cover of more than ten months" as on 3 January 2025 — effectively the same moment, and the point estimate sits inside the stated bound.

Both are upbeat FY2025-26 growth statements: the IMF's ensemble projects "well over 7 percent" y-o-y in FY26Q2, and the RBI says India is "poised to remain the fastest-growing major economy in 2025-26". They are consistent in direction, though one is a quarterly nowcast and the other a cross-country ranking rather than the same measured quantity.

The IMF fact is a quantitative nowcast (>7 percent y-o-y SA growth in the July-September 2025 quarter); the Survey's "prospects for FY26 are balanced" is a statement about the balance of risks, not a growth level. Different attributes despite the shared outlook framing.

Both are FY2025-26 outlook statements published for the same forward year and are mutually consistent — the RBI expects India to stay the fastest-growing major economy while the Survey calls prospects "balanced" — but they assert different things (relative ranking vs balance of risks), so the corroboration is directional rather than a matched value.

The IMF's 1.6 percent is a seasonally adjusted quarter-on-quarter growth rate for Jul-Sep 2025, while D3 cites the RBI's 7.2 percent annual GDP growth projection for FY25. Different growth concepts (q-o-q vs annual) and different periods, so the numbers are not comparable.

Both are real GDP growth projections on a year-on-year basis, but for different years and from different forecasters: the IMF's 7.9 percent (September vintage) is for the quarter Jul-Sep 2025 (FY26Q2), while Delhivery's 7.2 percent is the RBI's projection for the full year FY25 (Apr 2024-Mar 2025). A single quarter's y-o-y rate and a full-year rate a year apart need not match.

The IMF's 7.6 percent (July vintage) is a y-o-y projection for FY26Q2 (Jul-Sep 2025); the 7.2 percent quoted by Delhivery is the RBI's full-year FY25 projection made in its FY24 annual report. Different reference periods and different forecast origins explain the gap.

7.7 percent is the IMF ensemble's August-vintage y-o-y projection for the quarter Jul-Sep 2025, whereas 7.2 percent is the RBI's annual GDP growth projection for FY25 as cited in Delhivery's FY24 report. The periods (one quarter of FY26 vs all of FY25) and the forecasting institutions differ.

D4 reports a stock level ("Reserve money ... 48,292" INR billion, end-period FY2024/25); D1 reports a rate of change ("III.1 Reserve Money (% change) ... 3.3" for 2024-25, data pertaining to March 28, 2025). Different attributes, so not directly comparable. Note for follow-up: D4's own series (46,314 -> 48,292) implies ~4.3% growth, not 3.3%, but the reference dates (end-March vs March 28) and the underlying series would have to be aligned before calling that a disagreement.

"Reserve money" in D4 is the monetary base (₹48,292 billion, end-March 2025); D2's "foreign exchange reserves stood at USD 640.3 billion" is the RBI's external reserve assets at end-December 2024. Same word "reserve", entirely different attributes, units and dates.

D4's ₹48,292 billion is reserve money (monetary base) at end-March 2025; D2's "USD 640.3 billion as of the end of December 2024" is foreign exchange reserves. Different attribute, unit and reference date — a naive name match only.

D4 states reserve money of ₹48,292 billion (end-March 2025, monetary base); D2 states forex reserves "moderating to USD 634.6 billion as on 3 January 2025". Different concepts (central bank liabilities vs external reserve assets), different units and dates.

D4's reserve money (₹48,292 billion, end-March 2025) is not the same attribute as D2's "foreign exchange reserves ... USD 616.7 billion at the end of January 2024". Different measure, currency and period.

D1 gives reserve money growth of 3.3% for 2024-25 (a percentage change in the monetary base); D2 gives a stock of foreign exchange reserves, USD 640.3 billion at end-December 2024. Different attributes entirely.
D1's "Reserve Money (% change) ... 3.3" for 2024-25 measures growth of the monetary base; D2's "USD 634.6 billion as on 3 January 2025" is the level of forex reserves. No shared attribute.

Reserve money growth of 3.3% in 2024-25 (D1) and a forex reserve stock of USD 640.3 billion at end-December 2024 (D2) are different attributes in different units; the pair matches only on the word "reserve".
D1's 3.3% reserve money growth for 2024-25 and D2's USD 616.7 billion of forex reserves at end-January 2024 share neither attribute, unit nor period.

D4's "Broad money (M3) ... 272,866" INR billion = ₹272.87 trillion at end-period FY2024/25 (31 March 2025); D1 reports M3 outstanding of ₹272.1 trillion "as on March 21, 2025" (provisional). The two figures are 0.28% apart, consistent with the ten-day gap between the last reporting Friday (21 March) and the financial-year close (31 March), plus D1's provisional status.

D4 gives an M3 stock (₹272,866 billion at end-March 2025); D1 page 95 gives an M3 growth rate ("Broad Money (M3) ... 9.6" per cent y-o-y as of March 21, 2025). Level vs growth are different attributes. For information, D4's own series (249,398 -> 272,866) implies 9.4% growth, in the same neighbourhood as D1's 9.6%.

D4 reports the M3 level of ₹272,866 billion at end-March 2025, whereas D1 page 91 reports "Broad Money (M3) [% change] ... 9.6" for 2024-25 (data relate to March 21, 2025). Different attribute (stock vs percentage change); D4's implied 9.4% growth is broadly consistent but not the same measurement.

D4's figure is an M3 stock for FY2024/25 (₹272,866 billion at end-March 2025); D1's 11.2% is a y-o-y growth rate for the earlier date, 22 March 2024. Both the attribute (stock vs growth) and the period differ.

D4's "Central government debt ... 56.3" is central government liabilities as a percent of GDP for FY2024/25; D2's "external debt of USD 711.8 billion as of September 2024" is the whole economy's external (public plus private) debt in dollars. Different borrower universe, different unit, different date.

Central government debt of 56.3% of GDP (D4, FY2024/25 estimate) and India's external debt of USD 711.8 billion at September 2024 (D2) measure different things — government indebtedness relative to GDP vs total cross-border debt in USD. Only the word "debt" matches.

Both purport to be general government tax revenue for 2024-25: D4 shows "Taxes ... 17.6" percent of GDP (IMF staff consolidated general government estimate, report completed 6 Nov 2025), D1 cites a "rise in tax revenues to 18.8 per cent of GDP in 2024-25" on budget estimates. The 1.2pp gap reflects a different consolidation/definition (IMF nets intergovernmental flows and uses its own nominal GDP series of ₹330,682 billion) plus vintage — D1 is a pre-outturn BE figure, D4 an ex-post staff estimate. To confirm, one would compare the IMF's tax-revenue table footnote with the RBI's centre-plus-states BE aggregation.

D4: general government "Expenditure ... 28.3" percent of GDP for FY2024/25 (consolidated, staff estimate); D1: "moderation in total expenditure to 30.0 per cent of GDP from 30.2 per cent" for 2024-25 BE. Both show a small decline of similar size (D4: 28.6 -> 28.3; D1: 30.2 -> 30.0), so the direction agrees; the ~1.7pp level gap comes from IMF consolidation of centre and states (netting transfers) and a different GDP denominator, plus budget-estimate vs staff-estimate vintage.

Same subject and period: D4 shows "State and union territory governments' balance ... -3.3" percent of GDP for FY2024/25, D1 shows states' "Gross Fiscal Deficit (% of GDP) ... 3.6" for 2024-25 (28 states and 3 UTs). D4's own scope note explains the 0.3pp gap: it "excludes zero-interest 50-year loans to avoid double counting" of the centre's capex loans to states, which D1's gross figure includes.

D4 expresses the states/UTs deficit as -3.3 percent of GDP for FY2024/25; D1 expresses the same aggregate as a rupee amount, "V. Fiscal Deficit ... 10.4" lakh crore (₹10.4 trillion) on 2024-25 BE. Against D4's own nominal GDP of ₹330,682 billion, ₹10.4 trillion is about 3.1% of GDP, close to -3.3% once D4's exclusion of the interest-free 50-year loans and the differing GDP denominator are allowed for.

D4's -3.3 percent of GDP covers state and UT governments only; D1's "Gross Fiscal Deficit ... 2,473" thousand crore (₹24.7 trillion, 2024-25 BE) is the combined centre-plus-states figure, i.e. roughly 7.5% of D4's ₹330,682 billion GDP. The states' -3.3% (~₹10.9 trillion) is one component of that combined total, so the figures differ by scope rather than disagreeing.

D4 gives "Nominal GDP in billions of Rupees ... 330,682" for FY2024/25 (₹330.7 trillion); D3 quotes the IMF for "India's GDP was US$3.9 trillion in 2024". At roughly ₹85/USD, ₹330.7 trillion converts to about US$3.9 trillion, so the two agree once currency is aligned; a residual difference remains because D3's figure is calendar year 2024 while D4's is the April-March fiscal year.

D4 reports aggregate nominal GDP (₹330,682 billion, FY2024/25); D3 reports "per capita GDP reached US$2.73 thousand in 2024". Aggregate and per-head measures are different attributes (they differ by population), though they are mutually consistent: US$3.9 trillion over ~1.43 billion people gives ~US$2.7 thousand.
D4 states a nominal GDP level (₹330,682 billion for FY2024/25); D3 states a real growth rate ("of 8.2%") for FY24. Different attribute (level vs growth) and different year.

D4's ₹330,682 billion is a nominal GDP level for FY2024/25; D2's "real GDP is estimated to grow by 6.4 per cent in FY25" is a real growth rate. Level vs growth, and nominal vs real — not the same attribute.

D4 reports full-year nominal GDP in rupees (₹330,682 billion, FY2024/25); D2 reports "real GDP growth of 6.0 per cent in the first half of the current fiscal". Different attribute (nominal level vs real growth) and different span (full year vs H1).

D3 gives a GDP level in dollars ("US$3.9 trillion in 2024"); D2 gives a real growth rate (6.4 per cent for FY25). Different attributes; a level and a growth rate cannot corroborate or contradict each other.
D3's US$3.9 trillion GDP for calendar 2024 is a level; D2's 6.0 per cent is a half-year real growth rate for H1 FY25. Different attribute and different period basis.
Per capita GDP of US$2.73 thousand in 2024 (D3) and real GDP growth of 6.4 per cent in FY25 (D2) are different attributes — a dollar level per head vs an aggregate growth rate.
D3's per capita GDP level (US$2.73 thousand, 2024) has no attribute overlap with D2's H1 FY25 real GDP growth of 6.0 per cent.

Same attribute (India's real GDP growth) measured for different fiscal years: D3 reports "of 8.2%" for FY24 (1 Apr 2023-31 Mar 2024), D2 reports "6.4 per cent in FY25" (1 Apr 2024-31 Mar 2025, first advance estimates). The lower FY25 number is a later year, not a competing estimate of the same year — consistent with D1's own comparison of 6.5% in 2024-25 against 9.2% a year earlier.

D3's 8.2% is full-year FY24 real growth; D2's 6.0 per cent covers only "the first half of the current fiscal" (H1 FY25, Apr-Sep 2024). Different, non-overlapping periods and different span (12 months vs 6 months), so the gap is a timing difference rather than a disagreement.

Both report India's real GDP growth for the year ended March 2025 at the same value: D4's table row "Real GDP (at market prices) ... 6.5" for FY2024/25 and D1's "real GDP growth moderated to 6.5 per cent ... in 2024-25". Same period, same attribute, identical figure.

D4 reports FY2024/25 real GDP growth of 6.5% at market prices; D1 page 8 reports "real gross domestic product (GDP) growth moderated to 6.5 per cent in 2024-25" on Second Advance Estimates. Identical value for the identical April-March year; the IMF figure is explicitly the FY2024/25 outturn.
D1 states the economy "grown by 6.5 per cent in 2024-25" at constant prices, matching D4's "Real GDP (at market prices) ... 6.5" for FY2024/25. Same period, same measure, same number.

D1's 9.2 per cent is explicitly the prior-year comparator ("with 9.2 per cent a year ago", i.e. 2023-24), while D4's 6.5% is FY2024/25. D4's own series carries 9.2 in the FY2023/24 slot ("9.7 7.6 9.2 6.5 ..."), confirming that the two numbers describe consecutive years rather than conflicting estimates of one year.

Both describe FY2024-25 real GDP growth: D2 (published 31 Jan 2025) gives 6.4 per cent from the First Advance Estimates, D4 (staff report completed 6 Nov 2025) gives 6.5 per cent as the outturn. The 0.1pp difference is a successive-estimate revision — the FAE preceded the Second Advance Estimates/provisional actuals D1 and D4 rely on.

D2's "India's real GDP is estimated to grow by 6.4 per cent in FY25" is a January 2025 first-advance estimate; D4's 6.5% for FY2024/25 is the later outturn cited in a November 2025 staff report. Same year and attribute, 0.1pp apart because of the estimate-to-actual revision.

D2's 6.0 per cent covers only H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024) — "the first half of the current fiscal" — whereas D4's 6.5% is the full FY2024/25 year. A stronger second half lifts the full-year figure above the half-year one, so the two are compatible measurements of different windows.

Same year, different estimate vintage: D2 (31 Jan 2025) reports "real gross domestic product (GDP) growth for FY25 is estimated to be 6.4 per cent" on First Advance Estimates; D1's Annual Report for 2024-25 states growth "moderated to 6.5 per cent" using later (Second Advance/provisional) data. A 0.1pp official revision, not a conflict.

The bases are stated in the facts themselves: D2's 6.4 per cent is the First Advance Estimate for FY25, D1's 6.5 per cent is the Second Advance Estimate for the same 2024-25 year. Successive NSO estimates of one period, differing by 0.1pp.

D2's FAE-based 6.4 per cent for FY25 and D1's constant-price 6.5 per cent for 2024-25 refer to the identical April 2024-March 2025 year; the gap is the revision between the January 2025 advance estimate and the later estimate used in the RBI Annual Report.

D2's 6.4 per cent is FY25 (2024-25); D1's 9.2 per cent is expressly the year before ("9.2 per cent a year ago", 2023-24). Different fiscal years, so the large gap is a genuine year-on-year slowdown rather than disagreement.

D2 (Jan 2025) estimates FY25 real GDP growth at 6.4 per cent on first advance estimates; D1's Annual Report puts 2024-25 growth at 6.5 per cent on later data. Identical period, 0.1pp apart because of the successive official estimates.

The two facts label their own vintages: First Advance Estimates (D2, 6.4 per cent for FY25) versus Second Advance Estimates (D1, 6.5 per cent for 2024-25). Same April-March year, standard 0.1pp revision between estimate rounds.

D2's 6.4 per cent (FY25, first advance estimates) and D1's 6.5 per cent (2024-25, constant prices) measure the same year with data of different vintages, the RBI figure incorporating the later revision.
D1's 9.2 per cent is the 2023-24 comparator ("a year ago"), while D2's 6.4 per cent is FY25 (2024-25). The two refer to consecutive fiscal years, so the 2.8pp difference is the slowdown between them.

D2's 6.0 per cent is explicitly "the first half of the current fiscal" (Apr-Sep 2024), while D1's 6.5 per cent is the whole of 2024-25. Half-year versus full-year coverage of the same fiscal year explains the difference.

H1 FY25 growth of 6.0 per cent (D2) is a subperiod of the 6.5 per cent full-year 2024-25 SAE figure reported by D1; stronger H2 momentum lifts the annual number above the half-year one, so the two are compatible.
D2 measures April-September 2024 (6.0 per cent), D1 the full 2024-25 year at constant prices (6.5 per cent). Different windows within the same fiscal year, not competing estimates of one window.

D2's 6.0 per cent covers H1 FY25 (Apr-Sep 2024); D1's 9.2 per cent is full-year 2023-24, quoted as the prior-year comparator. Both the year and the span differ, so the gap reflects timing, not conflicting measurement.

D1 identifies Sahil Barua as one of the company's founders in the context of a founder employment undertaking; D3 p.68 records his signing office, "Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer DIN: 05131571". Founder status is a historical attribute, not a board position, so the two facts address different attributes of the same person.

D1 asserts founder status; D3 p.49 asserts the office held in his declaration, "Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of the Company". These are separate attributes about the same individual and the pair is a surface-level name match rather than a claim about the same fact.

D1 states a physical volume (5.26 million heavy-goods shipments in Fiscal 2021); D4 states a rupee revenue figure (Rs 15,174.05 million PTL revenue in FY24). Different attributes entirely (shipment count vs revenue), plus different periods — this is a false match rather than a numeric conflict.

Both cover FY24 but measure different profit lines: D3's 11.6% is 'Service EBITDA' margin, struck before corporate/overhead and other non-service costs, whereas D4's 1.56% is consolidated EBITDA as a percentage of revenue from customers, after those costs. The ~10 point gap is the overhead layer between the two definitions, not a conflicting measurement of one metric.

D1's (2.75)% is a Fiscal 2021 company EBITDA margin; D3's 11.6% is an FY24 total Service EBITDA margin. Both period (FY21 vs FY24) and metric definition (full EBITDA after overheads vs Service EBITDA before them) differ, so the two figures are not measuring the same thing at the same time.

D3's Rs 8,142 Cr is FY24 total revenue from services for the group; D4's Rs 7,760.29 million (Rs 776.0 Cr) is FY24 supply chain segment revenue only. Same period, different scope — the segment figure is a component of the group total, not a competing measure of it.

D3's Rs 2,076 Cr is total company revenue from services for the single quarter Q4 FY24; D4's Rs 7,760.29 million (Rs 776.0 Cr) is Supply Chain segment revenue for the full FY24 year. Both scope (all services vs one segment) and span (one quarter vs full year) differ.

D3's Rs 2,076 Cr is total revenue from services for Q4 FY24; D1's Rs 3,505.92 million (~Rs 351 Cr) is Supply Chain Services revenue for the nine months ended 31 Dec 2021. Different scope (group total vs one segment), different period, and different reporting unit (crore vs million).

D1 reports a PAT *margin* of (18.14)% for the nine months ended 31 Dec 2021; D3 reports an absolute PAT of Rs. (249) Cr for FY24. Different attribute (ratio vs rupee amount) and non-overlapping periods, so the two cannot be checked against each other.

D1's (10.83)% is a PAT margin for Fiscal 2021 (Apr 2020–Mar 2021); D3's (249) is an absolute PAT in Rs. crore for FY24. Different attribute and a three-year gap in period — no common measurement to compare.
D1's ₹29,587.59 million is Express Parcel revenue for 9M ended Dec 2021; D3's 740 Mn is a count of express parcel shipments in FY24. Money versus units shipped — different attributes entirely.

Both cover FY24, but D4's ₹50,765.87 million is Express Parcel revenue while D3's 740 Mn is express parcel shipment count. Same period and segment, different attribute, so they are not competing values (they are consistent inputs to a realisation-per-shipment calculation).
D4's FY24 figure of ₹50,765.87 million measures revenue; D3's FY24 figure of 740 Mn measures shipment volume. Matching period and segment, but different units of account.
D4's ₹45,522.22 million is FY23 Express Parcel revenue; D3's 740 Mn is FY24 shipment count. Both the attribute (revenue vs volume) and the fiscal year differ.
D1's 438,795 tonnes is PTL freight volume for 9M ended Dec 2021; D4's ₹15,174.05 million is PTL revenue for FY24. Tonnage versus rupees — different attributes, and different periods.

D1 reports an absolute PTL tonnage of 438,795 tonnes for 9M FY22; D4's fact is a 31% FY24 revenue growth rate (its quote also mentions 30% tonnage growth, but as a rate). A volume level from FY22 and a growth rate for FY24 measure different things over different periods.

D1 in May 2022 only proposes an NSE listing ("NSE is the Designated Stock Exchange"), while D4's FY24 annual report records the settled NSE code DELHIVERY. The prospectus predates the listing; the annual report reports it as accomplished.

D1 anticipates a BSE listing but, being pre-listing, carries no scrip code; D4 supplies the BSE code 543529 assigned after listing. The absence in D1 versus the presence in D4 reflects the documents' timing, not conflicting claims.
